original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Official container images are published on GHCR (ghcr.io/mermaid-js/mermaid-cli/mermaid-cli) and Docker Hub (minlag/mermaid-cli) for local Docker or Podman execution.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
111: ```sh
112: docker pull ghcr.io/mermaid-js/mermaid-cli/mermaid-cli
113: ```
114: or e.g. version 8.8.0
115: ```sh
116: docker pull minlag/mermaid-cli:8.8.0
117: ```
118: The container looks for input files in `/data`. So for example, if you have a
119: diagram defined on your system in `/path/to/diagrams/diagram.mmd`, you can use
120: the container to generate an SVG file as follows:
121: ```sh
122: docker run --rm -u `id -u`:`id -g` -v /path/to/diagrams:/data minlag/mermaid-cli -i diagram.mmd
123: ```
124: Or, if using [Podman](https://podman.io/), instead do:
125: ```sh
126: podman run --userns keep-id --user ${UID} --rm -v /path/to/diagrams:/data:z ghcr.io/mermaid-js/mermaid-cli/mermaid-cli -i diagram.mmd
127: ```
128: The key differences in the podman command versus the docker command are:
129: - The addition of the `--userns keep-id` argument. This allows the container to keep the same UID as the current user's UID in the container namespace instead of mapping to a subuid. To learn more, see the [`userns=mode` documentation](https://docs.podman.io/en/v4.4/markdown/options/userns.container.html).
130: - The addition of `:z` to the end of the volume mapping. This instructs podman to relabel the files in the volume with the SELinux label `container_file_t`, which allows processes in the container to access the files. See the "Labeling Volume Mounts" section of [podman-run (1)](https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-run.1.html#volume-v-source-volume-host-dir-container-dir-options) for more info.
131: In previous version, the input files were mounted in `/home/mermaidcli`. You can
132: restore this behaviour with the `--workdir` option:
133: ```sh
134: docker run [...] --workdir=/home/mermaidcli minlag/mermaid-cli [...]
135: ```

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Exposes a local Node.js API (import { run } from "@mermaid-js/mermaid-cli", explicitly not covered by semver) as well as local npm and npx invocation.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
136: ## Use Node.JS API
137: It's possible to call `mermaid-cli` via a Node.JS API.
138: Please be aware that **the NodeJS API is not covered by semver**, as `mermaid-cli` follows
139: `mermaid`'s versioning.
140: ```js
141: import { run } from "@mermaid-js/mermaid-cli";
142: await run(
143: "input.mmd",
144: "output.svg", // {optional options},
145: );
146: ```
147: ## Install locally
148: Some people are [having issues](https://github.com/mermaidjs/mermaid.cli/issues/15)
149: installing this tool globally. Installing it locally is an alternative solution:
150: ```
151: npm install @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli
152: ./node_modules/.bin/mmdc -h
153: ```
154: ### Run with npx
155: [`npx`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/npx) is installed by default with NPM. It
156: downloads and runs commands at the same time. To use Mermaid CLI with npx, you
157: need to use the `-p` flag because the package name is different than the command
158: it installs (`mmdc`). `npx -p @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli mmdc -h`

136: ## Use Node.JS API

139: `mermaid`'s versioning.
140: ```js
141: import { run } from "@mermaid-js/mermaid-cli";
142: await run(
143: "input.mmd",
144: "output.svg", // {optional options},
145: );

148: Some people are [having issues](https://github.com/mermaidjs/mermaid.cli/issues/15)
149: installing this tool globally. Installing it locally is an alternative solution:
150: ```
151: npm install @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli
152: ./node_modules/.bin/mmdc -h
153: ```
154: ### Run with npx
155: [`npx`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/npx) is installed by default with NPM. It
156: downloads and runs commands at the same time. To use Mermaid CLI with npx, you
157: need to use the `-p` flag because the package name is different than the command
158: it installs (`mmdc`). `npx -p @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli mmdc -h`

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Official container images are published on GHCR (ghcr.io/mermaid-js/mermaid-cli/mermaid-cli) and Docker Hub (minlag/mermaid-cli) for local Docker or Podman execution.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
111: ```sh
112: docker pull ghcr.io/mermaid-js/mermaid-cli/mermaid-cli
113: ```
114: or e.g. version 8.8.0
115: ```sh
116: docker pull minlag/mermaid-cli:8.8.0
117: ```
118: The container looks for input files in `/data`. So for example, if you have a
119: diagram defined on your system in `/path/to/diagrams/diagram.mmd`, you can use
120: the container to generate an SVG file as follows:
121: ```sh
122: docker run --rm -u `id -u`:`id -g` -v /path/to/diagrams:/data minlag/mermaid-cli -i diagram.mmd
123: ```
124: Or, if using [Podman](https://podman.io/), instead do:
125: ```sh
126: podman run --userns keep-id --user ${UID} --rm -v /path/to/diagrams:/data:z ghcr.io/mermaid-js/mermaid-cli/mermaid-cli -i diagram.mmd
127: ```
128: The key differences in the podman command versus the docker command are:
129: - The addition of the `--userns keep-id` argument. This allows the container to keep the same UID as the current user's UID in the container namespace instead of mapping to a subuid. To learn more, see the [`userns=mode` documentation](https://docs.podman.io/en/v4.4/markdown/options/userns.container.html).
130: - The addition of `:z` to the end of the volume mapping. This instructs podman to relabel the files in the volume with the SELinux label `container_file_t`, which allows processes in the container to access the files. See the "Labeling Volume Mounts" section of [podman-run (1)](https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-run.1.html#volume-v-source-volume-host-dir-container-dir-options) for more info.
131: In previous version, the input files were mounted in `/home/mermaidcli`. You can
132: restore this behaviour with the `--workdir` option:
133: ```sh
134: docker run [...] --workdir=/home/mermaidcli minlag/mermaid-cli [...]
135: ```

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Supports PNG/SVG/PDF output, themes, transparent backgrounds, custom icon packs (npm or URI), custom CSS animation, sizing, and transforming Markdown files with embedded Mermaid code blocks.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
25: ### Create A PNG With A Dark Theme And Transparent Background
26: ```sh
27: mmdc -i input.mmd -o output.png -t dark -b transparent
28: ```
29: ### Adding custom icon packs to Mermaid
30: `mermaid-cli` supports two different ways to add [custom icon packs to mermaid](https://mermaid.js.org/config/icons.html):
31: - Icon packs installed via `npm install`, e.g. [@iconify-json/logos](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@iconify-json/logos). These can be used via the `--iconPacks @iconify-json/logos`.
32: - Icon packs accessible via URI. These can either be URLs or local `file://` URIs to local files. For example, to download the above [@iconify-json/logos](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@iconify-json/logos) package from a CDN like [jsDelivr](https://www.jsdelivr.com/), you can do `--iconPacksAndUrls logos#https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@iconify-json/logos@1.2.14/icons.json`.
33: ### Animating an SVG file with custom CSS
34: The `--cssFile` option can be used to inline some custom CSS. It's passed to [Mermaid's `themeCSS` config option](https://mermaid.js.org/config/schema-docs/config.html#themecss).
35: Please see [./test-positive/flowchart1.css](test-positive/flowchart1.css) for an example of a CSS file that has animations.
36: **Warning**: Inline CSS files may be blocked by your browser, depending on the [HTTP Content-Security-Policy header](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy) of the website that hosts your SVG.
37: ```sh
38: mmdc --input test-positive/flowchart1.mmd --cssFile test-positive/flowchart1.css -o docs/animated-flowchart.svg
39: ```

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: API billing is prepaid pay-as-you-go in US dollars with a $5 minimum top-up (funds expire after 1 year, failed requests refunded); generation is asynchronous via polling or webhooks and outputs stay stored for at least 7 days.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
60: How is API usage billed?
61: Billing is pay-as-you-go from a US dollar balance, and the minimum top-up is $5. Video models are priced per second of output and image models per image; DoP is the exception, priced per generation. Each model has a fixed rate for every configuration: the rate depends on settings like resolution and audio, is listed publicly, and stays the same regardless of how much you top up. An estimate endpoint returns the cost of a request before you run it. Funds expire one year after they are added to the balance. The balance can't go below zero: once it's empty, new requests wait until you add funds, or you can turn on auto top-up so production traffic never stops.
62: You're only charged for generations that finish successfully. If a request fails, its cost returns to your balance automatically.
63: How does generation work?
64: Generation is asynchronous. You submit a request and receive a request ID, then track progress by polling the status or by receiving a webhook when the result is ready. Once the generation completes, you download the output file.
65: How long are generated files stored?
66: Generated output files stay available for at least 7 days after creation and may be removed from Higgsfield servers after that period. For long-term retention, download completed files to your own storage as part of your integration.

110: What You Need Before Installing
111: You need three things:
112: A paid Higgsfield subscription.

123: npm install -g @higgsfield/cli

60: How is API usage billed?
61: Billing is pay-as-you-go from a US dollar balance, and the minimum top-up is $5. Video models are priced per second of output and image models per image; DoP is the exception, priced per generation. Each model has a fixed rate for every configuration: the rate depends on settings like resolution and audio, is listed publicly, and stays the same regardless of how much you top up. An estimate endpoint returns the cost of a request before you run it. Funds expire one year after they are added to the balance. The balance can't go below zero: once it's empty, new requests wait until you add funds, or you can turn on auto top-up so production traffic never stops.
62: You're only charged for generations that finish successfully. If a request fails, its cost returns to your balance automatically.
63: How does generation work?
64: Generation is asynchronous. You submit a request and receive a request ID, then track progress by polling the status or by receiving a webhook when the result is ready. Once the generation completes, you download the output file.
65: How long are generated files stored?
66: Generated output files stay available for at least 7 days after creation and may be removed from Higgsfield servers after that period. For long-term retention, download completed files to your own storage as part of your integration.

60: How is API usage billed?
61: Billing is pay-as-you-go from a US dollar balance, and the minimum top-up is $5. Video models are priced per second of output and image models per image; DoP is the exception, priced per generation. Each model has a fixed rate for every configuration: the rate depends on settings like resolution and audio, is listed publicly, and stays the same regardless of how much you top up. An estimate endpoint returns the cost of a request before you run it. Funds expire one year after they are added to the balance. The balance can't go below zero: once it's empty, new requests wait until you add funds, or you can turn on auto top-up so production traffic never stops.
62: You're only charged for generations that finish successfully. If a request fails, its cost returns to your balance automatically.
63: How does generation work?
64: Generation is asynchronous. You submit a request and receive a request ID, then track progress by polling the status or by receiving a webhook when the result is ready. Once the generation completes, you download the output file.
65: How long are generated files stored?
66: Generated output files stay available for at least 7 days after creation and may be removed from Higgsfield servers after that period. For long-term retention, download completed files to your own storage as part of your integration.

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
110: What You Need Before Installing
111: You need three things:
112: A paid Higgsfield subscription.
113: A terminal on macOS, Linux or Windows.
114: One package route: curl (macOS and Linux, nothing else required), Homebrew (needs Homebrew) or npm (needs Node.js).
115: A coding agent is optional. If you plan to call the CLI from Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw or Hermes, the agent can run the installation itself. That is covered in the agents section below.
116: How to Install Higgsfield CLI
117: All three methods install the same tool. Pick the one that matches the rest of your setup, because updates go through the same method you installed with.
118: 1. Install with curl (macOS and Linux). The installer may ask for your system password.
119: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/higgsfield-ai/cli/main/install.sh | sh
120: 2. Or install with Homebrew. Later updates: brew update && brew upgrade higgsfield.
121: brew install higgsfield-ai/tap/higgsfield
122: 3. Or install with npm (any platform, including Windows). The package name is @higgsfield/cli.
123: npm install -g @higgsfield/cli
124: 4. Check the version. It prints the release number, for example higgsfield 1.1.26, with a build date.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: API billing is prepaid pay-as-you-go in US dollars with a $5 minimum top-up (funds expire after 1 year, failed requests refunded); generation is asynchronous via polling or webhooks and outputs stay stored for at least 7 days.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
60: How is API usage billed?
61: Billing is pay-as-you-go from a US dollar balance, and the minimum top-up is $5. Video models are priced per second of output and image models per image; DoP is the exception, priced per generation. Each model has a fixed rate for every configuration: the rate depends on settings like resolution and audio, is listed publicly, and stays the same regardless of how much you top up. An estimate endpoint returns the cost of a request before you run it. Funds expire one year after they are added to the balance. The balance can't go below zero: once it's empty, new requests wait until you add funds, or you can turn on auto top-up so production traffic never stops.
62: You're only charged for generations that finish successfully. If a request fails, its cost returns to your balance automatically.
63: How does generation work?
64: Generation is asynchronous. You submit a request and receive a request ID, then track progress by polling the status or by receiving a webhook when the result is ready. Once the generation completes, you download the output file.
65: How long are generated files stored?
66: Generated output files stay available for at least 7 days after creation and may be removed from Higgsfield servers after that period. For long-term retention, download completed files to your own storage as part of your integration.

7: Connect your AI tools to Attio using the [Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/introduction), an open standard that lets AI assistants interact with your Attio CRM workspace.
8: ## What is Attio MCP?
9: Attio MCP is Attio's hosted MCP server that gives AI tools secure access to your Attio workspace. It's designed to work seamlessly with popular AI assistants like Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and more.
10: ### Why use Attio MCP?
11: * **Easy setup** — Connect through simple OAuth with one-click installation for supported AI tools
12: * **Natural language CRM management** — Manage your entire Attio workspace through conversational AI instead of clicking through multiple screens
13: * **Full workspace access** — AI tools can search, read, create, and update records across your CRM—people, companies, deals, tasks, and notes
14: * **Optimized for AI** — Built specifically for AI agents with efficient data formatting and human-readable responses
15: * **Secure by design** — Authenticates as your Attio user with OAuth, and read operations are auto-approved while write operations request confirmation

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Documents callable MCP tools across Records & Objects (list-objects, search-records, create-record, upsert-record), Activities, and Lists.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
49: ### Records & Objects
50: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
51: | - | - | - |
52: | `list-objects` | List all objects in the workspace (e.g. companies, people, deals), with optional fuzzy search by name or API slug | • "What objects do we have?" • "Find the object for tracking deals" |
53: | `search-records` | Full-text search for records (people, companies, deals, etc.) by name, email, domain, or other indexed attributes | • "Find all contacts at Stripe" • "What's the email for Namit Chadha?" • "Show me everything we know about TheSwarm" |
54: | `list-records` | List records in a given object with optional filtering and sorting | • "List all open deals" • "Show me companies created this month" |
55: | `get-records-by-ids` | Retrieve full details for specific records by their IDs | • "Get the complete profile for this contact" • "Show me all details for these three companies" |
56: | `create-record` | Create a new record (person, company, deal, or custom object) | • "Add a new contact: John Smith, CTO at Acme Corp" • "Create a company record for Linear" |
57: | `upsert-record` | Create or update a record using a matching attribute (e.g., email or domain) | • "Update the company record for stripe.com with their new funding info" • "Add or update Sarah's contact with her new title" |
58: | `update-record` | Update an existing record by `record_id` | • "Update this company record with the new ARR" • "Change Sarah's title to VP Product" |
59: | `merge-records` | Merge two records of the same object into one new record. Where both records have a value for the same attribute, the primary record's value takes precedence | • "Merge these two duplicate Acme company records" • "Combine John Smith's duplicate contact records into one" |
60: | `list-attribute-definitions` | List all attributes available on an object type, including their types and valid options | • "What fields are available on company records?" • "Show me the status options for deals" |
61: ### Activities
62: [Activities](https://docs.attio.com/docs/activities.md) model things that happen over time, such as phone calls or site visits. Each activity holds activity records, such as one specific phone call.
63: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
64: | - | - | - |
65: | `list-activities` | List all activities in the workspace, with optional fuzzy search by name or API slug | • "What activities do we track?" • "Find the activity for site visits" |
66: | `list-activity-attribute-definitions` | List the attributes available on an activity, including their types and valid options | • "What fields are available on phone calls?" • "Show me the direction options for calls" |
67: | `list-activity-records` | List records of a given activity with optional filtering and sorting | • "Show me all outbound calls from last week" • "List site visits linked to Acme" |
68: | `create-activity-record` | Create a new record for an activity | • "Log an outbound call with Sarah from Acme today at 2pm" • "Record a site visit at the Linear office" |
69: | `update-activity-record` | Update an existing activity record by `record_id` | • "Change the title of this call to Renewal call" • "Add Stripe to the linked records of this site visit" |
70: | `upsert-activity-record` | Create or update an activity record using a unique matching attribute, such as an ID from your own system | • "Log this call, or update it if it already exists with call ID 4821" • "Upsert the site visit with external ID SV-1029" |
71: ### Lists
72: | Tool | Description | Example Prompts |
73: | - | - | - |
74: | `list-lists` | List all lists in the workspace, with optional filtering by name or slug | • "What lists do we have?" • "Find lists related to recruiting" |
75: | `create-list` | Create a new list to group and track records of a single object type | • "Create a list called Enterprise Sales for companies" • "Set up a new pipeline list for deals, private to me" |
76: | `list-list-attribute-definitions` | List the available entry attributes for a given list, including their types and options | • "What fields can I update on the sales pipeline list?" • "Show me the status options for this list" |
77: | `list-records-in-list` | List entries in a given list with optional filtering and sorting, including their parent records | • "Show me all entries in the sales pipeline" • "List recruiting candidates in the onsite stage" |
78: | `add-record-to-list` | Add a record to a list as a new list entry | • "Add Acme to the sales pipeline" • "Add this candidate to the interview pipeline" |

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
3: OAuth 2.0 allows third-party applications to access Close data on behalf of users without exposing passwords or sharing API keys. You can create custom OAuth apps for Close to add bespoke features, automate tasks, and enhance data analytics, tailored to your business needs.
4: ## Create a new OAuth app
5: #### Go to OAuth Apps settings
6: Navigate to [**Settings** → **Developer** → **OAuth Apps**](https://app.close.com/settings/developer/oauth-apps) and click **Create App**.
7: #### Fill in your app details
8: * **App Name** — Your application name that users will see on the consent screen.
9: * **App Description** — 1–2 sentence description of what your app does.
10: * **Redirect URL** — The http**s** URL where users are redirected after authorizing your app (e.g. `https://yourapp.com/callback/close`). Must use TLS/SSL — plain `http://` URLs are not accepted.
11: * **Terms of Service URL** — Optional for internal-only apps
12: * **Privacy Policy URL** — Optional for internal-only apps
13: #### Get your credentials
14: Click **Create**, then copy your **Client ID** and **Client Secret** — you'll need these to implement the [OAuth 2.0 flow](/api/overview/oauth-authentication).
15: ### Scopes
16: All OAuth applications are granted the `all.full_access offline_access` scopes, providing the same level of access as API keys. If you have a use case for different scopes, we'd like to [hear about it](mailto:support@close.com?Subject=OAuth%20App%20Scopes).
17: ## Make authenticated requests
18: Once you have your Client ID and Client Secret, you're ready to follow the [OAuth 2.0 authorization flow guide](/api/overview/oauth-authentication) to obtain access tokens and make authenticated requests to the Close API on behalf of your users.
19: ## Making your app public (optional)
20: OAuth apps are **Private** by default, meaning only members of your own Close organization can authorize them. This is fine if you and your teammates (in the same organization) are the only users.
21: If you want other Close customers to authorize it, you'll need to request to [make it public and optionally get listed](/integrations/publish).

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
3: OAuth 2.0 allows third-party applications to access Close data on behalf of users without exposing passwords or sharing API keys. You can create custom OAuth apps for Close to add bespoke features, automate tasks, and enhance data analytics, tailored to your business needs.
4: ## Create a new OAuth app
5: #### Go to OAuth Apps settings
6: Navigate to [**Settings** → **Developer** → **OAuth Apps**](https://app.close.com/settings/developer/oauth-apps) and click **Create App**.
7: #### Fill in your app details
8: * **App Name** — Your application name that users will see on the consent screen.
9: * **App Description** — 1–2 sentence description of what your app does.
10: * **Redirect URL** — The http**s** URL where users are redirected after authorizing your app (e.g. `https://yourapp.com/callback/close`). Must use TLS/SSL — plain `http://` URLs are not accepted.
11: * **Terms of Service URL** — Optional for internal-only apps
12: * **Privacy Policy URL** — Optional for internal-only apps
13: #### Get your credentials
14: Click **Create**, then copy your **Client ID** and **Client Secret** — you'll need these to implement the [OAuth 2.0 flow](/api/overview/oauth-authentication).
15: ### Scopes
16: All OAuth applications are granted the `all.full_access offline_access` scopes, providing the same level of access as API keys. If you have a use case for different scopes, we'd like to [hear about it](mailto:support@close.com?Subject=OAuth%20App%20Scopes).
17: ## Make authenticated requests
18: Once you have your Client ID and Client Secret, you're ready to follow the [OAuth 2.0 authorization flow guide](/api/overview/oauth-authentication) to obtain access tokens and make authenticated requests to the Close API on behalf of your users.
19: ## Making your app public (optional)
20: OAuth apps are **Private** by default, meaning only members of your own Close organization can authorize them. This is fine if you and your teammates (in the same organization) are the only users.
21: If you want other Close customers to authorize it, you'll need to request to [make it public and optionally get listed](/integrations/publish).

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: RPC-style HTTPS GET/POST method calls at /bot<token>/METHOD_NAME returning JSON {ok, result}.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
130: All queries to the Telegram Bot API must be served over HTTPS and need to be presented in this form: https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/METHOD_NAME. Like this for example:
131: https://api.telegram.org/bot123456:ABC-DEF1234ghIkl-zyx57W2v1u123ew11/getMe
132: We support GET and POST HTTP methods. We support four ways of passing parameters in Bot API requests:
133: URL query string
134: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
135: application/json (except for uploading files)
136: multipart/form-data (use to upload files)
137: The response contains a JSON object, which always has a Boolean field 'ok' and may have an optional String field 'description' with a human-readable description of the result. If 'ok' equals True, the request was successful and the result of the query can be found in the 'result' field. In case of an unsuccessful request, 'ok' equals False and the error is explained in the 'description'. An Integer 'error_code' field is also returned, but its contents are subject to change in the future. Some errors may also have an optional field 'parameters' of the type ResponseParameters, which can help to automatically handle the error.

155: Getting updates
156: There are two mutually exclusive ways of receiving updates for your bot - the getUpdates method on one hand and webhooks on the other. Incoming updates are stored on the server until the bot receives them either way, but they will not be kept longer than 24 hours.
157: Regardless of which option you choose, you will receive JSON-serialized Update objects as a result.
158: Update
159: This object represents an incoming update.
160: At most one of the optional fields can be present in any given update.
161: Field
162: Type
163: Description
164: update_id
165: Integer
166: The update's unique identifier. Update identifiers start from a certain positive number and increase sequentially. This identifier becomes especially handy if you're using webhooks, since it allows you to ignore repeated updates or to restore the correct update sequence, should they get out of order. If there are no new updates for at least a week, then identifier of the next update will be chosen randomly instead of sequentially.
167: message
168: Message
169: Optional. New incoming message of any kind - text, photo, sticker, etc.
170: edited_message
171: Message
172: Optional. New version of a message that is known to the bot and was edited. This update may at times be triggered by changes to message fields that are either unavailable or not actively used by your bot.
173: channel_post
174: Message
175: Optional. New incoming channel post of any kind - text, photo, sticker, etc.
176: edited_channel_post
177: Message
178: Optional. New version of a channel post that is known to the bot and was edited. This update may at times be triggered by changes to message fields that are either unavailable or not actively used by your bot.
179: business_connection
180: BusinessConnection
181: Optional. The bot was connected to or disconnected from a business account, or a user edited an existing connection with the bot
182: business_message
183: Message
184: Optional. New message from a connected business account
185: edited_business_message
186: Message
187: Optional. New version of a message from a connected business account
188: deleted_business_messages
189: BusinessMessagesDeleted
190: Optional. Messages were deleted from a connected business account
191: guest_message
192: Message
193: Optional. New guest message. The bot can use the field Message.guest_query_id and the method answerGuestQuery to send a message in response.
194: message_reaction
195: MessageReactionUpdated
196: Optional. A reaction to a message was changed by a user. The bot must be an administrator in the chat and must explicitly specify "message_reaction" in the list of allowed_updates to receive these updates. The update isn't received for reactions set by bots.
197: message_reaction_count
198: MessageReactionCountUpdated
199: Optional. Reactions to a message with anonymous reactions were changed. The bot must be an administrator in the chat and must explicitly specify "message_reaction_count" in the list of allowed_updates to receive these updates. The updates are grouped and can be sent with delay up to a few minutes.
200: inline_query
201: InlineQuery
202: Optional. New incoming inline query
203: chosen_inline_result
204: ChosenInlineResult
205: Optional. The result of an inline query that was chosen by a user and sent to their chat partner. Please see our documentation on the feedback collecting for details on how to enable these updates for your bot. The updates can also be enabled using the parameter inline_feedback_share_denominator of the method setMySettings.
206: callback_query
207: CallbackQuery
208: Optional. New incoming callback query
209: widget_query
210: WidgetQuery
211: Optional. New incoming query from a widget in a message sent by the bot or via the bot
212: shared_widget_query
213: SharedWidgetQuery
214: Optional. New incoming query from a forwarded message with a shared widget
215: shipping_query
216: ShippingQuery
217: Optional. New incoming shipping query. Only for invoices with flexible price.
218: pre_checkout_query
219: PreCheckoutQuery
220: Optional. New incoming pre-checkout query. Contains full information about checkout.

28: Replace Entire Websites
29: Telegram bots can host Mini Apps built with JavaScript. This allows for infinitely flexible interfaces that can power everything from online stores to arcade games. Unlike websites, bots support seamless authorization and notifications through Telegram out of the box.
30: Try @DurgerKingBot – or check out the dedicated guide to Mini Apps to build your own.
31: Natively Integrate AI Agents and Chatbots
32: On Telegram, AI bots can natively meet, chat and compete: users can summon assistants into the same chat, watch their responses stream in real time, coordinate multiple agents at once or have them manage their whole account.
33: Bots also support threaded conversations to manage several different topics in parallel — letting users easily access information from previous chats.
34: See here to check out more tools and integrations available for AI-powered bots on Telegram.
35: Manage Your Business
36: Telegram Business users can connect Telegram bots to process and answer messages on their behalf, via their personal account. This allows businesses to seamlessly integrate any existing tools and workflows, or add new AI assistants to increase productivity.
37: As we continue to expand the set of free tools available to bots through this integration, we encourage all developers to innovate and develop useful applications and services for businesses on Telegram.
38: Developers can turn on Business Mode in @BotFather if their bot supports integration with Telegram Business accounts.
39: Receive Payments
40: Bots can sell all kinds of goods and services on Telegram – to anyone in the world. Telegram Stars allow users to securely and effortlessly buy digital products via in-app purchases. In addition, physical products can be easily purchased through third-party providers that support integration with Mini Apps.
41: Try @ShopBot – or check out our dedicated guides for digital and physical products to build your own.
42: Create Custom Tools
43: Increase your productivity by creating bots for specific tasks – like converting files, managing chats or fetching today’s forecast. Users can chat directly with bots, or add them to groups and channels to introduce extra features.
44: Mini apps can generate media and files – that users can effortlessly share to other chats or a post as a story.
45: Integrate with Services and Devices
46: Mini apps can seamlessly integrate with third-party services, APIs and devices to instantly process and update information – like changing a user's emoji status when they start a game or get in a taxi .
47: By default, Mini Apps seamlessly integrate with Android and iOS, allowing users to add direct shortcuts to their device’s home screen.
48: Likewise, many popular platforms already have official Telegram bots, which allow users to comfortably access content in one app – or perform quick searches using inline mode.
49: Try @GMailBot, @GitHubBot, @Bing, @YouTube, @wiki and more.
50: Host Games
51: Developers can create both lightweight HTML5 Games and immersive full-screen modern games with support for detailed motion controls, location-based points of interest and dynamic hardware optimizations.
52: Try some of the games in the @Gamee library – or check out the HTML5 and Mini App manuals to build your own.
53: Build Social Networks
54: Bots can serve as an intermediary to connect users based on shared interests, location, and more. Coordinate meetups, show local services, or help people sell second-hand items.
55: Users can place direct shortcuts to specific mini apps on the home screen of their devices – accessing services in one tap.

57: Telegram offers a robust ecosystem of monetization features, allowing any bot to support its development with multiple revenue streams. Popular bots can passively earn income through Revenue Sharing from Telegram Ads, implement subscription plans for users – or offer paid content and digital products for Telegram Stars.
58: Telegram Stars in your bot's balance can be used to increase message limits, send gifts to users or accept rewards in Toncoin.
59: Promote Your Project
60: Bots can host affiliate marketing programs – giving developers a transparent way to quickly scale with organic growth from user referrals.
61: Affiliate Programs support custom revenue sharing rates and variable commission periods, allowing you to customize your offers and update your campaign over time.
62: To learn more and get started in just a few taps, check out our dedicated guide.

108: Introduced support for Ephemeral Messages, allowing bots to send group messages and receive commands that are visible only to a specific user and the bot.
109: Added the field is_ephemeral to the class BotCommand.
110: Added the field receiver_user to the class Message.
111: Added the field ephemeral_message_id to the class Message.
112: Added the parameters receiver_user_id and callback_query_id to the methods sendMessage, sendAnimation, sendAudio, sendDocument, sendLivePhoto, sendPhoto, sendSticker, sendVideo, sendVideoNote, sendVoice, sendContact, sendLocation, sendVenue.
113: Added the field ephemeral_message_id to the class ReplyParameters, allowing bots to reply to ephemeral messages.
114: Marked the field message_id in the class ReplyParameters as optional if the field ephemeral_message_id is present.
115: Added the methods editEphemeralMessageText, editEphemeralMessageMedia, editEphemeralMessageCaption, and editEphemeralMessageReplyMarkup allowing bots to edit ephemeral messages.
116: Added the method deleteEphemeralMessage allowing bots to delete ephemeral messages.
117: Communities
118: Introduced initial support for Communities - several supergroups, channels, and bots linked together around a shared topic or audience.
119: Added the class Community which represents a community.
120: Added the class CommunityChatAdded and the field community_chat_added to the class Message.
121: Added the class CommunityChatRemoved and the field community_chat_removed to the class Message.
122: Added the field community to the class ChatFullInfo.
123: General
124: Added updates about changes to a user payment subscription, represented by the class BotSubscriptionUpdated and the field subscription in the class Update.
125: Hardened the security of Mini Apps by disallowing the usage of Mini App methods from origins different from the original Mini App domain. The protection will be automatically enabled for all Mini Apps on July 20, 2026. You can opt-out from the protection through the @BotFather Mini App. If you do so, you acknowledge that it is the responsibility of the bot to ensure that the Mini App has no links to untrusted sites.
126: See earlier changes »
127: Authorizing your bot
128: Each bot is given a unique authentication token when it is created. The token looks something like 123456:ABC-DEF1234ghIkl-zyx57W2v1u123ew11, but we'll use simply <token> in this document instead. You can learn about obtaining tokens and generating new ones in this document.
129: Making requests
130: All queries to the Telegram Bot API must be served over HTTPS and need to be presented in this form: https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/METHOD_NAME. Like this for example:
131: https://api.telegram.org/bot123456:ABC-DEF1234ghIkl-zyx57W2v1u123ew11/getMe
132: We support GET and POST HTTP methods. We support four ways of passing parameters in Bot API requests:
133: URL query string
134: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
135: application/json (except for uploading files)
136: multipart/form-data (use to upload files)
137: The response contains a JSON object, which always has a Boolean field 'ok' and may have an optional String field 'description' with a human-readable description of the result. If 'ok' equals True, the request was successful and the result of the query can be found in the 'result' field. In case of an unsuccessful request, 'ok' equals False and the error is explained in the 'description'. An Integer 'error_code' field is also returned, but its contents are subject to change in the future. Some errors may also have an optional field 'parameters' of the type ResponseParameters, which can help to automatically handle the error.
138: All methods in the Bot API are case-insensitive.
139: All queries must be made using UTF-8.
140: Making requests when getting updates
141: If you're using webhooks, you can perform a request to the Bot API while sending an answer to the webhook. Use either application/json or application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data response content type for passing parameters. Specify the method to be invoked in the method parameter of the request. It's not possible to know that such a request was successful or get its result.
142: Please see our FAQ for examples.
143: Using a Local Bot API Server
144: The Bot API server source code is available at telegram-bot-api. You can run it locally and send the requests to your own server instead of https://api.telegram.org. If you switch to a local Bot API server, your bot will be able to:
145: Download files without a size limit.
146: Upload files up to 2000 MB.
147: Upload files using their local path and the file URI scheme.
148: Use an HTTP URL for the webhook.
149: Use any local IP address for the webhook.
150: Use any port for the webhook.
151: Set max_webhook_connections up to 100000.
152: Receive the absolute local path as a value of the file_path field without the need to download the file after a getFile request.
153: Do I need a Local Bot API Server
154: The majority of bots will be OK with the default configuration, running on our servers. But if you feel that you need one of these features, you're welcome to switch to your own at any time.
155: Getting updates
156: There are two mutually exclusive ways of receiving updates for your bot - the getUpdates method on one hand and webhooks on the other. Incoming updates are stored on the server until the bot receives them either way, but they will not be kept longer than 24 hours.
157: Regardless of which option you choose, you will receive JSON-serialized Update objects as a result.
158: Update
159: This object represents an incoming update.
160: At most one of the optional fields can be present in any given update.
161: Field
162: Type
163: Description
164: update_id
165: Integer
166: The update's unique identifier. Update identifiers start from a certain positive number and increase sequentially. This identifier becomes especially handy if you're using webhooks, since it allows you to ignore repeated updates or to restore the correct update sequence, should they get out of order. If there are no new updates for at least a week, then identifier of the next update will be chosen randomly instead of sequentially.
167: message

176: edited_channel_post

179: business_connection

191: guest_message

194: message_reaction

197: message_reaction_count

The bot must be an administrator in the chat and must explicitly specify "message_reaction_count" in the list of allowed_updates to receive these updates. The updates are grouped and can be sent with delay up to a few minutes.
200: inline_query

Please see our documentation on the feedback collecting for details on how to enable these updates for your bot. The updates can also be enabled using the parameter inline_feedback_share_denominator of the method setMySettings.

11: We offer three kinds of APIs for developers. The Bot API allows you to easily create programs that use Telegram messages for an interface. The Telegram API and TDLib allow you to build your own customized Telegram clients. You are welcome to use both APIs free of charge. Lastly, the Gateway API allows any business, app or website to send verification codes through Telegram instead of traditional SMS.
12: You can also add Telegram Widgets to your website.
13: Designers are welcome to create Animated Stickers and Emoji or Custom Themes for Telegram.
14: Bot API
15: This API allows you to connect bots to our system. Telegram Bots are special accounts that do not require an additional phone number to set up. These accounts serve as an interface for code running somewhere on your server.
16: To use this, you don't need to know anything about how our MTProto encryption protocol works — our intermediary server will handle all encryption and communication with the Telegram API for you. You communicate with this server via a simple HTTPS interface that offers a simplified version of the Telegram API.
17: Learn more about the Bot API here »
18: Bot developers can also make use of our Payments API to accept payments from Telegram users around the world.
19: TDLib – build your own Telegram
20: Even if you're looking for maximum customization, you don't have to create your app from scratch. Try our Telegram Database Library (or simply TDLib), a tool for third-party developers that makes it easy to build fast, secure and feature-rich Telegram apps.
21: TDLib takes care of all network implementation details, encryption and local data storage, so that you can dedicate more time to design, responsive interfaces and beautiful animations.
22: TDLib supports all Telegram features and makes developing Telegram apps a breeze on any platform. It can be used on Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, Linux and virtually any other system. The library is open source and compatible with virtually any programming language.
23: Learn more about TDLib here »
24: Gateway API
25: The Telegram Gateway API allows any business, app or website to send authorization codes through Telegram instead of traditional SMS – offering a powerful and convenient way to lower costs while increasing the security and delivery speed of your codes to Telegram’s 1 billion monthly active users. Users will instantly receive messages with codes in a special chat inside Telegram.
26: Telegram's Gateway API is completely free to test. Learn more here »
27: Telegram API
28: This API allows you to build your own customized Telegram clients. It is 100% open for all developers who wish to create Telegram applications on our platform. Feel free to study the open source code of existing Telegram applications for examples of how things work here. Don't forget to register your application in our system.

103: AI features
104: Telegram offers many AI features powered by Cocoon — a decentralized network designed to maximize privacy.
105: Bot API dialog IDs
106: A bot API dialog ID is a single, unique 64-bit peer ID sequence derived from the user, chat, channel and secret chat ID sequences, maintaining uniqueness across all of them.
107: This page specifies how to convert MTProto peer IDs to bot API dialog IDs and vice versa.
108: Managed bots
109: Users can create managed bots (which are controlled by a specific manager bot) directly through the MTProto API, without interacting with @BotFather.
110: Commands
111: Bots offer a set of commands that can be used by users in private, or in a chat.
112: Buttons
113: Users can interact with your bot via buttons or even inline buttons, straight from inline messages in any chat.
114: Menu button
115: Bots can choose the behavior of the menu button shown next to the text input field.
116: Inline queries
117: Users can interact with your bot via inline queries, straight from the text input field in any chat.
118: Games
119: Bots can offer users HTML5 games to play solo or to compete against each other in groups and one-on-one chats; how to work with games in the MTProto API.
120: Mini apps
121: Bots can offer users interactive HTML5 mini apps to completely replace any website.
122: Affiliate programs
123: Developers can open affiliate programs for their mini app – allowing content creators, other mini app developers and any Telegram user to promote it and earn commissions on purchases made by people they referred.
124: Attachment menu
125: Bots can install attachment menu entries, offering conveniently accessible, versatile mini apps.
126: Editing bot info
127: Users can edit and localize the profile picture, name, about text and description of bots they own; the same can be done by the bots themselves.
128: AI bots
129: Telegram bots offer a number of features for AI chatbots.
130: Guest mode
131: Guest bots can be queried by username from any non-secret private chat, group and supergroup, posting their results directly into the chat, even if they're not a member.
132: Bot-to-bot communication »
133: Bots may receive and send messages to and from other bots in groups, private chats and chats, if Bot-to-Bot Communication Mode is enabled.
134: Stories
135: Telegram users and channels can easily post and view stories through the API.
136: Similar channels and bots
137: The API offers a method to obtain a list of similarly themed public channels and bots, selected based on similarities in their subscriber bases.
138: Accent colors
139: Telegram users and channels can change the accent color and background pattern of their profile page and their messages!
140: Privacy settings
141: Telegram allows users to specify granular privacy settings, choosing which users can or can't interact with them in certain ways.
142: Search & filters
143: Telegram allows applying detailed message filters while looking for messages in chats.
144: This allows the server to filter messages based on a text query, and even on their type, and this feature is often used by graphical clients to implement features like the chat gallery, chat profile pictures and more.
145: Polls
146: Telegram allows sending polls and quizzes, that can be voted on by thousands, if not millions of users in chats and channels.
147: Checklists
148: Premium users can now create collaborative checklists in any chat to track tasks and coordinate teams — or manage shopping and to-do lists.
149: Reactions
150: Telegram allows users to react to any message using specific emojis, triggering cute Lottie animations.
151: Animated message effects
152: Telegram allows adding spectacular animated effects to messages you send.
153: Emoji categories
154: Sticker, custom emoji and GIF selection UIs should offer a list of categories to quickly filter results by a (list of) emojis, or by some other criteria.
155: Emoji status
156: Telegram allows users to set an emoticon or a custom emoji as status, to show next to their name in chats and profiles.
157: Invite links and join requests
158: Channels, basic groups and supergroups may have a public username or a private invite link: private invite links may be further enhanced with per-user join requests.
159: Admin, banned and default rights for channels, supergroups and groups
160: How to handle admin permissions, granular bans and global permissions in channels, groups and supergroups.
161: Discussion groups
162: Groups can be associated with a channel as a discussion group, allowing users to discuss posts.
163: Channel comments and message threads
164: Telegram allows commenting on a channel post or on a generic group message, thanks to message threads.
165: Admin log
166: Both supergroups and channels offer a so-called admin log, a log of recent relevant supergroup and channel actions, like the modification of group/channel settings or information on behalf of an admin, user kicks and bans, and more.
167: Pinned messages
168: Telegram allows pinning multiple messages on top of a specific chat.
169: Group member/admin tags
170: Members in group chats (both basic groups and supergroups) can now add a tag next to their name — to show their role at work, what they study in school, and more.
171: Mentions
172: Telegram allows mentioning other users in case of urgent duckling matters, and quickly navigating to those mentions in order to read them as swiftly as possible.
173: Scheduled messages
174: Telegram allows scheduling messages.
175: Live geolocations
176: Telegram allows sending the live geolocation of a user in a chat, optionally setting a proximity alert.
177: Peer database
178: How to work with peer information in the API.
179: Min constructors
180: Sometimes, user and channel constructors encountered in group chat updates may not contain full info about the user: this page explains how to handle such constructors.
181: Account deletion
182: How to delete a Telegram account.
183: Imported messages
184: Telegram allows importing messages and media from foreign chat apps.
185: Telegram Passport
186: How to work with Telegram Passport directly using the MTProto API.
187: Telegram Payments
188: How to work with Telegram Payments directly using the MTProto API.

202: Telegram API Configuration
203: Before you can use the server, you need to connect to the Telegram API.
204: Get the API ID and hash from Telegram API
205: Run the following command:
206: mcp-telegram sign-in --api-id <your-api-id> --api-hash <your-api-hash> --phone-number <your-phone-number>
207: Enter the code you received from Telegram to connect to the API.
208: The password may be required if you have two-factor authentication enabled.
209: Note
210: To log out from the Telegram API, use the mcp-telegram logout command.
211: Claude Desktop Configuration
212: Configure Claude Desktop to recognize the Exa MCP server.
213: Open the Claude Desktop configuration file:
214: in MacOS, the configuration file is located at ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json
215: in Windows, the configuration file is located at %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json
216: Note:
217: You can also find claude_desktop_config.json inside the settings of Claude Desktop app
218: Add the server configuration
219: {
220: "mcpServers": {
221: "mcp-telegram": {
222: "command": "mcp-server",
223: "env": {
224: "TELEGRAM_API_ID": "<your-api-id>",
225: "TELEGRAM_API_HASH": "<your-api-hash>",
226: },
227: }
228: }
229: }
230: }

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
127: Authorizing your bot
128: Each bot is given a unique authentication token when it is created. The token looks something like 123456:ABC-DEF1234ghIkl-zyx57W2v1u123ew11, but we'll use simply <token> in this document instead. You can learn about obtaining tokens and generating new ones in this document.
129: Making requests
130: All queries to the Telegram Bot API must be served over HTTPS and need to be presented in this form: https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/METHOD_NAME. Like this for example:
131: https://api.telegram.org/bot123456:ABC-DEF1234ghIkl-zyx57W2v1u123ew11/getMe
132: We support GET and POST HTTP methods. We support four ways of passing parameters in Bot API requests:
133: URL query string
134: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
135: application/json (except for uploading files)
136: multipart/form-data (use to upload files)
137: The response contains a JSON object, which always has a Boolean field 'ok' and may have an optional String field 'description' with a human-readable description of the result. If 'ok' equals True, the request was successful and the result of the query can be found in the 'result' field. In case of an unsuccessful request, 'ok' equals False and the error is explained in the 'description'. An Integer 'error_code' field is also returned, but its contents are subject to change in the future. Some errors may also have an optional field 'parameters' of the type ResponseParameters, which can help to automatically handle the error.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Slack apps use OAuth 2.0 v2 flow to request bot and user scopes.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
41: Slack apps are installed with a v2 OAuth 2.0 flow. Your app can act with its own identity instead of acting on behalf of users, without requesting excessive permissions that could cause installations to be rejected.
42: OAuth 2.0 refers to the 2.0 version of the OAuth spec, and this is our second version of OAuth 2.0. For the rest of this guide, we'll just refer to it as "OAuth".
43: How it works: a high-level overview​
44: OAuth allows a user in any Slack workspace to install your app. At the end of the OAuth flow, your app gains an access token. Your app's access token allows your app to open doors to the Slack platform. During the OAuth flow, you specify which scopes your app needs. Those scopes determine exactly which doors your app can open.
45: Implementing an OAuth flow can feel hard because there are a lot of steps, but your app really only has to worry about three steps to make OAuth work: requesting scopes, waiting for a user to give their approval, and exchanging a temporary authorization code for an access token. Redirecting a user to Slack can be done with a single link. For example:
46: [Add to Slack](https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?scope=incoming-webhook&client_id=33336676.569200954261)
47: Replace the client_id with your app's client ID, and add the scopes you'd like. Bot scopes should be added as scope=<bot_scope>, and user scopes should be added as user_scope=<user_scope>.
48: For example, if your app only has one bot scope and it is incoming-webhook, the redirect would look like that shown above. If your app has a user scope, it might look like this instead:
49: https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?user_scope=search%3Aread&client_id=33336676.569200954261
50: If your app has both a bot and a user scope, it might look like this:
51: https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?scope=incoming-webhook&user_scope=search%3Aread&client_id=33336676.569200954261

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: OAuth 2.0 v2 flow requests bot scopes (scope) and user scopes (user_scope) at /oauth/v2/authorize.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
41: Slack apps are installed with a v2 OAuth 2.0 flow. Your app can act with its own identity instead of acting on behalf of users, without requesting excessive permissions that could cause installations to be rejected.
42: OAuth 2.0 refers to the 2.0 version of the OAuth spec, and this is our second version of OAuth 2.0. For the rest of this guide, we'll just refer to it as "OAuth".
43: How it works: a high-level overview​
44: OAuth allows a user in any Slack workspace to install your app. At the end of the OAuth flow, your app gains an access token. Your app's access token allows your app to open doors to the Slack platform. During the OAuth flow, you specify which scopes your app needs. Those scopes determine exactly which doors your app can open.
45: Implementing an OAuth flow can feel hard because there are a lot of steps, but your app really only has to worry about three steps to make OAuth work: requesting scopes, waiting for a user to give their approval, and exchanging a temporary authorization code for an access token. Redirecting a user to Slack can be done with a single link. For example:
46: [Add to Slack](https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?scope=incoming-webhook&client_id=33336676.569200954261)
47: Replace the client_id with your app's client ID, and add the scopes you'd like. Bot scopes should be added as scope=<bot_scope>, and user scopes should be added as user_scope=<user_scope>.
48: For example, if your app only has one bot scope and it is incoming-webhook, the redirect would look like that shown above. If your app has a user scope, it might look like this instead:
49: https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?user_scope=search%3Aread&client_id=33336676.569200954261
50: If your app has both a bot and a user scope, it might look like this:
51: https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?scope=incoming-webhook&user_scope=search%3Aread&client_id=33336676.569200954261
52: Obtaining access tokens with OAuth​
53: Your app obtains an access token in three steps:
54: Requesting scopes.
55: Waiting for a user to approve your requested scopes.
56: Exchanging a temporary authorization code for an access token.
57: Why is there a third exchanging step in OAuth at all? Why doesn't Slack send your app an access token directly after the user okays your app? The reason is two-factor authentication. You have to prove both that you have the right temporary authorization code, and that you have your app's client secret.
58: 1. Request scopes​
59: While developing your app, you'll determine a minimum list of scopes that your app requires to work. When a user installs your app in their workspace, you'll request those scopes.
60: To request scopes, redirect Slack users to https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize. If you're developing a GovSlack app for use by public sector customers, redirect users to https://slack-gov.com/oauth/v2/authorize.
61: A scope conflict occurs when attempting to combine Sign in with Slack (SIWS) user scopes with non-Sign in with Slack scopes in the same OAuth flow
62: Each set of scopes must be requested in a separate OAuth flow.
63: Include both your app's client ID, which is found in the App Management page, and a comma-separated list of scopes, such as: scope=incoming-webhook,commands. The full redirect URL will look something like this:
64: https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize?scope=incoming-webhook,commands&client_id=3336676.569200954261
65: The scope list requests scopes for your app's bot user. If you have specific need for a user token (for example, so that you can act on behalf of a user), provide a user_scope parameter with requested user scopes instead of, or in addition to, the scope parameter.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: User-centric /oauth/v2_user/authorize and /api/oauth.v2.user.access flow for user tokens and MCP clients.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
194: The user-centric flow: the oauth.v2.user.access method​
195: In addition to the standard workspace installation flow, Slack provides a dedicated flow for obtaining user-specific access tokens. To initiate a user-specific flow, redirect users to the v2_user authorization endpoint:
196: https://slack.com/oauth/v2_user/authorize?client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&scope=chat:write,channels:history
197: Unlike the the standard v2/authorize endpoint, this flow focuses exclusively on the user's identity and personal permissions. After approval, Slack redirects back to your redirect_uri with a temporary code, just like the standard flow.
198: Exchanging the code with oauth.v2.user.access​
199: Once you have the temporary authorization code, you must exchange it using the oauth.v2.user.access API method. This method is compliant to the OAuth 2.0 RFC.
200: Comparing oauth.v2.access and oauth.v2.user.access endpoints​
201: The oauth.v2.access API method supports generating either a bot token or user token or both.
202: The oauth.v2.user.access API method generates a user token by default following the standard OAuth spec and works out-of-the-box with MCP authorization flows.
203: The oauth.v2.user.access endpoint should be used in scenarios where:
204: You only need user tokens, not bot tokens
205: You're building MCP integrations with desktop IDE clients like Cursor or Claude Code
206: Use the oauth.v2.access API method unless your client cannot support passing scope and scope_user in the same request.

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
68: You must explicitly set the Content-type HTTP header to application/json. We won't interpret your POST body as such without it.
69: You must transmit your token as a bearer token in the Authorization HTTP header.
70: You cannot send your token as part of the query string or as an attribute in your posted JSON.
71: Do not mix arguments between query string, URL-encoded POST body, and JSON attributes. Choose one approach per request.
72: Providing an explicitly null value for an attribute will result in whichever default behavior is assigned to it.
73: For example, to send the same request above to the conversations.create method with a JSON POST body, send something like this:
74: POST /api/conversations.create
75: Content-type: application/json
76: Authorization: Bearer xoxp-xxxxxxxxx-xxxx
77: {"name":"something-urgent"}
78: Note how we present the token with the string Bearer pre-pended to it, indicating the OAuth 2.0 authentication scheme. Consult your favorite HTTP tool or library's manual for further detail on setting HTTP headers.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Web API requests authenticate via bearer token identifying a user or bot user.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
112: Authentication​
113: Authenticate your Web API requests by providing a bearer token, which identifies a single user or bot user relationship.
114: Register your application with Slack to obtain credentials for use with our OAuth 2.0 implementation, which allows you to negotiate tokens on behalf of users and workspaces.
115: We prefer tokens to be sent in the Authorization HTTP header of your outbound requests. However, you may also pass tokens in all Web API calls as a POST body parameter called token. Tokens cannot be sent as a query parameter.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Access tokens presented as Authorization: Bearer xoxb-... header or form POST token parameter.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
221: Using tokens​
222: The best way to communicate your access tokens — also known as bearer tokens — to Slack is by presenting them in a request's Authorization HTTP header where the full value, including "Bearer", is case-sensitive. This approach is required when using application/json with a write method.
223: GET /api/conversations.list?limit=50
224: Authorization: Bearer xoxb-1234-abcdefgh
225: Alternatively, you may send the token as a POST body attribute of the application/x-www-form-urlencoded variety.
226: POST body:
227: POST /api/conversations.list
228: Content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
229: token=xoxb-1234-abcdefgh&limit=50

61: For example, a POST request to the conversations.create method might look something like this:
62: POST /api/conversations.create
63: Content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
64: token=xoxp-xxxxxxxxx-xxxx&name=something-urgent
65: JSON-encoded bodies​
66: For write methods that support JSON, you may alternatively send your HTTP POST data as Content-type: application/json.
67: There are some ground rules:
68: You must explicitly set the Content-type HTTP header to application/json. We won't interpret your POST body as such without it.
69: You must transmit your token as a bearer token in the Authorization HTTP header.
70: You cannot send your token as part of the query string or as an attribute in your posted JSON.
71: Do not mix arguments between query string, URL-encoded POST body, and JSON attributes. Choose one approach per request.
72: Providing an explicitly null value for an attribute will result in whichever default behavior is assigned to it.
73: For example, to send the same request above to the conversations.create method with a JSON POST body, send something like this:
74: POST /api/conversations.create
75: Content-type: application/json
76: Authorization: Bearer xoxp-xxxxxxxxx-xxxx
77: {"name":"something-urgent"}
78: Note how we present the token with the string Bearer pre-pended to it, indicating the OAuth 2.0 authentication scheme. Consult your favorite HTTP tool or library's manual for further detail on setting HTTP headers.
79: Here's a more complicated example — posting a message with menus using chat.postMessage:
80: POST /api/chat.postMessage
81: Content-type: application/json
82: Authorization: Bearer xoxp-xxxxxxxxx-xxxx
83: {"channel":"C123ABC456","text":"I hope the tour went well, Mr. Wonka.","attachments":[{"text":"Who wins the lifetime supply of chocolate?","fallback":"You could be telling the computer exactly what it can do with a lifetime supply of chocolate.","color":"#3AA3E3","attachment_type":"default","callback_id":"select_simple_1234","actions":[{"name":"winners_list","text":"Who should win?","type":"select","data_source":"users"}]}]}
84: The attachments argument is sent a straightforward JSON array.
85: Here's how to do that with cURL:
86: curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer xoxb-1234-56789abcdefghijklmnop' \
87: -H 'Content-type: application/json' \
88: --data '{"channel":"C123ABC456","text":"I hope the tour went well, Mr. Wonka.","attachments": [{"text":"Who wins the lifetime supply of chocolate?","fallback":"You could be telling the computer exactly what it can do with a lifetime supply of chocolate.","color":"#3AA3E3","attachment_type":"default","callback_id":"select_simple_1234","actions":[{"name":"winners_list","text":"Who should win?","type":"select","data_source":"users"}]}]}' \

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
43: Slack MCP server overview
44: With the Slack MCP server, your integrated apps can search channels, send messages, and perform other Slack actions through MCP clients. Workspace admins can approve and manage all MCP client integrations, keeping your Slack data safe. This guide discusses the MCP server offerings from Slack and how to develop with the Slack MCP server.
45: Slack MCP server features​
46: The Slack MCP server provides tools for searching through Slack, retrieving and sending messages, managing canvases, managing users, uploading files, and working with lists. Each of these tools provides useful functionality for interacting with Slack; combine them for comprehensive integrations that grasp your team's context and history.
47: Searching throughout Slack​
48: The MCP server can search for a variety of information found throughout a Slack workspace:
49: Messages and files — filter by date, user, and content type. Retrieve metadata and content.
50: Users in a workspace — filter by name (with partial name matching), email, and user ID. Retrieve user details and statuses.
51: Private and public channels — filter by channel name and description. Retrieve channel metadata.
52: List user channels — list the channels you're a member of, filterable by type (public, private, DMs, group DMs), name prefix, and workspace. Supports pagination and can return full details, names only, or IDs only. Archived channels are included by default.
53: Emoji — returns the list of custom emoji available in the workspace.
54: Retrieving and sending messages​
55: The MCP server can retrieve and send messages throughout a Slack workspace:
56: Send messages — send messages to any type of conversation in Slack.
57: Schedule messages — schedule a message to be sent to a conversation at a future time.
58: Draft messages — draft, format, and preview messages directly within AI clients.
59: Read channels — grab the complete message history of channels.
60: Read threads — grab complete message thread conversations.
61: Create a conversation/channel — creates a new Slack channel, group DM, or IM conversation on behalf of the authenticated user.
62: Add reactions — adds an emoji reaction to a Slack message on behalf of the authenticated user.
63: Get reactions — retrieve the emoji reactions on a Slack message.
64: Managing canvases​
65: The MCP server can interact and modify Slack canvases:
66: Create/update a canvas — create and share rich, formatted documents.
67: Read a canvas — export canvases as markdown files.
68: Managing users​
69: Fetch user info — access complete user profile info, including custom profile fields and statuses.
70: List channel members — retrieve a list of user IDs for members of a given Slack channel or conversation.
71: Managing files​
72: Upload files — upload files to Slack via a two-step process. The file isn't visible until the second step completes.
73: Call the slack_get_file_upload_url tool to get a signed upload URL and file ID, then POST your file bytes to that URL.
74: Call the slack_complete_file_upload tool with the file ID to finalize it, optionally sharing the file to a channel with a message.
75: Working with lists​
76: The MCP server can work with Slack lists, which hold structured tabular data with typed columns (text, date, select, user, and more):
77: Create and read lists — create lists with custom schemas and read their contents.
78: Update lists and records — update list metadata and columns, and add or update individual records (rows). Columns are addressed by display name or internal key. Column types include select/multi_select with color-coded options.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Hosted JSON-RPC 2.0 Streamable HTTP endpoint at https://mcp.slack.com/mcp using confidential OAuth 2.0 (no SSE or DCR).
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
107: Transport protocol and endpoint​
108: Slack supports JSON-RPC 2.0 over Streamable HTTP. All requests should be sent to:
109: https://mcp.slack.com/mcp
110: We do not support SSE-based connections or Dynamic Client Registration at this time.
111: App Identity​
112: MCP clients must be backed by a registered Slack app with a fixed app ID and hardcode that app ID. This allows Slack to:
113: Let admins manage and approve your app/MCP client app using standard Slack app approval process.
114: Associate requests with your app for logging, rate limits, and access control.
115: Provide better support and visibility into usage.
116: If you're already using a Slack app for your integration, you can reuse it for MCP access.
117: Only directory-published apps or internal apps may use MCP.
118: Security concerns​
119: When using the Slack MCP server, please be mindful about connecting to or utilizing other MCP servers at the same time. Different servers may have their own security, stability, and usage characteristics, so think carefully before mixing them together. Use judgment when evaluating what to connect and share across environments. Using these clients means giving them access to your Slack data so you can use it as context while interacting with those apps.
120: Audit MCP activity with the associated audit logs.
121: Only apps published in the Slack Marketplace and internal apps can use MCP at this time; unlisted apps are prohibited from using MCP.
122: IP allowlist​
123: If your app has allowed IP address ranges configured, requests to the Slack MCP server are subject to the same restrictions. API calls originating from IP addresses not on your allowlist will be rejected. Ensure that the IP addresses your MCP client uses are included in your app's allowed list.
124: Authentication and Token Handling​
125: Slack supports confidential OAuth for MCP clients. You'll need to use your app's client_id and client_secret for Slack OAuth.
126: If your MCP client supports OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414) per MCP spec, you can rely on that. Users go through OAuth consent and authorize the app. You can initiate this OAuth request from your UX following standard MCP metadata discovery files:
127: https://mcp.slack.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
128: https://mcp.slack.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
129: OAuth URL and endpoints​
130: Authorization endpoint for Slack user tokens: https://slack.com/oauth/v2_user/authorize
131: Token endpoint for Slack user tokens: https://slack.com/api/oauth.v2.user.access (method docs here)
132: If you also want to generate bot tokens (for in-Slack experience), follow instructions here.

4: # Overview
5: > Use Clay from agents, terminals, backend services, internal tools, and custom apps.
6: Clay used to live primarily in the Clay UI. Now Clay also works where your agents, developers, and business systems already are.
7: Use the developer platform to search Clay's GTM data, run reusable Clay logic, read table data, and work with Audiences programmatically.
8: ## Start here
9: > [card] [Install the Clay plugin](https://developers.clay.com/quickstart.md#agent-plugin)
10: >
11: > Best for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and agent-first work. The plugin ships skills and the Clay CLI.
12: > [card] [Call the API directly](https://developers.clay.com/quickstart.md#api)
13: >
14: > Best for backend jobs, internal tools, custom apps, queues, and product workflows.
15: ## Core primitives
16: | Primitive | Use it for |
17: | - | - |
18: | [Searches](https://developers.clay.com/searches.md) | Find companies and people using Clay's GTM database |
19: | [Routines](https://developers.clay.com/routines.md) | Run Clay-managed functions, custom functions, and Workflows |
20: | [Tables (Enterprise)](https://developers.clay.com/tables.md) | Query existing Clay table data from known tables |
21: | [Audiences](https://developers.clay.com/audiences.md) | Work with records, saved segments, activities, and signal events |
22: | [Signals](https://developers.clay.com/signals.md) | Create triggers that detect relevant changes across records |
23: Start with the primitive that matches where your data lives and what you want to do.
24: ## Choose the right primitive
25: * Need a target list? Use [Searches](https://developers.clay.com/searches.md).
26: * Need enrichment, scoring, routing, or reusable logic? Use [Routines](https://developers.clay.com/routines.md).
27: * Need existing table data? Use [Tables](https://developers.clay.com/tables.md). Tables are Enterprise only.
28: * Need Audiences records, saved segments, activities, or signal events? Use [Audiences](https://developers.clay.com/audiences.md).
29: * Need triggers that watch records and produce signal events? Use [Signals](https://developers.clay.com/signals.md).
