4: # Authentication
5: > Authenticate requests with a Clay API key.
6: Every request to the Clay Public API must include a Clay API key in the `clay-api-key` header. Store your key in an environment variable and pass it in the header:
7: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
8: export CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY="your_api_key"
9: curl https://api.clay.com/public/v0/me \
10: -H "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY"
11: ```
12: API keys are tied to a Clay user and workspace access. Create one under [API and CLI → API keys](https://app.clay.com/workspaces/~/api-and-cli?tab=api-keys), with `clay api-keys create --name "<key name>"` in the CLI, or by asking your agent after installing the [agent plugin](https://developers.clay.com/quickstart.md#agent-plugin). Keep keys server-side and do not expose them in browser code, mobile apps, public repositories, logs, or analytics tools.
13: ## Header
14: | Header | Required | Description |
15: | - | - | - |
16: | `clay-api-key` | Yes | Personal API key for the Clay Public API. |
17: ## Failed authentication
18: Requests without a valid API key return a non-2xx response with the standard error shape:
19: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
20: {
21: "message": "Authentication failed"
22: }
23: ```

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: The JSON-first Clay CLI (`clay`) writes machine-readable JSON to stdout and authenticates per workspace via `clay login` (browser OAuth) or `clay login --device` for headless environments.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
4: # CLI basics
5: > Understand the Clay CLI output contract, exit codes, environment variables, and authentication.
6: The Clay CLI (`clay`) is JSON-first: every command writes machine-readable JSON to stdout on success and a structured error envelope to stderr on failure. There are no spinners, colors, or progress bars, so agents and scripts can branch on the output and exit code directly.
7: ## Output contract
8: | Result | Behavior |
9: | - | - |
10: | Success | JSON is written to stdout, exit code `0`. |
11: | Failure | `{ "error": { "code", "message", "details"? } }` is written to stderr, non-zero exit code. |
12: Pipe stdout straight into `jq`, and read the exit code (`$?`) to decide what to do next.
13: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
14: clay whoami | jq -r '.user.id'
15: ```
16: ## Exit codes
17: Branch on these from agents and scripts instead of parsing error text.
18: | Exit | Meaning |
19: | - | - |
20: | `0` | Success. |
21: | `1` | Generic or unrecoverable (`server_error`, `contract_mismatch`, `conflict`, `internal_error`, `invalid_config_file`). |
22: | `2` | `validation_error` — input was rejected as malformed. |
23: | `3` | `auth_required` \| `auth_invalid` \| `auth_forbidden` — run `clay login` to (re)authenticate. |
24: | `4` | `rate_limited` (HTTP 429) — `details` has `retryAfter` (seconds), plus `limit`/`remaining`/`reset` when Clay sends the `X-RateLimit-*` headers. |
25: | `5` | `network_error` \| `network_timeout` — could not reach Clay. |
26: | `6` | `not_found` (HTTP 404). |
27: ## Environment variables
28: | Variable | Purpose |
29: | - | - |
30: | `CLAY_CONFIG_HOME` | Highest-precedence config directory parent; `config.json` and the identity cache live under `<CLAY_CONFIG_HOME>/clay`. |
31: | `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | Used when `CLAY_CONFIG_HOME` is unset (`<XDG_CONFIG_HOME>/clay`), falling back to `~/.config/clay` when neither is set. |
32: | `CLAY_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` | Per-request network timeout in milliseconds (default `60000`). |
33: | `CLAY_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT_MS` | Bulk file-upload timeout in milliseconds (default `600000`). |
34: ## Authentication
35: `clay login` opens a browser to authorize the CLI with OAuth — this works from a human terminal or an agent's shell tool. Use `clay whoami` as the canonical check that authentication is working, and `clay logout` to clear a stored credential.
36: Each sign-in covers one workspace — the one you pick on the consent screen. To work across several, run `clay login` once per workspace: signing into a second keeps the first. `clay workspaces list` shows what you are signed into, `clay workspaces current` shows which one commands run against, and `clay workspaces switch <id>` switches. Signing in makes the workspace just added the active one, so switch back explicitly if you were working in another. `clay logout` signs out of the active workspace and leaves the rest.
37: On machines where a local browser can't open — SSH sessions, containers, headless machines — use `clay login --device` instead. It prints a link and a short code; open the link in a browser on any device to approve the sign-in, and the CLI completes automatically. Run `clay login --help` for details.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Routines API runs Clay-managed functions and custom functions via POST https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/{routine_id}/run and polls GET .../routines/run/{id}/results; Workflows are also routines and are in Alpha.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
4: # Routines API
5: > Run Clay-managed functions and custom functions through the Public API.
6: Routines are the programmable way to run Clay logic. Through the Public API, you can run Clay-managed functions and custom functions from backend services, queue workers, internal tools, and custom apps.
7: Use [Clay-managed functions](https://developers.clay.com/routines/clay-managed-functions.md) for common enrichment and research jobs. Use [custom functions](https://developers.clay.com/routines/custom-functions.md) for team-specific Clay logic built in the Clay UI.
8: ## Run a function routine
9: Custom function routine ids use the format `function:t_...`. To start a run, call `POST /routines/{routine_id}/run`.
10: Replace `function:t_abc123` and the input names with your function's routine id and inputs. Give each item an id you can use to match its result later.
11: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
12: ROUTINE_RUN_ID=$(curl --request POST \
13: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/function:t_abc123/run" \
14: --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
15: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY" \
16: --data '{
17: "items": [
18: {
19: "id": "row-1",
20: "inputs": {
21: "domain": "clay.com"
22: }
23: },
24: {
25: "id": "row-2",
26: "inputs": {
27: "domain": "example.com"
28: }
29: }
30: ]
31: }' | jq -r '.routine_run_id')
32: ```
33: ## Read the results
34: Use the returned `routine_run_id` to request the run's results:
35: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
36: curl --request GET \
37: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/run/$ROUTINE_RUN_ID/results" \
38: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY"
39: ```
40: While the run is processing, the endpoint returns **HTTP 202** with progress counters. There is no `data` array yet:
41: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
42: {
43: "routine_run_id": "run_xyz789",
44: "status": "in_progress",
45: "total": 2,
46: "finished": 1
47: }
48: ```
49: Repeat the GET request until it returns **HTTP 200** with `status: "complete"`. Use a delay between polls and a timeout appropriate for your application. For HTTP errors, follow the [error handling](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/errors.md) and [rate limit](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/rate-limits.md) guidance rather than continuing to poll unchanged.
50: Read individual results from **`data`**. Each item's `id` matches an id you supplied in the run request. Check each item's `status`: a completed run can contain failed items. For example, a function with a `company_name` output could return:
51: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
52: {
53: "routine_run_id": "run_xyz789",
54: "status": "complete",
55: "total": 2,
56: "finished": 2,
57: "data": [
58: {
59: "id": "row-1",
60: "status": "complete",
61: "result": {
62: "company_name": "Clay"
63: }
64: },
65: {
66: "id": "row-2",
67: "status": "failed",
68: "error": {
69: "message": "Provider request failed"
70: }
71: }
72: ]
73: }
74: ```
75: The keys inside `result` depend on your function's outputs. Use item ids to associate results with inputs rather than relying on response order. `finished` counts finished items, including failures; it is not a count of successful results.
76: ### Retrieve every page
77: A completed run's results can span multiple pages. If the response includes `cursor`, pass that value to the same endpoint to retrieve the next page:
78: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
79: NEXT_CURSOR="<cursor from the previous response>"
80: curl --get \
81: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/run/$ROUTINE_RUN_ID/results" \
82: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY" \
83: --data-urlencode "cursor=$NEXT_CURSOR" \
84: --data-urlencode "limit=20"
85: ```
86: Collect `data` from each page and continue with each returned cursor until `cursor` is omitted. Treat cursors as opaque values. `total` and `finished` describe the whole run, not the current page. See [pagination](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/pagination.md) for the general cursor pattern.
87: This polling flow applies to runs started with `/routines/{routine_id}/run`. Runs started through the batch API use the separate [batch results endpoint](https://developers.clay.com/routines/batch-runs.md).
88: ## Webhook notifications
89: The `run` and `run-batch/start` requests accept an optional `webhook_id`. Clay notifies that webhook when the run finishes, so your system can react without polling.
90: Run `clay webhooks --help` for webhook creation, testing, delivery payloads, and signature verification.
91: ## Batch run a function routine
92: For large input sets, create an upload URL, upload JSONL input, then start a batch run.
93: > [card] [Batch runs](https://developers.clay.com/routines/batch-runs.md)
94: >
95: > Learn how batch runs fit into Routines.
96: ## When to use Workflows
97: Workflows are also routines, but they are in Alpha and are built differently. Use Workflows when you want to build, edit, validate, run, inspect, or batch-run Clay logic from the plugin or CLI instead of building the logic in the Clay UI.
98: > [card] [Workflows (Alpha)](https://developers.clay.com/routines/workflows-alpha.md)
99: >
100: > Compare Workflows with functions.

4: # Quickstart
5: > Build with Clay from your coding agent, or call the Clay API from your own applications.
6: There are two ways to use Clay as a developer: install the agent plugin to build with Clay inside your coding agent, or call the Public API directly from your own applications and services.
7: ## Agent plugin
8: The agent plugin gives your coding agent Clay's skills and the `clay` CLI — the fastest way to build with Clay from a coding agent.
9: It requires a coding-agent host with a shell — Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor — and doesn't work in general-purpose chat apps like Claude Desktop, claude.ai, or ChatGPT that can't run the CLI.
10: Copy this into your agent of choice and let it install and set up the plugin for you:
11: ```
12: Set up the Clay plugin by following the steps in
13: https://github.com/clay-run/agent-plugins
14: ```
15: This runs the plugin's `cli-setup` skill, which puts `clay` on your PATH, signs you in, and verifies the CLI. Sign-in opens a browser to authorize the CLI.
16: > [card] [Agent plugin repository](https://github.com/clay-run/agent-plugins)
17: >
18: > Manual install and setup instructions for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.
19: ## API
20: Use the Public API to call Clay from your own applications and services — backend jobs, internal tools, queues, and product features. Requests authenticate with a Clay API key in the `clay-api-key` header.
21: > [card] [API reference](https://developers.clay.com/api-reference/me/get-the-authenticated-user.md)
22: >
23: > Endpoint paths, request bodies, response schemas, and an interactive try-it console.
24: ### Get an API key
25: You can create an API key three ways:
26: * Ask your agent to generate one for you after installing the [agent plugin](#agent-plugin).
27: * Run `clay api-keys create --name "<key name>"` with the `clay` CLI. The key is returned once, in the `apiKey` field.
28: * Create one yourself in Clay under [API and CLI → API keys](https://app.clay.com/workspaces/~/api-and-cli?tab=api-keys).
29: Keep keys server-side. Do not expose them in browser code, mobile apps, public repositories, logs, or analytics tools. See [Authentication](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/authentication.md) for details.

4: # Authentication
5: > Authenticate requests with a Clay API key.
6: Every request to the Clay Public API must include a Clay API key in the `clay-api-key` header. Store your key in an environment variable and pass it in the header:
7: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
8: export CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY="your_api_key"
9: curl https://api.clay.com/public/v0/me \
10: -H "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY"
11: ```
12: API keys are tied to a Clay user and workspace access. Create one under [API and CLI → API keys](https://app.clay.com/workspaces/~/api-and-cli?tab=api-keys), with `clay api-keys create --name "<key name>"` in the CLI, or by asking your agent after installing the [agent plugin](https://developers.clay.com/quickstart.md#agent-plugin). Keep keys server-side and do not expose them in browser code, mobile apps, public repositories, logs, or analytics tools.
13: ## Header
14: | Header | Required | Description |
15: | - | - | - |
16: | `clay-api-key` | Yes | Personal API key for the Clay Public API. |
17: ## Failed authentication
18: Requests without a valid API key return a non-2xx response with the standard error shape:
19: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
20: {
21: "message": "Authentication failed"
22: }
23: ```

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
4: # Rate limits
5: > Understand Clay Public API rate limits and how to handle 429 responses.
6: The Clay Public API enforces per-workspace request rate limits. When you exceed a limit, Clay returns HTTP `429` and you should back off before retrying.
7: ## Limits
8: The default limit is **300 requests per minute per workspace** (about 5 requests per second), shared across all API keys and OAuth credentials in the workspace.
9: Spread requests evenly over time. Sending many requests at once can return `429` even when you're under the per-minute total.
10: Some endpoints, such as `POST /workflows/runs/query`, also have their own per-endpoint limits.
11: Limits may differ for specific workspaces. Contact Clay if you need higher limits.
12: ## Reading the limit
13: When a request is rate limited, Clay returns `429` with a `Retry-After` header (seconds to wait). When available, Clay also sends `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, and `X-RateLimit-Reset` so you can pace requests before you hit the ceiling.
14: The CLI surfaces the same signal: rate-limited commands exit with code `4`, and the error `details` include `retryAfter` (seconds), plus `limit`, `remaining`, and `reset` when Clay sends the `X-RateLimit-*` headers.
15: ## Recommended handling

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: The JSON-first Clay CLI (`clay`) writes machine-readable JSON to stdout and authenticates per workspace via `clay login` (browser OAuth) or `clay login --device` for headless environments.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
4: # CLI basics
5: > Understand the Clay CLI output contract, exit codes, environment variables, and authentication.
6: The Clay CLI (`clay`) is JSON-first: every command writes machine-readable JSON to stdout on success and a structured error envelope to stderr on failure. There are no spinners, colors, or progress bars, so agents and scripts can branch on the output and exit code directly.
7: ## Output contract
8: | Result | Behavior |
9: | - | - |
10: | Success | JSON is written to stdout, exit code `0`. |
11: | Failure | `{ "error": { "code", "message", "details"? } }` is written to stderr, non-zero exit code. |
12: Pipe stdout straight into `jq`, and read the exit code (`$?`) to decide what to do next.
13: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
14: clay whoami | jq -r '.user.id'
15: ```
16: ## Exit codes
17: Branch on these from agents and scripts instead of parsing error text.
18: | Exit | Meaning |
19: | - | - |
20: | `0` | Success. |
21: | `1` | Generic or unrecoverable (`server_error`, `contract_mismatch`, `conflict`, `internal_error`, `invalid_config_file`). |
22: | `2` | `validation_error` — input was rejected as malformed. |
23: | `3` | `auth_required` \| `auth_invalid` \| `auth_forbidden` — run `clay login` to (re)authenticate. |
24: | `4` | `rate_limited` (HTTP 429) — `details` has `retryAfter` (seconds), plus `limit`/`remaining`/`reset` when Clay sends the `X-RateLimit-*` headers. |
25: | `5` | `network_error` \| `network_timeout` — could not reach Clay. |
26: | `6` | `not_found` (HTTP 404). |
27: ## Environment variables
28: | Variable | Purpose |
29: | - | - |
30: | `CLAY_CONFIG_HOME` | Highest-precedence config directory parent; `config.json` and the identity cache live under `<CLAY_CONFIG_HOME>/clay`. |
31: | `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | Used when `CLAY_CONFIG_HOME` is unset (`<XDG_CONFIG_HOME>/clay`), falling back to `~/.config/clay` when neither is set. |
32: | `CLAY_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` | Per-request network timeout in milliseconds (default `60000`). |
33: | `CLAY_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT_MS` | Bulk file-upload timeout in milliseconds (default `600000`). |
34: ## Authentication
35: `clay login` opens a browser to authorize the CLI with OAuth — this works from a human terminal or an agent's shell tool. Use `clay whoami` as the canonical check that authentication is working, and `clay logout` to clear a stored credential.
36: Each sign-in covers one workspace — the one you pick on the consent screen. To work across several, run `clay login` once per workspace: signing into a second keeps the first. `clay workspaces list` shows what you are signed into, `clay workspaces current` shows which one commands run against, and `clay workspaces switch <id>` switches. Signing in makes the workspace just added the active one, so switch back explicitly if you were working in another. `clay logout` signs out of the active workspace and leaves the rest.
37: On machines where a local browser can't open — SSH sessions, containers, headless machines — use `clay login --device` instead. It prints a link and a short code; open the link in a browser on any device to approve the sign-in, and the CLI completes automatically. Run `clay login --help` for details.

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
17: ## Result limits
18: Clay caps how many search results a workspace can return through the API. These limits apply to results returned across the CLI and Public API, and they scale with your plan.
19: | Plan | Results per request | Results per search | Results per period | Reset date |
20: | - | - | - | - | - |
21: | Free | 50 | 50 | 100 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
22: | Trial | 50 | 50 | 10,000 for trial duration | Not applicable |
23: | Paid | 500 | Up to your period limit | 1,000,000 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
24: | Legacy paid (Starter, Explorer, Pro) | 500 | Up to your period limit | 1,000,000 per year | January 1 (UTC) |
25: | Enterprise | 500 | Up to your period limit | 10,000,000 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
26: * **Per request** is the largest limit you can request in a single call.
27: * **Per search** is the total results you can fetch across all pages of one `search_id`.
28: * **Reset date** is when the period limit resets. For rolling windows, usage ages out of the window daily at midnight UTC rather than resetting on a fixed calendar date.
29: Legacy Starter, Explorer, and Pro plans keep the yearly period limit. Legacy Enterprise plans use the Enterprise row. Moving to a current paid plan or Enterprise is what switches a workspace to the rolling 30-day limit.
30: When you exceed a limit, Clay returns HTTP `402` with a message naming the limit you hit. Period-limit errors also state when the limit resets. Malformed filters or other invalid input still return HTTP `400`. To increase a limit, paid customers can contact Clay Support; Enterprise customers should contact their assigned Clay GTME.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Searches API/CLI result limits scale by plan: Free (50 per request/search, 100 per 30 days), Trial (50 per request/search, 10,000 for trial), Paid (500 per request, 1,000,000 per 30 days), and Enterprise (500 per request, 10,000,000 per 30 days).
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
17: ## Result limits
18: Clay caps how many search results a workspace can return through the API. These limits apply to results returned across the CLI and Public API, and they scale with your plan.
19: | Plan | Results per request | Results per search | Results per period | Reset date |
20: | - | - | - | - | - |
21: | Free | 50 | 50 | 100 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
22: | Trial | 50 | 50 | 10,000 for trial duration | Not applicable |
23: | Paid | 500 | Up to your period limit | 1,000,000 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
24: | Legacy paid (Starter, Explorer, Pro) | 500 | Up to your period limit | 1,000,000 per year | January 1 (UTC) |
25: | Enterprise | 500 | Up to your period limit | 10,000,000 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
26: * **Per request** is the largest limit you can request in a single call.
27: * **Per search** is the total results you can fetch across all pages of one `search_id`.
28: * **Reset date** is when the period limit resets. For rolling windows, usage ages out of the window daily at midnight UTC rather than resetting on a fixed calendar date.
29: Legacy Starter, Explorer, and Pro plans keep the yearly period limit. Legacy Enterprise plans use the Enterprise row. Moving to a current paid plan or Enterprise is what switches a workspace to the rolling 30-day limit.
30: When you exceed a limit, Clay returns HTTP `402` with a message naming the limit you hit. Period-limit errors also state when the limit resets. Malformed filters or other invalid input still return HTTP `400`. To increase a limit, paid customers can contact Clay Support; Enterprise customers should contact their assigned Clay GTME.

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
4: # Quickstart
5: > Build with Clay from your coding agent, or call the Clay API from your own applications.
6: There are two ways to use Clay as a developer: install the agent plugin to build with Clay inside your coding agent, or call the Public API directly from your own applications and services.
7: ## Agent plugin
8: The agent plugin gives your coding agent Clay's skills and the `clay` CLI — the fastest way to build with Clay from a coding agent.
9: It requires a coding-agent host with a shell — Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor — and doesn't work in general-purpose chat apps like Claude Desktop, claude.ai, or ChatGPT that can't run the CLI.
10: Copy this into your agent of choice and let it install and set up the plugin for you:
11: ```
12: Set up the Clay plugin by following the steps in
13: https://github.com/clay-run/agent-plugins
14: ```
15: This runs the plugin's `cli-setup` skill, which puts `clay` on your PATH, signs you in, and verifies the CLI. Sign-in opens a browser to authorize the CLI.
16: > [card] [Agent plugin repository](https://github.com/clay-run/agent-plugins)
17: >
18: > Manual install and setup instructions for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.
19: ## API
20: Use the Public API to call Clay from your own applications and services — backend jobs, internal tools, queues, and product features. Requests authenticate with a Clay API key in the `clay-api-key` header.
21: > [card] [API reference](https://developers.clay.com/api-reference/me/get-the-authenticated-user.md)
22: >
23: > Endpoint paths, request bodies, response schemas, and an interactive try-it console.
24: ### Get an API key
25: You can create an API key three ways:
26: * Ask your agent to generate one for you after installing the [agent plugin](#agent-plugin).
27: * Run `clay api-keys create --name "<key name>"` with the `clay` CLI. The key is returned once, in the `apiKey` field.
28: * Create one yourself in Clay under [API and CLI → API keys](https://app.clay.com/workspaces/~/api-and-cli?tab=api-keys).
29: Keep keys server-side. Do not expose them in browser code, mobile apps, public repositories, logs, or analytics tools. See [Authentication](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/authentication.md) for details.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Routines API runs Clay-managed functions and custom functions via POST https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/{routine_id}/run and polls GET .../routines/run/{id}/results; Workflows are also routines and are in Alpha.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
4: # Routines API
5: > Run Clay-managed functions and custom functions through the Public API.
6: Routines are the programmable way to run Clay logic. Through the Public API, you can run Clay-managed functions and custom functions from backend services, queue workers, internal tools, and custom apps.
7: Use [Clay-managed functions](https://developers.clay.com/routines/clay-managed-functions.md) for common enrichment and research jobs. Use [custom functions](https://developers.clay.com/routines/custom-functions.md) for team-specific Clay logic built in the Clay UI.
8: ## Run a function routine
9: Custom function routine ids use the format `function:t_...`. To start a run, call `POST /routines/{routine_id}/run`.
10: Replace `function:t_abc123` and the input names with your function's routine id and inputs. Give each item an id you can use to match its result later.
11: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
12: ROUTINE_RUN_ID=$(curl --request POST \
13: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/function:t_abc123/run" \
14: --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
15: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY" \
16: --data '{
17: "items": [
18: {
19: "id": "row-1",
20: "inputs": {
21: "domain": "clay.com"
22: }
23: },
24: {
25: "id": "row-2",
26: "inputs": {
27: "domain": "example.com"
28: }
29: }
30: ]
31: }' | jq -r '.routine_run_id')
32: ```
33: ## Read the results
34: Use the returned `routine_run_id` to request the run's results:
35: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
36: curl --request GET \
37: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/run/$ROUTINE_RUN_ID/results" \
38: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY"
39: ```
40: While the run is processing, the endpoint returns **HTTP 202** with progress counters. There is no `data` array yet:
41: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
42: {
43: "routine_run_id": "run_xyz789",
44: "status": "in_progress",
45: "total": 2,
46: "finished": 1
47: }
48: ```
49: Repeat the GET request until it returns **HTTP 200** with `status: "complete"`. Use a delay between polls and a timeout appropriate for your application. For HTTP errors, follow the [error handling](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/errors.md) and [rate limit](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/rate-limits.md) guidance rather than continuing to poll unchanged.
50: Read individual results from **`data`**. Each item's `id` matches an id you supplied in the run request. Check each item's `status`: a completed run can contain failed items. For example, a function with a `company_name` output could return:
51: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
52: {
53: "routine_run_id": "run_xyz789",
54: "status": "complete",
55: "total": 2,
56: "finished": 2,
57: "data": [
58: {
59: "id": "row-1",
60: "status": "complete",
61: "result": {
62: "company_name": "Clay"
63: }
64: },
65: {
66: "id": "row-2",
67: "status": "failed",
68: "error": {
69: "message": "Provider request failed"
70: }
71: }
72: ]
73: }
74: ```
75: The keys inside `result` depend on your function's outputs. Use item ids to associate results with inputs rather than relying on response order. `finished` counts finished items, including failures; it is not a count of successful results.
76: ### Retrieve every page
77: A completed run's results can span multiple pages. If the response includes `cursor`, pass that value to the same endpoint to retrieve the next page:
78: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
79: NEXT_CURSOR="<cursor from the previous response>"
80: curl --get \
81: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/run/$ROUTINE_RUN_ID/results" \
82: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY" \
83: --data-urlencode "cursor=$NEXT_CURSOR" \
84: --data-urlencode "limit=20"
85: ```
86: Collect `data` from each page and continue with each returned cursor until `cursor` is omitted. Treat cursors as opaque values. `total` and `finished` describe the whole run, not the current page. See [pagination](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/pagination.md) for the general cursor pattern.
87: This polling flow applies to runs started with `/routines/{routine_id}/run`. Runs started through the batch API use the separate [batch results endpoint](https://developers.clay.com/routines/batch-runs.md).
88: ## Webhook notifications
89: The `run` and `run-batch/start` requests accept an optional `webhook_id`. Clay notifies that webhook when the run finishes, so your system can react without polling.
90: Run `clay webhooks --help` for webhook creation, testing, delivery payloads, and signature verification.
91: ## Batch run a function routine
92: For large input sets, create an upload URL, upload JSONL input, then start a batch run.
93: > [card] [Batch runs](https://developers.clay.com/routines/batch-runs.md)
94: >
95: > Learn how batch runs fit into Routines.
96: ## When to use Workflows
97: Workflows are also routines, but they are in Alpha and are built differently. Use Workflows when you want to build, edit, validate, run, inspect, or batch-run Clay logic from the plugin or CLI instead of building the logic in the Clay UI.
98: > [card] [Workflows (Alpha)](https://developers.clay.com/routines/workflows-alpha.md)
99: >
100: > Compare Workflows with functions.

4: # Quickstart
5: > Build with Clay from your coding agent, or call the Clay API from your own applications.
6: There are two ways to use Clay as a developer: install the agent plugin to build with Clay inside your coding agent, or call the Public API directly from your own applications and services.
7: ## Agent plugin
8: The agent plugin gives your coding agent Clay's skills and the `clay` CLI — the fastest way to build with Clay from a coding agent.
9: It requires a coding-agent host with a shell — Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor — and doesn't work in general-purpose chat apps like Claude Desktop, claude.ai, or ChatGPT that can't run the CLI.
10: Copy this into your agent of choice and let it install and set up the plugin for you:
11: ```
12: Set up the Clay plugin by following the steps in
13: https://github.com/clay-run/agent-plugins
14: ```
15: This runs the plugin's `cli-setup` skill, which puts `clay` on your PATH, signs you in, and verifies the CLI. Sign-in opens a browser to authorize the CLI.
16: > [card] [Agent plugin repository](https://github.com/clay-run/agent-plugins)
17: >
18: > Manual install and setup instructions for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.
19: ## API
20: Use the Public API to call Clay from your own applications and services — backend jobs, internal tools, queues, and product features. Requests authenticate with a Clay API key in the `clay-api-key` header.
21: > [card] [API reference](https://developers.clay.com/api-reference/me/get-the-authenticated-user.md)
22: >
23: > Endpoint paths, request bodies, response schemas, and an interactive try-it console.
24: ### Get an API key
25: You can create an API key three ways:
26: * Ask your agent to generate one for you after installing the [agent plugin](#agent-plugin).
27: * Run `clay api-keys create --name "<key name>"` with the `clay` CLI. The key is returned once, in the `apiKey` field.
28: * Create one yourself in Clay under [API and CLI → API keys](https://app.clay.com/workspaces/~/api-and-cli?tab=api-keys).
29: Keep keys server-side. Do not expose them in browser code, mobile apps, public repositories, logs, or analytics tools. See [Authentication](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/authentication.md) for details.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: The JSON-first Clay CLI (`clay`) writes machine-readable JSON to stdout and authenticates per workspace via `clay login` (browser OAuth) or `clay login --device` for headless environments.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
4: # CLI basics
5: > Understand the Clay CLI output contract, exit codes, environment variables, and authentication.
6: The Clay CLI (`clay`) is JSON-first: every command writes machine-readable JSON to stdout on success and a structured error envelope to stderr on failure. There are no spinners, colors, or progress bars, so agents and scripts can branch on the output and exit code directly.
7: ## Output contract
8: | Result | Behavior |
9: | - | - |
10: | Success | JSON is written to stdout, exit code `0`. |
11: | Failure | `{ "error": { "code", "message", "details"? } }` is written to stderr, non-zero exit code. |
12: Pipe stdout straight into `jq`, and read the exit code (`$?`) to decide what to do next.
13: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
14: clay whoami | jq -r '.user.id'
15: ```
16: ## Exit codes
17: Branch on these from agents and scripts instead of parsing error text.
18: | Exit | Meaning |
19: | - | - |
20: | `0` | Success. |
21: | `1` | Generic or unrecoverable (`server_error`, `contract_mismatch`, `conflict`, `internal_error`, `invalid_config_file`). |
22: | `2` | `validation_error` — input was rejected as malformed. |
23: | `3` | `auth_required` \| `auth_invalid` \| `auth_forbidden` — run `clay login` to (re)authenticate. |
24: | `4` | `rate_limited` (HTTP 429) — `details` has `retryAfter` (seconds), plus `limit`/`remaining`/`reset` when Clay sends the `X-RateLimit-*` headers. |
25: | `5` | `network_error` \| `network_timeout` — could not reach Clay. |
26: | `6` | `not_found` (HTTP 404). |
27: ## Environment variables
28: | Variable | Purpose |
29: | - | - |
30: | `CLAY_CONFIG_HOME` | Highest-precedence config directory parent; `config.json` and the identity cache live under `<CLAY_CONFIG_HOME>/clay`. |
31: | `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | Used when `CLAY_CONFIG_HOME` is unset (`<XDG_CONFIG_HOME>/clay`), falling back to `~/.config/clay` when neither is set. |
32: | `CLAY_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` | Per-request network timeout in milliseconds (default `60000`). |
33: | `CLAY_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT_MS` | Bulk file-upload timeout in milliseconds (default `600000`). |
34: ## Authentication
35: `clay login` opens a browser to authorize the CLI with OAuth — this works from a human terminal or an agent's shell tool. Use `clay whoami` as the canonical check that authentication is working, and `clay logout` to clear a stored credential.
36: Each sign-in covers one workspace — the one you pick on the consent screen. To work across several, run `clay login` once per workspace: signing into a second keeps the first. `clay workspaces list` shows what you are signed into, `clay workspaces current` shows which one commands run against, and `clay workspaces switch <id>` switches. Signing in makes the workspace just added the active one, so switch back explicitly if you were working in another. `clay logout` signs out of the active workspace and leaves the rest.
37: On machines where a local browser can't open — SSH sessions, containers, headless machines — use `clay login --device` instead. It prints a link and a short code; open the link in a browser on any device to approve the sign-in, and the CLI completes automatically. Run `clay login --help` for details.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Searches API/CLI result limits scale by plan: Free (50 per request/search, 100 per 30 days), Trial (50 per request/search, 10,000 for trial), Paid (500 per request, 1,000,000 per 30 days), and Enterprise (500 per request, 10,000,000 per 30 days).
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
17: ## Result limits
18: Clay caps how many search results a workspace can return through the API. These limits apply to results returned across the CLI and Public API, and they scale with your plan.
19: | Plan | Results per request | Results per search | Results per period | Reset date |
20: | - | - | - | - | - |
21: | Free | 50 | 50 | 100 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
22: | Trial | 50 | 50 | 10,000 for trial duration | Not applicable |
23: | Paid | 500 | Up to your period limit | 1,000,000 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
24: | Legacy paid (Starter, Explorer, Pro) | 500 | Up to your period limit | 1,000,000 per year | January 1 (UTC) |
25: | Enterprise | 500 | Up to your period limit | 10,000,000 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
26: * **Per request** is the largest limit you can request in a single call.
27: * **Per search** is the total results you can fetch across all pages of one `search_id`.
28: * **Reset date** is when the period limit resets. For rolling windows, usage ages out of the window daily at midnight UTC rather than resetting on a fixed calendar date.
29: Legacy Starter, Explorer, and Pro plans keep the yearly period limit. Legacy Enterprise plans use the Enterprise row. Moving to a current paid plan or Enterprise is what switches a workspace to the rolling 30-day limit.

4: # Routines API
5: > Run Clay-managed functions and custom functions through the Public API.
6: Routines are the programmable way to run Clay logic. Through the Public API, you can run Clay-managed functions and custom functions from backend services, queue workers, internal tools, and custom apps.
7: Use [Clay-managed functions](https://developers.clay.com/routines/clay-managed-functions.md) for common enrichment and research jobs. Use [custom functions](https://developers.clay.com/routines/custom-functions.md) for team-specific Clay logic built in the Clay UI.
8: ## Run a function routine
9: Custom function routine ids use the format `function:t_...`. To start a run, call `POST /routines/{routine_id}/run`.
10: Replace `function:t_abc123` and the input names with your function's routine id and inputs. Give each item an id you can use to match its result later.
11: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
12: ROUTINE_RUN_ID=$(curl --request POST \
13: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/function:t_abc123/run" \
14: --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
15: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY" \
16: --data '{
17: "items": [
18: {
19: "id": "row-1",
20: "inputs": {
21: "domain": "clay.com"
22: }
23: },
24: {
25: "id": "row-2",
26: "inputs": {
27: "domain": "example.com"
28: }
29: }
30: ]
31: }' | jq -r '.routine_run_id')
32: ```
33: ## Read the results
34: Use the returned `routine_run_id` to request the run's results:
35: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
36: curl --request GET \
37: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/run/$ROUTINE_RUN_ID/results" \
38: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY"
39: ```
40: While the run is processing, the endpoint returns **HTTP 202** with progress counters. There is no `data` array yet:
41: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
42: {
43: "routine_run_id": "run_xyz789",
44: "status": "in_progress",
45: "total": 2,
46: "finished": 1
47: }
48: ```
49: Repeat the GET request until it returns **HTTP 200** with `status: "complete"`. Use a delay between polls and a timeout appropriate for your application. For HTTP errors, follow the [error handling](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/errors.md) and [rate limit](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/rate-limits.md) guidance rather than continuing to poll unchanged.
50: Read individual results from **`data`**. Each item's `id` matches an id you supplied in the run request. Check each item's `status`: a completed run can contain failed items. For example, a function with a `company_name` output could return:
51: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
52: {
53: "routine_run_id": "run_xyz789",
54: "status": "complete",
55: "total": 2,
56: "finished": 2,
57: "data": [
58: {
59: "id": "row-1",
60: "status": "complete",
61: "result": {
62: "company_name": "Clay"
63: }
64: },
65: {
66: "id": "row-2",
67: "status": "failed",
68: "error": {
69: "message": "Provider request failed"
70: }
71: }
72: ]
73: }
74: ```
75: The keys inside `result` depend on your function's outputs. Use item ids to associate results with inputs rather than relying on response order. `finished` counts finished items, including failures; it is not a count of successful results.
76: ### Retrieve every page
77: A completed run's results can span multiple pages. If the response includes `cursor`, pass that value to the same endpoint to retrieve the next page:
78: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
79: NEXT_CURSOR="<cursor from the previous response>"
80: curl --get \
81: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/run/$ROUTINE_RUN_ID/results" \
82: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY" \
83: --data-urlencode "cursor=$NEXT_CURSOR" \
84: --data-urlencode "limit=20"
85: ```
86: Collect `data` from each page and continue with each returned cursor until `cursor` is omitted. Treat cursors as opaque values. `total` and `finished` describe the whole run, not the current page. See [pagination](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/pagination.md) for the general cursor pattern.
87: This polling flow applies to runs started with `/routines/{routine_id}/run`. Runs started through the batch API use the separate [batch results endpoint](https://developers.clay.com/routines/batch-runs.md).
88: ## Webhook notifications
89: The `run` and `run-batch/start` requests accept an optional `webhook_id`. Clay notifies that webhook when the run finishes, so your system can react without polling.
90: Run `clay webhooks --help` for webhook creation, testing, delivery payloads, and signature verification.
91: ## Batch run a function routine
92: For large input sets, create an upload URL, upload JSONL input, then start a batch run.
93: > [card] [Batch runs](https://developers.clay.com/routines/batch-runs.md)
94: >
95: > Learn how batch runs fit into Routines.
96: ## When to use Workflows
97: Workflows are also routines, but they are in Alpha and are built differently. Use Workflows when you want to build, edit, validate, run, inspect, or batch-run Clay logic from the plugin or CLI instead of building the logic in the Clay UI.

99: >
100: > Compare Workflows with functions.

25: 3. Open **Details**.
26: 4. Enable the integrations you need, such as **API** or **MCP**.
27: 5. Copy the `t_...` function id.
28: 6. Prefix it with `function:` when you call it from the plugin, CLI, MCP, or API.
29: Custom function routine ids use the format `function:t_...`.
30: Each access setting enables a separate way to call the function:
31: | How you call the function | Access to enable |
32: | - | - |
33: | Public API, `clay` CLI, or an agent using the CLI | API access |
34: | Clay's MCP connector | MCP access |
35: | As a routine in a Claygent | Claygent access |
36: An agent can use either the CLI or MCP, so choose access based on its connection. Enabling one does not enable the others. Workspace and role permissions still apply.
37: ## Access a published function through MCP
38: Publishing a function does not automatically enable MCP access. Enable MCP access in the function's settings before calling it through an MCP client. API access alone is not sufficient.
39: Call `list_subroutines` to find functions available to the connected MCP client. Use the returned `id` as `subroutine_id` when running a function through MCP.
40: ### A published function is missing or cannot run by id
41: MCP access is required both to list a function and to run it by id. Supplying a known id does not bypass that requirement.
42: If a function is missing from `list_subroutines` or a run returns a not-found error:
43: 1. Confirm the MCP client is connected to the workspace that contains the function.
44: 2. Check that MCP access is enabled in the function's settings.
45: 3. If access cannot be changed, ask a workspace admin to check the integration and role access settings.
46: 4. Call `list_subroutines` again and use an id returned by that call.
47: A not-found error does not distinguish a nonexistent function from one unavailable to the connected client.

4: # Authentication
5: > Authenticate requests with a Clay API key.
6: Every request to the Clay Public API must include a Clay API key in the `clay-api-key` header. Store your key in an environment variable and pass it in the header:
7: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
8: export CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY="your_api_key"
9: curl https://api.clay.com/public/v0/me \
10: -H "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY"
11: ```
12: API keys are tied to a Clay user and workspace access. Create one under [API and CLI → API keys](https://app.clay.com/workspaces/~/api-and-cli?tab=api-keys), with `clay api-keys create --name "<key name>"` in the CLI, or by asking your agent after installing the [agent plugin](https://developers.clay.com/quickstart.md#agent-plugin). Keep keys server-side and do not expose them in browser code, mobile apps, public repositories, logs, or analytics tools.
13: ## Header
14: | Header | Required | Description |
15: | - | - | - |
16: | `clay-api-key` | Yes | Personal API key for the Clay Public API. |
17: ## Failed authentication
18: Requests without a valid API key return a non-2xx response with the standard error shape:
19: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
20: {
21: "message": "Authentication failed"
22: }
23: ```

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Searches API/CLI result limits scale by plan: Free (50 per request/search, 100 per 30 days), Trial (50 per request/search, 10,000 for trial), Paid (500 per request, 1,000,000 per 30 days), and Enterprise (500 per request, 10,000,000 per 30 days).
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
17: ## Result limits
18: Clay caps how many search results a workspace can return through the API. These limits apply to results returned across the CLI and Public API, and they scale with your plan.
19: | Plan | Results per request | Results per search | Results per period | Reset date |
20: | - | - | - | - | - |
21: | Free | 50 | 50 | 100 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
22: | Trial | 50 | 50 | 10,000 for trial duration | Not applicable |
23: | Paid | 500 | Up to your period limit | 1,000,000 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
24: | Legacy paid (Starter, Explorer, Pro) | 500 | Up to your period limit | 1,000,000 per year | January 1 (UTC) |
25: | Enterprise | 500 | Up to your period limit | 10,000,000 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
26: * **Per request** is the largest limit you can request in a single call.
27: * **Per search** is the total results you can fetch across all pages of one `search_id`.
28: * **Reset date** is when the period limit resets. For rolling windows, usage ages out of the window daily at midnight UTC rather than resetting on a fixed calendar date.
29: Legacy Starter, Explorer, and Pro plans keep the yearly period limit. Legacy Enterprise plans use the Enterprise row. Moving to a current paid plan or Enterprise is what switches a workspace to the rolling 30-day limit.
30: When you exceed a limit, Clay returns HTTP `402` with a message naming the limit you hit. Period-limit errors also state when the limit resets. Malformed filters or other invalid input still return HTTP `400`. To increase a limit, paid customers can contact Clay Support; Enterprise customers should contact their assigned Clay GTME.

4: # Routines API
5: > Run Clay-managed functions and custom functions through the Public API.
6: Routines are the programmable way to run Clay logic. Through the Public API, you can run Clay-managed functions and custom functions from backend services, queue workers, internal tools, and custom apps.
7: Use [Clay-managed functions](https://developers.clay.com/routines/clay-managed-functions.md) for common enrichment and research jobs. Use [custom functions](https://developers.clay.com/routines/custom-functions.md) for team-specific Clay logic built in the Clay UI.
8: ## Run a function routine
9: Custom function routine ids use the format `function:t_...`. To start a run, call `POST /routines/{routine_id}/run`.
10: Replace `function:t_abc123` and the input names with your function's routine id and inputs. Give each item an id you can use to match its result later.

14: --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
15: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY" \
16: --data '{
17: "items": [
18: {
19: "id": "row-1",
20: "inputs": {
21: "domain": "clay.com"
22: }
23: },
24: {
25: "id": "row-2",

29: }
30: ]
31: }' | jq -r '.routine_run_id')
32: ```
33: ## Read the results
34: Use the returned `routine_run_id` to request the run's results:
35: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
36: curl --request GET \
37: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/run/$ROUTINE_RUN_ID/results" \
38: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY"
39: ```
40: While the run is processing, the endpoint returns **HTTP 202** with progress counters. There is no `data` array yet:
41: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
42: {
43: "routine_run_id": "run_xyz789",
44: "status": "in_progress",
45: "total": 2,
46: "finished": 1
47: }
48: ```
49: Repeat the GET request until it returns **HTTP 200** with `status: "complete"`. Use a delay between polls and a timeout appropriate for your application. For HTTP errors, follow the [error handling](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/errors.md) and [rate limit](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/rate-limits.md) guidance rather than continuing to poll unchanged.
50: Read individual results from **`data`**. Each item's `id` matches an id you supplied in the run request. Check each item's `status`: a completed run can contain failed items. For example, a function with a `company_name` output could return:
51: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
52: {
53: "routine_run_id": "run_xyz789",
54: "status": "complete",
55: "total": 2,
56: "finished": 2,
57: "data": [
58: {
59: "id": "row-1",
60: "status": "complete",
61: "result": {
62: "company_name": "Clay"
63: }
64: },
65: {
66: "id": "row-2",
67: "status": "failed",
68: "error": {
69: "message": "Provider request failed"
70: }
71: }
72: ]
73: }
74: ```
75: The keys inside `result` depend on your function's outputs. Use item ids to associate results with inputs rather than relying on response order. `finished` counts finished items, including failures; it is not a count of successful results.
76: ### Retrieve every page
77: A completed run's results can span multiple pages. If the response includes `cursor`, pass that value to the same endpoint to retrieve the next page:
78: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
79: NEXT_CURSOR="<cursor from the previous response>"
80: curl --get \
81: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/run/$ROUTINE_RUN_ID/results" \
82: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY" \
83: --data-urlencode "cursor=$NEXT_CURSOR" \
84: --data-urlencode "limit=20"
85: ```
86: Collect `data` from each page and continue with each returned cursor until `cursor` is omitted. Treat cursors as opaque values. `total` and `finished` describe the whole run, not the current page. See [pagination](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/pagination.md) for the general cursor pattern.
87: This polling flow applies to runs started with `/routines/{routine_id}/run`. Runs started through the batch API use the separate [batch results endpoint](https://developers.clay.com/routines/batch-runs.md).
88: ## Webhook notifications
89: The `run` and `run-batch/start` requests accept an optional `webhook_id`. Clay notifies that webhook when the run finishes, so your system can react without polling.
90: Run `clay webhooks --help` for webhook creation, testing, delivery payloads, and signature verification.
91: ## Batch run a function routine
92: For large input sets, create an upload URL, upload JSONL input, then start a batch run.
93: > [card] [Batch runs](https://developers.clay.com/routines/batch-runs.md)
94: >
95: > Learn how batch runs fit into Routines.
96: ## When to use Workflows
97: Workflows are also routines, but they are in Alpha and are built differently. Use Workflows when you want to build, edit, validate, run, inspect, or batch-run Clay logic from the plugin or CLI instead of building the logic in the Clay UI.
98: > [card] [Workflows (Alpha)](https://developers.clay.com/routines/workflows-alpha.md)
99: >
100: > Compare Workflows with functions.

21: ## Expose a function
22: To call a custom function:
23: 1. Open [Functions](https://app.clay.com/functions).
24: 2. Create or select a function.
25: 3. Open **Details**.
26: 4. Enable the integrations you need, such as **API** or **MCP**.
27: 5. Copy the `t_...` function id.
28: 6. Prefix it with `function:` when you call it from the plugin, CLI, MCP, or API.
29: Custom function routine ids use the format `function:t_...`.
30: Each access setting enables a separate way to call the function:
31: | How you call the function | Access to enable |
32: | - | - |
33: | Public API, `clay` CLI, or an agent using the CLI | API access |
34: | Clay's MCP connector | MCP access |
35: | As a routine in a Claygent | Claygent access |
36: An agent can use either the CLI or MCP, so choose access based on its connection. Enabling one does not enable the others. Workspace and role permissions still apply.
37: ## Access a published function through MCP
38: Publishing a function does not automatically enable MCP access. Enable MCP access in the function's settings before calling it through an MCP client. API access alone is not sufficient.
39: Call `list_subroutines` to find functions available to the connected MCP client. Use the returned `id` as `subroutine_id` when running a function through MCP.
40: ### A published function is missing or cannot run by id
41: MCP access is required both to list a function and to run it by id. Supplying a known id does not bypass that requirement.
42: If a function is missing from `list_subroutines` or a run returns a not-found error:
43: 1. Confirm the MCP client is connected to the workspace that contains the function.
44: 2. Check that MCP access is enabled in the function's settings.
45: 3. If access cannot be changed, ask a workspace admin to check the integration and role access settings.
46: 4. Call `list_subroutines` again and use an id returned by that call.
47: A not-found error does not distinguish a nonexistent function from one unavailable to the connected client.

39: Call `list_subroutines` to find functions available to the connected MCP client. Use the returned `id` as `subroutine_id` when running a function through MCP.
40: ### A published function is missing or cannot run by id
41: MCP access is required both to list a function and to run it by id. Supplying a known id does not bypass that requirement.
42: If a function is missing from `list_subroutines` or a run returns a not-found error:
43: 1. Confirm the MCP client is connected to the workspace that contains the function.
44: 2. Check that MCP access is enabled in the function's settings.
45: 3. If access cannot be changed, ask a workspace admin to check the integration and role access settings.
46: 4. Call `list_subroutines` again and use an id returned by that call.
47: A not-found error does not distinguish a nonexistent function from one unavailable to the connected client.

4: # Quickstart
5: > Build with Clay from your coding agent, or call the Clay API from your own applications.
6: There are two ways to use Clay as a developer: install the agent plugin to build with Clay inside your coding agent, or call the Public API directly from your own applications and services.
7: ## Agent plugin
8: The agent plugin gives your coding agent Clay's skills and the `clay` CLI — the fastest way to build with Clay from a coding agent.
9: It requires a coding-agent host with a shell — Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor — and doesn't work in general-purpose chat apps like Claude Desktop, claude.ai, or ChatGPT that can't run the CLI.
10: Copy this into your agent of choice and let it install and set up the plugin for you:
11: ```
12: Set up the Clay plugin by following the steps in
13: https://github.com/clay-run/agent-plugins
14: ```
15: This runs the plugin's `cli-setup` skill, which puts `clay` on your PATH, signs you in, and verifies the CLI. Sign-in opens a browser to authorize the CLI.
16: > [card] [Agent plugin repository](https://github.com/clay-run/agent-plugins)
17: >
18: > Manual install and setup instructions for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.
19: ## API
20: Use the Public API to call Clay from your own applications and services — backend jobs, internal tools, queues, and product features. Requests authenticate with a Clay API key in the `clay-api-key` header.
21: > [card] [API reference](https://developers.clay.com/api-reference/me/get-the-authenticated-user.md)
22: >
23: > Endpoint paths, request bodies, response schemas, and an interactive try-it console.
24: ### Get an API key
25: You can create an API key three ways:
26: * Ask your agent to generate one for you after installing the [agent plugin](#agent-plugin).
27: * Run `clay api-keys create --name "<key name>"` with the `clay` CLI. The key is returned once, in the `apiKey` field.
28: * Create one yourself in Clay under [API and CLI → API keys](https://app.clay.com/workspaces/~/api-and-cli?tab=api-keys).
29: Keep keys server-side. Do not expose them in browser code, mobile apps, public repositories, logs, or analytics tools. See [Authentication](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/authentication.md) for details.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Every request to the Clay Public API (e.g., https://api.clay.com/public/v0/me) requires a personal API key in the clay-api-key HTTP header, tied to a Clay user and workspace access.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
4: # Authentication
5: > Authenticate requests with a Clay API key.
6: Every request to the Clay Public API must include a Clay API key in the `clay-api-key` header. Store your key in an environment variable and pass it in the header:
7: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
8: export CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY="your_api_key"
9: curl https://api.clay.com/public/v0/me \
10: -H "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY"
11: ```
12: API keys are tied to a Clay user and workspace access. Create one under [API and CLI → API keys](https://app.clay.com/workspaces/~/api-and-cli?tab=api-keys), with `clay api-keys create --name "<key name>"` in the CLI, or by asking your agent after installing the [agent plugin](https://developers.clay.com/quickstart.md#agent-plugin). Keep keys server-side and do not expose them in browser code, mobile apps, public repositories, logs, or analytics tools.
13: ## Header
14: | Header | Required | Description |
15: | - | - | - |
16: | `clay-api-key` | Yes | Personal API key for the Clay Public API. |
17: ## Failed authentication
18: Requests without a valid API key return a non-2xx response with the standard error shape:
19: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
20: {
21: "message": "Authentication failed"
22: }
23: ```

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: The JSON-first Clay CLI (`clay`) writes machine-readable JSON to stdout and authenticates per workspace via `clay login` (browser OAuth) or `clay login --device` for headless environments.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
4: # CLI basics
5: > Understand the Clay CLI output contract, exit codes, environment variables, and authentication.
6: The Clay CLI (`clay`) is JSON-first: every command writes machine-readable JSON to stdout on success and a structured error envelope to stderr on failure. There are no spinners, colors, or progress bars, so agents and scripts can branch on the output and exit code directly.
7: ## Output contract
8: | Result | Behavior |
9: | - | - |
10: | Success | JSON is written to stdout, exit code `0`. |
11: | Failure | `{ "error": { "code", "message", "details"? } }` is written to stderr, non-zero exit code. |
12: Pipe stdout straight into `jq`, and read the exit code (`$?`) to decide what to do next.
13: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
14: clay whoami | jq -r '.user.id'
15: ```
16: ## Exit codes
17: Branch on these from agents and scripts instead of parsing error text.
18: | Exit | Meaning |
19: | - | - |
20: | `0` | Success. |
21: | `1` | Generic or unrecoverable (`server_error`, `contract_mismatch`, `conflict`, `internal_error`, `invalid_config_file`). |
22: | `2` | `validation_error` — input was rejected as malformed. |
23: | `3` | `auth_required` \| `auth_invalid` \| `auth_forbidden` — run `clay login` to (re)authenticate. |
24: | `4` | `rate_limited` (HTTP 429) — `details` has `retryAfter` (seconds), plus `limit`/`remaining`/`reset` when Clay sends the `X-RateLimit-*` headers. |
25: | `5` | `network_error` \| `network_timeout` — could not reach Clay. |
26: | `6` | `not_found` (HTTP 404). |
27: ## Environment variables
28: | Variable | Purpose |
29: | - | - |
30: | `CLAY_CONFIG_HOME` | Highest-precedence config directory parent; `config.json` and the identity cache live under `<CLAY_CONFIG_HOME>/clay`. |
31: | `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | Used when `CLAY_CONFIG_HOME` is unset (`<XDG_CONFIG_HOME>/clay`), falling back to `~/.config/clay` when neither is set. |
32: | `CLAY_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` | Per-request network timeout in milliseconds (default `60000`). |
33: | `CLAY_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT_MS` | Bulk file-upload timeout in milliseconds (default `600000`). |
34: ## Authentication
35: `clay login` opens a browser to authorize the CLI with OAuth — this works from a human terminal or an agent's shell tool. Use `clay whoami` as the canonical check that authentication is working, and `clay logout` to clear a stored credential.
36: Each sign-in covers one workspace — the one you pick on the consent screen. To work across several, run `clay login` once per workspace: signing into a second keeps the first. `clay workspaces list` shows what you are signed into, `clay workspaces current` shows which one commands run against, and `clay workspaces switch <id>` switches. Signing in makes the workspace just added the active one, so switch back explicitly if you were working in another. `clay logout` signs out of the active workspace and leaves the rest.
37: On machines where a local browser can't open — SSH sessions, containers, headless machines — use `clay login --device` instead. It prints a link and a short code; open the link in a browser on any device to approve the sign-in, and the CLI completes automatically. Run `clay login --help` for details.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Searches API/CLI result limits scale by plan: Free (50 per request/search, 100 per 30 days), Trial (50 per request/search, 10,000 for trial), Paid (500 per request, 1,000,000 per 30 days), and Enterprise (500 per request, 10,000,000 per 30 days).
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
17: ## Result limits
18: Clay caps how many search results a workspace can return through the API. These limits apply to results returned across the CLI and Public API, and they scale with your plan.
19: | Plan | Results per request | Results per search | Results per period | Reset date |
20: | - | - | - | - | - |
21: | Free | 50 | 50 | 100 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
22: | Trial | 50 | 50 | 10,000 for trial duration | Not applicable |
23: | Paid | 500 | Up to your period limit | 1,000,000 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
24: | Legacy paid (Starter, Explorer, Pro) | 500 | Up to your period limit | 1,000,000 per year | January 1 (UTC) |
25: | Enterprise | 500 | Up to your period limit | 10,000,000 per 30 days | Rolling (ages out daily at midnight UTC) |
26: * **Per request** is the largest limit you can request in a single call.
27: * **Per search** is the total results you can fetch across all pages of one `search_id`.
28: * **Reset date** is when the period limit resets. For rolling windows, usage ages out of the window daily at midnight UTC rather than resetting on a fixed calendar date.
29: Legacy Starter, Explorer, and Pro plans keep the yearly period limit. Legacy Enterprise plans use the Enterprise row. Moving to a current paid plan or Enterprise is what switches a workspace to the rolling 30-day limit.
30: When you exceed a limit, Clay returns HTTP `402` with a message naming the limit you hit. Period-limit errors also state when the limit resets. Malformed filters or other invalid input still return HTTP `400`. To increase a limit, paid customers can contact Clay Support; Enterprise customers should contact their assigned Clay GTME.

4: # Tables (Enterprise)
5: > Query known Clay tables with structured filters, selected fields, ordering, and pagination.

7: > [!NOTE]
8: >
9: > Tables are available on Enterprise plans.
10: Clay tables can act as a GTM database for your downstream systems. You can build dashboards, internal tools, QA views, scoring jobs, and interactive apps on top of data that already exists in Clay.

14: * Power interactive apps that search, filter, and inspect Clay table data.
15: * Run QA checks against known Clay tables.
16: * Sync selected table fields into another system.
17: * Power alerts, scoring models, and warehouse jobs.

21: curl --request POST \
22: --url https://api.clay.com/public/v0/tables/query \
23: --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
24: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY" \

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Routines API runs Clay-managed functions and custom functions via POST https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/{routine_id}/run and polls GET .../routines/run/{id}/results; Workflows are also routines and are in Alpha.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
4: # Routines API
5: > Run Clay-managed functions and custom functions through the Public API.
6: Routines are the programmable way to run Clay logic. Through the Public API, you can run Clay-managed functions and custom functions from backend services, queue workers, internal tools, and custom apps.
7: Use [Clay-managed functions](https://developers.clay.com/routines/clay-managed-functions.md) for common enrichment and research jobs. Use [custom functions](https://developers.clay.com/routines/custom-functions.md) for team-specific Clay logic built in the Clay UI.
8: ## Run a function routine
9: Custom function routine ids use the format `function:t_...`. To start a run, call `POST /routines/{routine_id}/run`.
10: Replace `function:t_abc123` and the input names with your function's routine id and inputs. Give each item an id you can use to match its result later.
11: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
12: ROUTINE_RUN_ID=$(curl --request POST \
13: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/function:t_abc123/run" \
14: --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
15: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY" \
16: --data '{
17: "items": [
18: {
19: "id": "row-1",
20: "inputs": {
21: "domain": "clay.com"
22: }
23: },
24: {
25: "id": "row-2",
26: "inputs": {
27: "domain": "example.com"
28: }
29: }
30: ]
31: }' | jq -r '.routine_run_id')
32: ```
33: ## Read the results
34: Use the returned `routine_run_id` to request the run's results:
35: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
36: curl --request GET \
37: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/run/$ROUTINE_RUN_ID/results" \
38: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY"
39: ```
40: While the run is processing, the endpoint returns **HTTP 202** with progress counters. There is no `data` array yet:
41: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
42: {
43: "routine_run_id": "run_xyz789",
44: "status": "in_progress",
45: "total": 2,
46: "finished": 1
47: }
48: ```
49: Repeat the GET request until it returns **HTTP 200** with `status: "complete"`. Use a delay between polls and a timeout appropriate for your application. For HTTP errors, follow the [error handling](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/errors.md) and [rate limit](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/rate-limits.md) guidance rather than continuing to poll unchanged.
50: Read individual results from **`data`**. Each item's `id` matches an id you supplied in the run request. Check each item's `status`: a completed run can contain failed items. For example, a function with a `company_name` output could return:
51: ```json theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
52: {
53: "routine_run_id": "run_xyz789",
54: "status": "complete",
55: "total": 2,
56: "finished": 2,
57: "data": [
58: {
59: "id": "row-1",
60: "status": "complete",
61: "result": {
62: "company_name": "Clay"
63: }
64: },
65: {
66: "id": "row-2",
67: "status": "failed",
68: "error": {
69: "message": "Provider request failed"
70: }
71: }
72: ]
73: }
74: ```
75: The keys inside `result` depend on your function's outputs. Use item ids to associate results with inputs rather than relying on response order. `finished` counts finished items, including failures; it is not a count of successful results.
76: ### Retrieve every page
77: A completed run's results can span multiple pages. If the response includes `cursor`, pass that value to the same endpoint to retrieve the next page:
78: ```bash theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"github-dark"}}
79: NEXT_CURSOR="<cursor from the previous response>"
80: curl --get \
81: --url "https://api.clay.com/public/v0/routines/run/$ROUTINE_RUN_ID/results" \
82: --header "clay-api-key: $CLAY_PUBLIC_API_KEY" \
83: --data-urlencode "cursor=$NEXT_CURSOR" \
84: --data-urlencode "limit=20"
85: ```
86: Collect `data` from each page and continue with each returned cursor until `cursor` is omitted. Treat cursors as opaque values. `total` and `finished` describe the whole run, not the current page. See [pagination](https://developers.clay.com/public-api/pagination.md) for the general cursor pattern.
87: This polling flow applies to runs started with `/routines/{routine_id}/run`. Runs started through the batch API use the separate [batch results endpoint](https://developers.clay.com/routines/batch-runs.md).
88: ## Webhook notifications
89: The `run` and `run-batch/start` requests accept an optional `webhook_id`. Clay notifies that webhook when the run finishes, so your system can react without polling.
90: Run `clay webhooks --help` for webhook creation, testing, delivery payloads, and signature verification.
91: ## Batch run a function routine
92: For large input sets, create an upload URL, upload JSONL input, then start a batch run.
93: > [card] [Batch runs](https://developers.clay.com/routines/batch-runs.md)
94: >
95: > Learn how batch runs fit into Routines.
96: ## When to use Workflows

21: ## Expose a function
22: To call a custom function:
23: 1. Open [Functions](https://app.clay.com/functions).
24: 2. Create or select a function.
25: 3. Open **Details**.
26: 4. Enable the integrations you need, such as **API** or **MCP**.
27: 5. Copy the `t_...` function id.
28: 6. Prefix it with `function:` when you call it from the plugin, CLI, MCP, or API.
29: Custom function routine ids use the format `function:t_...`.
30: Each access setting enables a separate way to call the function:
31: | How you call the function | Access to enable |
32: | - | - |
33: | Public API, `clay` CLI, or an agent using the CLI | API access |
34: | Clay's MCP connector | MCP access |
35: | As a routine in a Claygent | Claygent access |
36: An agent can use either the CLI or MCP, so choose access based on its connection. Enabling one does not enable the others. Workspace and role permissions still apply.
37: ## Access a published function through MCP
38: Publishing a function does not automatically enable MCP access. Enable MCP access in the function's settings before calling it through an MCP client. API access alone is not sufficient.
39: Call `list_subroutines` to find functions available to the connected MCP client. Use the returned `id` as `subroutine_id` when running a function through MCP.
40: ### A published function is missing or cannot run by id
41: MCP access is required both to list a function and to run it by id. Supplying a known id does not bypass that requirement.
42: If a function is missing from `list_subroutines` or a run returns a not-found error:
43: 1. Confirm the MCP client is connected to the workspace that contains the function.
44: 2. Check that MCP access is enabled in the function's settings.
45: 3. If access cannot be changed, ask a workspace admin to check the integration and role access settings.
46: 4. Call `list_subroutines` again and use an id returned by that call.
47: A not-found error does not distinguish a nonexistent function from one unavailable to the connected client.

21: ## Available APIs
22: ### Data API
23: SEO data for any domain, URL or keyword:
24: - **Backlinks**: backlink profiles, referring domains, anchors, authority scores and historical trends
25: - **Domain Analysis**: organic and paid keyword rankings, competitors, traffic estimates and domain overviews
26: - **Keyword Research**: search volume, keyword difficulty, similar, related, question and long-tail keywords
27: - **AI Search**: brand and domain visibility in AI-generated answers, leaderboards and prompt-level data
28: - **SERP**: search engine results pages collected on demand
29: - **Website Audit**: technical SEO audits with crawl data, issues and page-level analysis
30: - **Account System**: subscription and credit balance
31: ### Project API
32: The SE Ranking projects in your account: projects and project groups, keywords and rankings, search engines,
33: competitors, URL tags, Google Search Console data, the marketing plan, website audits, Backlink Checker and
34: AI Results Tracker.
35: ### Local Marketing API
36: Read-only data for your Local Marketing locations: location profiles and overviews, local rankings, Google Business
37: Profile reports, business listings, reviews and Local Marketing audits.
38: ### SE Visible API
39: Brand visibility in AI engines: SE Visible projects, brands, topics and prompts, prompt results, sources, engines,
40: locations and the subscription.
41: ## Authentication
42: All four APIs are served from `https://api.seranking.com` and use the same SE Ranking API key. Send it in the
43: `Authorization` header with the `Token` scheme (recommended):
44: ```bash
45: curl 'https://api.seranking.com/v1/account/subscription' \
46: -H 'Authorization: Token YOUR_API_KEY'
47: ```
48: or as the `apikey` query parameter:
49: ```
50: https://api.seranking.com/v1/account/subscription?apikey=YOUR_API_KEY
51: ```
52: Create a key on the [API Dashboard](https://online.seranking.com/admin.api.dashboard.html). See
53: [Getting API access](https://seranking.com/api/how-to-get-api/), [API rate limits](https://seranking.com/api/rate-limits/)
54: and the [API credit system](https://seranking.com/api/api-credits-system/).
55: ## Usage Examples
56: ### Import in Swagger UI

13: | -------------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |

18: The YAML and JSON file of each API contain the same specification. Use whichever format your tooling prefers.
19: The specs follow the public API documentation: every endpoint, parameter and response field described there is in
20: the spec, with the documented request and response examples. Each operation links back to its documentation section.
21: ## Available APIs
22: ### Data API
23: SEO data for any domain, URL or keyword:
24: - **Backlinks**: backlink profiles, referring domains, anchors, authority scores and historical trends
25: - **Domain Analysis**: organic and paid keyword rankings, competitors, traffic estimates and domain overviews
26: - **Keyword Research**: search volume, keyword difficulty, similar, related, question and long-tail keywords
27: - **AI Search**: brand and domain visibility in AI-generated answers, leaderboards and prompt-level data
28: - **SERP**: search engine results pages collected on demand
29: - **Website Audit**: technical SEO audits with crawl data, issues and page-level analysis
30: - **Account System**: subscription and credit balance
31: ### Project API
32: The SE Ranking projects in your account: projects and project groups, keywords and rankings, search engines,
33: competitors, URL tags, Google Search Console data, the marketing plan, website audits, Backlink Checker and
34: AI Results Tracker.
35: ### Local Marketing API
36: Read-only data for your Local Marketing locations: location profiles and overviews, local rankings, Google Business
37: Profile reports, business listings, reviews and Local Marketing audits.
38: ### SE Visible API
39: Brand visibility in AI engines: SE Visible projects, brands, topics and prompts, prompt results, sources, engines,
40: locations and the subscription.
41: ## Authentication

51: ```

53: [Getting API access](https://seranking.com/api/how-to-get-api/), [API rate limits](https://seranking.com/api/rate-limits/)
