original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Official seranking/seo-skills repository distributes 32 open-source Claude/Cursor SEO skills configured for the hosted SE Ranking remote MCP server at https://api.seranking.com/mcp with OAuth sign-in.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
1: # Claude SEO Skills
2: **32 free, open-source Claude SEO skills** for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and any AI agent that supports Agent Skills and MCP. Each SEO skill turns live [SE Ranking](https://seranking.com) data into a finished deliverable: content briefs, technical audits, AI search share of voice, backlink gap lists, keyword clusters and 90-day SEO plans. <!-- dir-edition:line readme-intro -->
3: Overview, use cases and a no-terminal install guide: [Claude SEO Skills by SE Ranking](https://seranking.com/claude-seo-skills.html). <!-- dir-edition:line readme-overview-link -->
4: <!-- dir-edition:line readme-about-edition -->
5: Production-ready [Claude Agent Skills](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview) for SEO, powered by the [SE Ranking MCP](https://seranking.com/mcp.html). Each skill turns raw API data into a finished SEO deliverable — content briefs, AI Search share of voice, page intelligence, structured data, drift monitoring, SXO diagnostics, competitive analysis, and more.
6: These Claude Skills are designed to work with the SE Ranking MCP server, but they document every API call explicitly so they can also be adapted to other SEO data providers.
7: ## What are Claude SEO skills?
8: Claude SEO skills are reusable instructions that teach Claude how to run a specific SEO task end to end: which data to pull, in what order, and what file to produce. Instead of writing a long prompt each time, you ask for "a content brief for X" or "a backlink gap vs. these competitors", and Claude picks the matching skill. The skills in this repo get their data from the SE Ranking MCP server, so every brief, audit and report is based on live keyword, backlink, SERP and AI search data rather than the model's memory.
9: ## Install
10: <!-- dir-edition:begin readme-install -->
11: Pick the first option that fits.
12: ### 1. Claude Desktop (recommended)
13: The easiest setup — no terminal needed. Cowork in Claude Desktop installs the plugin from a marketplace through a UI flow.
14: 1. Open **Customize** in the sidebar.
15: 2. Click **Personal plugin** → **+ Create plugin**.
16: 3. Click **Add marketplace** and enter `seranking/seo-skills`.
17: 4. Install the plugin once the marketplace loads.
18: Skills are available in your next Cowork session. Trigger them by name — `seo-content-brief`, `seo-page`, etc. — or just describe what you want and Claude picks the right one.
19: ### 2. Claude Code (slash commands)
20: If you use Claude Code in the terminal:
21: ```bash
22: /plugin marketplace add seranking/seo-skills
23: /plugin install seo-skills@seranking
24: ```
25: Trigger skills with `/seo-content-brief`, `/seo-page`, etc. — no `seo-skills:` prefix needed. Or just describe what you want and Claude picks the right skill. Update the marketplace later with `/plugin marketplace update seranking`.
26: ### 3. Manual install (only if you want `seo-google` or the optional extensions)
27: Options 1 and 2 cover **31 of 32 skills**. The 32nd — `seo-google` — ships Python scripts that need a local clone. The optional Firecrawl + Google extensions also need this. **If neither matters to you, skip this option.**
28: ```bash
29: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/seranking/seo-skills.git
30: bash seo-skills/install.sh
31: ```
32: The installer is interactive — it asks which extensions to install. Accept the defaults and you're done. Re-running pulls the latest version and re-runs the chosen extensions. Requires `git`, `python3` 3.10+, and (for Firecrawl) `node` 20+. To skip the questions, pass `--all` (both extensions), `--firecrawl` or `--google` (one of them), or `--no-extensions`.
33: The manual install only wires your *environment* (extensions, Python deps, `~/.config/seo-skills/`). You still need Option 1 or 2 above so Claude can find the skill files.
34: ### 4. Cursor
35: SE Ranking is also packaged as a [Cursor plugin](.cursor-plugin/plugin.json). Once it is listed on [cursor.com/marketplace](https://cursor.com/marketplace), install it from the marketplace, or add it by name in Cursor:
36: ```
37: /add-plugin se-ranking
38: ```
39: The hosted SE Ranking MCP server is declared in [`mcp.json`](mcp.json) and is auto-detected when the plugin is installed — open Cursor's MCP settings and sign in via OAuth (no API token to manage). The same skills ship to the Cursor agent.
40: ### 5. Any other AI agent
41: The skills follow the open Agent Skills format (one SKILL.md per folder), so any agent that supports skills and MCP can use them:
42: 1. Copy the folders from skills/ into your agent's skills directory.
43: 2. Add the SE Ranking remote MCP server: https://api.seranking.com/mcp (OAuth sign-in).
44: 3. Ask for an SEO task in plain language. The agent picks the matching skill.
45: <!-- dir-edition:end readme-install -->
46: ### Connect SE Ranking (any install path)
47: The SE Ranking remote MCP auto-registers when you install the plugin — there's no separate `claude mcp add` step. On your first session, run `/mcp` and sign in via OAuth. No API token to manage. If you don't have an SE Ranking account yet, [start a free trial](https://seranking.com/sign-up.html?landing=claude_seo_skills&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=seo_skills) — it includes 100K API credits and MCP access for 14 days. <!-- dir-edition:line readme-connect -->
48: <details>
49: <summary>Manual fallback (older Claude Code, or troubleshooting)</summary>
50: If `/mcp` doesn't list `se-ranking` after install — typically because you're on a Claude Code build that pre-dates plugin-bundled MCP servers — register it directly:
51: ```bash
52: claude mcp add --transport http se-ranking https://api.seranking.com/mcp
53: ```
54: Then run `/mcp` and complete OAuth. (User-scope registrations [outrank plugin-bundled ones](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#scope-hierarchy-and-precedence), so this safely overrides whatever the plugin shipped with.)

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Official seranking/openapi repo publishes OpenAPI 3.0 specs (JSON and YAML) for Data API, Project API, Local Marketing API, and SE Visible API served from https://api.seranking.com and authenticated via Authorization: Token YOUR_API_KEY header or apikey query parameter.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
12: | API | YAML | JSON | Documentation |
13: | -------------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
14: | Data API | `data-api.yaml` | `data-api.json` | [seranking.com/api/data](https://seranking.com/api/data/) |
15: | Project API | `project-api.yaml` | `project-api.json` | [seranking.com/api/project](https://seranking.com/api/project/) |
16: | Local Marketing API | `local-marketing-api.yaml` | `local-marketing-api.json` | [seranking.com/api/local-marketing-api](https://seranking.com/api/local-marketing-api/) |
17: | SE Visible API | `se-visible-api.yaml` | `se-visible-api.json` | [seranking.com/api/se-visible](https://seranking.com/api/se-visible/) |
18: The YAML and JSON file of each API contain the same specification. Use whichever format your tooling prefers.
19: The specs follow the public API documentation: every endpoint, parameter and response field described there is in
20: the spec, with the documented request and response examples. Each operation links back to its documentation section.
21: ## Available APIs
22: ### Data API
23: SEO data for any domain, URL or keyword:
24: - **Backlinks**: backlink profiles, referring domains, anchors, authority scores and historical trends
25: - **Domain Analysis**: organic and paid keyword rankings, competitors, traffic estimates and domain overviews
26: - **Keyword Research**: search volume, keyword difficulty, similar, related, question and long-tail keywords
27: - **AI Search**: brand and domain visibility in AI-generated answers, leaderboards and prompt-level data
28: - **SERP**: search engine results pages collected on demand
29: - **Website Audit**: technical SEO audits with crawl data, issues and page-level analysis
30: - **Account System**: subscription and credit balance
31: ### Project API
32: The SE Ranking projects in your account: projects and project groups, keywords and rankings, search engines,
33: competitors, URL tags, Google Search Console data, the marketing plan, website audits, Backlink Checker and
34: AI Results Tracker.
35: ### Local Marketing API
36: Read-only data for your Local Marketing locations: location profiles and overviews, local rankings, Google Business
37: Profile reports, business listings, reviews and Local Marketing audits.
38: ### SE Visible API
39: Brand visibility in AI engines: SE Visible projects, brands, topics and prompts, prompt results, sources, engines,
40: locations and the subscription.
41: ## Authentication
42: All four APIs are served from `https://api.seranking.com` and use the same SE Ranking API key. Send it in the
43: `Authorization` header with the `Token` scheme (recommended):
44: ```bash
45: curl 'https://api.seranking.com/v1/account/subscription' \
46: -H 'Authorization: Token YOUR_API_KEY'
47: ```
48: or as the `apikey` query parameter:
49: ```
50: https://api.seranking.com/v1/account/subscription?apikey=YOUR_API_KEY
51: ```
52: Create a key on the [API Dashboard](https://online.seranking.com/admin.api.dashboard.html). See
53: [Getting API access](https://seranking.com/api/how-to-get-api/), [API rate limits](https://seranking.com/api/rate-limits/)
54: and the [API credit system](https://seranking.com/api/api-credits-system/).
55: ## Usage Examples
56: ### Import in Swagger UI
57: Point Swagger UI at the raw spec URL, for example:
58: ```
59: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seranking/openapi/main/openapi/data-api.yaml
60: ```
61: ### Generate a Client Library
62: Using [OpenAPI Generator](https://openapi-generator.tech/):
63: ```bash
64: openapi-generator-cli generate \
65: -i openapi/data-api.yaml \
66: -g python \
67: -o ./seranking-python-client
68: ```
69: ### Validate the Specs
70: ```bash
71: npx @redocly/cli lint openapi/*.yaml
72: ```
73: ## OpenAPI Version
74: The specs use **OpenAPI 3.0**. Both JSON and YAML formats are kept in sync.

444: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) server provides a standardized interface that allows any compatible AI model to access your SE Ranking and SE Visible data simply and securely.

446: What you can access

450: Local Marketing API: your locations, local rankings, Google Business Profile, business listings, and reviews
451: SE Visible API: your AI visibility projects, brands, topics, prompts, and sources

463: In the connection dialog, choose Enter API keys manually.
464: Paste the key when prompted.

12: | API | YAML | JSON | Documentation |
13: | -------------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
14: | Data API | `data-api.yaml` | `data-api.json` | [seranking.com/api/data](https://seranking.com/api/data/) |
15: | Project API | `project-api.yaml` | `project-api.json` | [seranking.com/api/project](https://seranking.com/api/project/) |
16: | Local Marketing API | `local-marketing-api.yaml` | `local-marketing-api.json` | [seranking.com/api/local-marketing-api](https://seranking.com/api/local-marketing-api/) |
17: | SE Visible API | `se-visible-api.yaml` | `se-visible-api.json` | [seranking.com/api/se-visible](https://seranking.com/api/se-visible/) |
18: The YAML and JSON file of each API contain the same specification. Use whichever format your tooling prefers.
19: The specs follow the public API documentation: every endpoint, parameter and response field described there is in
20: the spec, with the documented request and response examples. Each operation links back to its documentation section.
21: ## Available APIs
22: ### Data API
23: SEO data for any domain, URL or keyword:
24: - **Backlinks**: backlink profiles, referring domains, anchors, authority scores and historical trends
25: - **Domain Analysis**: organic and paid keyword rankings, competitors, traffic estimates and domain overviews
26: - **Keyword Research**: search volume, keyword difficulty, similar, related, question and long-tail keywords
27: - **AI Search**: brand and domain visibility in AI-generated answers, leaderboards and prompt-level data
28: - **SERP**: search engine results pages collected on demand
29: - **Website Audit**: technical SEO audits with crawl data, issues and page-level analysis
30: - **Account System**: subscription and credit balance
31: ### Project API
32: The SE Ranking projects in your account: projects and project groups, keywords and rankings, search engines,
33: competitors, URL tags, Google Search Console data, the marketing plan, website audits, Backlink Checker and
34: AI Results Tracker.
35: ### Local Marketing API
36: Read-only data for your Local Marketing locations: location profiles and overviews, local rankings, Google Business
37: Profile reports, business listings, reviews and Local Marketing audits.
38: ### SE Visible API
39: Brand visibility in AI engines: SE Visible projects, brands, topics and prompts, prompt results, sources, engines,
40: locations and the subscription.
41: ## Authentication
42: All four APIs are served from `https://api.seranking.com` and use the same SE Ranking API key. Send it in the
43: `Authorization` header with the `Token` scheme (recommended):
44: ```bash
45: curl 'https://api.seranking.com/v1/account/subscription' \
46: -H 'Authorization: Token YOUR_API_KEY'
47: ```
48: or as the `apikey` query parameter:
49: ```
50: https://api.seranking.com/v1/account/subscription?apikey=YOUR_API_KEY
51: ```
52: Create a key on the [API Dashboard](https://online.seranking.com/admin.api.dashboard.html). See
53: [Getting API access](https://seranking.com/api/how-to-get-api/), [API rate limits](https://seranking.com/api/rate-limits/)
54: and the [API credit system](https://seranking.com/api/api-credits-system/).
55: ## Usage Examples
56: ### Import in Swagger UI
57: Point Swagger UI at the raw spec URL, for example:
58: ```
59: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seranking/openapi/main/openapi/data-api.yaml
60: ```
61: ### Generate a Client Library
62: Using [OpenAPI Generator](https://openapi-generator.tech/):
63: ```bash
64: openapi-generator-cli generate \
65: -i openapi/data-api.yaml \
66: -g python \
67: -o ./seranking-python-client
68: ```
69: ### Validate the Specs
70: ```bash
71: npx @redocly/cli lint openapi/*.yaml
72: ```
73: ## OpenAPI Version
74: The specs use **OpenAPI 3.0**. Both JSON and YAML formats are kept in sync.

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
1: # Claude SEO Skills
2: **32 free, open-source Claude SEO skills** for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and any AI agent that supports Agent Skills and MCP. Each SEO skill turns live [SE Ranking](https://seranking.com) data into a finished deliverable: content briefs, technical audits, AI search share of voice, backlink gap lists, keyword clusters and 90-day SEO plans. <!-- dir-edition:line readme-intro -->
3: Overview, use cases and a no-terminal install guide: [Claude SEO Skills by SE Ranking](https://seranking.com/claude-seo-skills.html). <!-- dir-edition:line readme-overview-link -->
4: <!-- dir-edition:line readme-about-edition -->
5: Production-ready [Claude Agent Skills](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview) for SEO, powered by the [SE Ranking MCP](https://seranking.com/mcp.html). Each skill turns raw API data into a finished SEO deliverable — content briefs, AI Search share of voice, page intelligence, structured data, drift monitoring, SXO diagnostics, competitive analysis, and more.
6: These Claude Skills are designed to work with the SE Ranking MCP server, but they document every API call explicitly so they can also be adapted to other SEO data providers.
7: ## What are Claude SEO skills?
8: Claude SEO skills are reusable instructions that teach Claude how to run a specific SEO task end to end: which data to pull, in what order, and what file to produce. Instead of writing a long prompt each time, you ask for "a content brief for X" or "a backlink gap vs. these competitors", and Claude picks the matching skill. The skills in this repo get their data from the SE Ranking MCP server, so every brief, audit and report is based on live keyword, backlink, SERP and AI search data rather than the model's memory.
9: ## Install
10: <!-- dir-edition:begin readme-install -->
11: Pick the first option that fits.
12: ### 1. Claude Desktop (recommended)
13: The easiest setup — no terminal needed. Cowork in Claude Desktop installs the plugin from a marketplace through a UI flow.
14: 1. Open **Customize** in the sidebar.
15: 2. Click **Personal plugin** → **+ Create plugin**.
16: 3. Click **Add marketplace** and enter `seranking/seo-skills`.
17: 4. Install the plugin once the marketplace loads.
18: Skills are available in your next Cowork session. Trigger them by name — `seo-content-brief`, `seo-page`, etc. — or just describe what you want and Claude picks the right one.
19: ### 2. Claude Code (slash commands)
20: If you use Claude Code in the terminal:
21: ```bash
22: /plugin marketplace add seranking/seo-skills
23: /plugin install seo-skills@seranking
24: ```
25: Trigger skills with `/seo-content-brief`, `/seo-page`, etc. — no `seo-skills:` prefix needed. Or just describe what you want and Claude picks the right skill. Update the marketplace later with `/plugin marketplace update seranking`.
26: ### 3. Manual install (only if you want `seo-google` or the optional extensions)
27: Options 1 and 2 cover **31 of 32 skills**. The 32nd — `seo-google` — ships Python scripts that need a local clone. The optional Firecrawl + Google extensions also need this. **If neither matters to you, skip this option.**
28: ```bash
29: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/seranking/seo-skills.git
30: bash seo-skills/install.sh
31: ```
32: The installer is interactive — it asks which extensions to install. Accept the defaults and you're done. Re-running pulls the latest version and re-runs the chosen extensions. Requires `git`, `python3` 3.10+, and (for Firecrawl) `node` 20+. To skip the questions, pass `--all` (both extensions), `--firecrawl` or `--google` (one of them), or `--no-extensions`.
33: The manual install only wires your *environment* (extensions, Python deps, `~/.config/seo-skills/`). You still need Option 1 or 2 above so Claude can find the skill files.
34: ### 4. Cursor
35: SE Ranking is also packaged as a [Cursor plugin](.cursor-plugin/plugin.json). Once it is listed on [cursor.com/marketplace](https://cursor.com/marketplace), install it from the marketplace, or add it by name in Cursor:
36: ```
37: /add-plugin se-ranking
38: ```
39: The hosted SE Ranking MCP server is declared in [`mcp.json`](mcp.json) and is auto-detected when the plugin is installed — open Cursor's MCP settings and sign in via OAuth (no API token to manage). The same skills ship to the Cursor agent.
40: ### 5. Any other AI agent
41: The skills follow the open Agent Skills format (one SKILL.md per folder), so any agent that supports skills and MCP can use them:
42: 1. Copy the folders from skills/ into your agent's skills directory.
43: 2. Add the SE Ranking remote MCP server: https://api.seranking.com/mcp (OAuth sign-in).
44: 3. Ask for an SEO task in plain language. The agent picks the matching skill.
45: <!-- dir-edition:end readme-install -->
46: ### Connect SE Ranking (any install path)
47: The SE Ranking remote MCP auto-registers when you install the plugin — there's no separate `claude mcp add` step. On your first session, run `/mcp` and sign in via OAuth. No API token to manage. If you don't have an SE Ranking account yet, [start a free trial](https://seranking.com/sign-up.html?landing=claude_seo_skills&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=seo_skills) — it includes 100K API credits and MCP access for 14 days. <!-- dir-edition:line readme-connect -->
48: <details>
49: <summary>Manual fallback (older Claude Code, or troubleshooting)</summary>
50: If `/mcp` doesn't list `se-ranking` after install — typically because you're on a Claude Code build that pre-dates plugin-bundled MCP servers — register it directly:
51: ```bash
52: claude mcp add --transport http se-ranking https://api.seranking.com/mcp
53: ```
54: Then run `/mcp` and complete OAuth. (User-scope registrations [outrank plugin-bundled ones](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp#scope-hierarchy-and-precedence), so this safely overrides whatever the plugin shipped with.)

26: - **Keyword Research**: search volume, keyword difficulty, similar, related, question and long-tail keywords
27: - **AI Search**: brand and domain visibility in AI-generated answers, leaderboards and prompt-level data
28: - **SERP**: search engine results pages collected on demand
29: - **Website Audit**: technical SEO audits with crawl data, issues and page-level analysis

104: TypeFormatPrivilegesAvailabilityUse
105: Publishable keysb_publishable_...LowPlatform, CLISafe to expose online: web page, mobile or desktop app, GitHub actions, CLIs, source code.
106: Secret keyssb_secret_...ElevatedPlatform, CLIOnly use in backend components of your app, such as servers, APIs with their own authorization checks, Edge Functions, and microservices. They provide full access to your project's data, bypassing Row Level Security.
107: anonJWT (long-lived)LowPlatform, CLILegacy version of publishable keys.

109: Publishable and secret keys are short strings, not JWTs. If a tool, tutorial, or AI assistant tells you to copy a long key that begins with eyJ, it was written for the legacy keys.

111: Legacy anon and service_role keys

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Publishable/secret keys use apikey header, not JWT Bearer; root OpenAPI route requires secret key.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
315: Publishable and secret keys aren't JWTs, which creates a few compatibility differences to plan for:
316: Send publishable and secret keys on the apikey header, not on Authorization: Bearer. Because the keys aren't JWTs, anything that tries to verify one as a JWT fails. For migration compatibility the verify_jwt platform check accepts them on either header, but passing that check doesn't authenticate the caller. See Authorization headers.
317: Edge Functions need to authorize API keys in code. The verify_jwt check alone doesn't authenticate a caller that sends only an API key. Use the @supabase/server SDK, as shown in Securing Edge Functions, rather than relying on the platform check.
318: The Data API's OpenAPI root, GET /rest/v1/, accepts only secret keys. A publishable key gets a 401 there, even though it works on table routes such as /rest/v1/<table>. To check that a publishable key works, call a table route or /auth/v1/health instead.

59: Configure your MCP client to connect with your Supabase project
60: Installation
61: Add the MCP server to your project config using the command line:
62: claude mcp add --scope project --transport http supabase "https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp?features=docs%2Caccount%2Cdatabase%2Cdebugging%2Cdevelopment%2Cfunctions%2Cbranching%2Cfeedback%2Cnotebooks"
63: Alternatively, add this configuration to .mcp.json:
64: 1{
65: 2 "mcpServers": {
66: 3 "supabase": {
67: 4 "type": "http",
68: 5 "url": "https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp?features=docs%2Caccount%2Cdatabase%2Cdebugging%2Cdevelopment%2Cfunctions%2Cbranching%2Cfeedback%2Cnotebooks"
69: 6 }
70: 7 }
71: 8}
72: After configuring the MCP server, you need to authenticate. In a regular terminal (not the IDE extension) run:
73: claude /mcp
74: Select the "supabase" server, then "Authenticate" to begin the authentication flow.
75: Need help?View Claude Code docs
76: Authentication
77: Some MCP clients automatically prompt you to log in during setup. Others require manual authentication steps. Either method opens a browser window where you log in to your Supabase account and grant the MCP client access to your organization. You don't need a personal access token (PAT).
78: Next steps
79: Your MCP client automatically redirects you to sign in to Supabase during setup. This opens a browser window where you can sign in to your Supabase account and grant access to the MCP client. Be sure to choose the organization that contains the project you wish to work with.

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
104: TypeFormatPrivilegesAvailabilityUse
105: Publishable keysb_publishable_...LowPlatform, CLISafe to expose online: web page, mobile or desktop app, GitHub actions, CLIs, source code.
106: Secret keyssb_secret_...ElevatedPlatform, CLIOnly use in backend components of your app, such as servers, APIs with their own authorization checks, Edge Functions, and microservices. They provide full access to your project's data, bypassing Row Level Security.
107: anonJWT (long-lived)LowPlatform, CLILegacy version of publishable keys.
108: service_roleJWT (long-lived)ElevatedPlatform, CLILegacy version of secret keys.
109: Publishable and secret keys are short strings, not JWTs. If a tool, tutorial, or AI assistant tells you to copy a long key that begins with eyJ, it was written for the legacy keys.
110: Running supabase start prints a publishable key and a secret key for your local project. The local secret key takes the place of the local service_role key. See the CLI getting started guide for the full output.
111: Legacy anon and service_role keys
112: Creating publishable and secret keys doesn't revoke your legacy keys. Both key systems work at the same time.
113: Creating a publishable or secret key adds it alongside your existing anon and service_role keys without affecting them, so your legacy keys keep working. They stay valid until you disable them in the Settings > API Keys section of the Dashboard, which is a separate step.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Secret key bypasses RLS; user JWT and application key are separate.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
122: Postgres roles and Row Level Security
123: Every key resolves to a built-in Postgres role, and that role is what your Row Level Security policies match on. Using a publishable key doesn't mean your user is anonymous: your application authenticates with the publishable key while your user authenticates separately through Supabase Auth with their own JWT.
124: KeyUser signed in through Supabase AuthPostgres role
125: Publishable keyNoanon
126: Publishable keyYesauthenticated
127: Secret keyNot applicableservice_role
128: Write your Row Level Security policies for the anon and authenticated roles. Policies never apply to a secret key, because service_role has the BYPASSRLS attribute.
129: Postgres evaluates table grants first, and only then applies Row Level Security. The two failures look different. A missing grant returns a permission error, including for service_role, whereas a policy that matches no rows returns an empty result. Check the grant before you debug the policy. See Securing your API.
130: Secret keys and elevated access
131: Unlike publishable keys, secret keys allow elevated access to your project's data. Use them only in secure, developer-controlled components of your application, such as:
132: Servers that run their own authorization checks, such as Edge Functions, microservices, and web servers.
133: Periodic jobs, queue processors, topic subscribers.
134: Admin and back-office tools that run authorization checks first.
135: Data processing pipelines, such as for analytics, reports, backups, or database synchronization.
136: A leaked secret key exposes all of your project's data
137: A secret key bypasses every Row Level Security policy you have. Never put one in a browser, a shipped application, or source control. For the full list of places a secret key must never go, see Handling secret keys safely.
138: If a secret key leaks, see Rotate a leaked or compromised API key.
139: Secret keys authorize access to your project's data through the built-in service_role Postgres role. By design, this role has full access to your project's data. It also has the BYPASSRLS attribute, so it skips every Row Level Security policy you attach.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Production MCP recommendations include project scope, read-only and feature restrictions; developer context not customer-facing.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
242: Recommendations
243: We recommend the following best practices to mitigate security risks when using the Supabase MCP server:
244: Protect production data: Connect to a production project only when the task requires production evidence. Use project scoping, read-only mode, restricted feature groups, and the narrowest data query that can answer the question. Do not include secrets or unrelated personal data in prompts or reports.
245: Don't give to your customers: The MCP server operates under the context of your developer permissions, so you should not give it to your customers or end users. Instead, use it internally as a developer tool to help you build and test your applications.
246: Read-only mode: Set unattended monitoring and diagnostic routines to read-only mode, which executes SQL queries as a read-only Postgres user.
247: Project scoping: Scope your MCP server to a specific project, limiting access to only that project's resources. This prevents LLMs from accessing data from other projects in your Supabase account.
248: Branching: Use Supabase's branching feature to create a development branch for your database. This allows you to test changes in a safe environment before merging them to production.
249: Cost confirmation: When your connection uses cost confirmation dialogs, the server asks for confirmation through your client before it creates resources that incur charges. This is a guardrail on top of authentication and authorization, not a replacement for them.
250: Feature groups: Restrict which tool groups are available using the features configuration option. This helps reduce the attack surface and limits the actions that LLMs can perform to only those that you need.

15: Prerequisite
16: Before you begin, find your zone and account IDs.
17: Determine if you want a user token or an Account API token. Use Account API tokens if you prefer service tokens that are not associated with users and your desired API endpoints are compatible.
18: From the Cloudflare dashboard ↗︎, go to My Profile > API Tokens for user tokens. For Account Tokens, go to Manage Account > API Tokens.
19: Select Create Token.
20: Add a token name to describe why or how the token is used.
21: Select a template from the available API token templates or start from scratch. Templates include policies with predefined permissions. The following example uses the Edit zone DNS template.
22: Create a policy to organize the token's permissions. Select a policy type (Account, User, or Zone), then select resource rules within the policy to specify which resources the permissions apply to, such as specific accounts or zones.
23: Choose the permissions to grant within the policy. Most permissions offer Edit or Read access. Edit is full CRUDL (create, read, update, delete, list) access, while Read is the read permission and list where appropriate. For example, Zone DNS Read for example.com allows the token to read DNS records only for that zone. Refer to the available token permissions for more information.
24: (Optional) Restrict how a token is used in the Token expiration and Client IP Address Filtering fields.
25: Select Continue to summary.
26: Review the token summary. Select Back to make adjustments. You can also edit a token after creation.
27: Select Create Token to generate the token's secret.
28: Copy the secret to a secure place.
29: Warning
30: The token secret is only shown once. Do not store the secret in plaintext where others can access it. Anyone with this token can perform the authorized actions against the resources that the token has access to.
31: The token secret page also includes an example command to test the token. Use the /user/tokens/verify endpoint to fetch the current status of the given token.
32: curl "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/user/tokens/verify" \
33: --header "Authorization: Bearer <API_TOKEN>"

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Cloudflare MCP servers can inspect and change services across application development, security and performance.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
1: # Cloudflare MCP Server
2: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a [new, standardized protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/introduction) for managing context between large language models (LLMs) and external systems. In this repository, you can find several MCP servers allowing you to connect to Cloudflare's service from an MCP client (e.g. Cursor, Claude) and use natural language to accomplish tasks through your Cloudflare account.
3: These MCP servers allow your [MCP Client](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/clients) to read configurations from your account, process information, make suggestions based on data, and even make those suggested changes for you. All of these actions can happen across Cloudflare's many services including application development, security and performance.
4: Every server in this repository exposes a stateless Streamable HTTP handler at `/mcp` through a fresh SDK v2 server factory. The retired `/sse` URL answers every request with a `410 Gone` Problem Details response that names the `/mcp` URL; MCP clients show its message in their connection error. Modern 2026 requests and stateless 2025 requests share the same request-scoped implementation without an MCP protocol session. OAuth, credentials, account selection, application caches, and product Durable Objects remain application/security state where required.
5: Cloudflare offers the following MCP servers. The domain-specific servers are included in this repository, while the recommended Cloudflare API MCP Server is maintained in [`cloudflare/mcp`](https://github.com/cloudflare/mcp):
6: | Server Name | Description | Server URL |
7: | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
8: | [**Cloudflare API MCP Server (recommended)**](https://github.com/cloudflare/mcp) | Best when you want broad access across Cloudflare's APIs through code execution | `https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp` |

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
1: # Cloudflare MCP Server
2: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a [new, standardized protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/introduction) for managing context between large language models (LLMs) and external systems. In this repository, you can find several MCP servers allowing you to connect to Cloudflare's service from an MCP client (e.g. Cursor, Claude) and use natural language to accomplish tasks through your Cloudflare account.
3: These MCP servers allow your [MCP Client](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/clients) to read configurations from your account, process information, make suggestions based on data, and even make those suggested changes for you. All of these actions can happen across Cloudflare's many services including application development, security and performance.
4: Every server in this repository exposes a stateless Streamable HTTP handler at `/mcp` through a fresh SDK v2 server factory. The retired `/sse` URL answers every request with a `410 Gone` Problem Details response that names the `/mcp` URL; MCP clients show its message in their connection error. Modern 2026 requests and stateless 2025 requests share the same request-scoped implementation without an MCP protocol session. OAuth, credentials, account selection, application caches, and product Durable Objects remain application/security state where required.
5: Cloudflare offers the following MCP servers. The domain-specific servers are included in this repository, while the recommended Cloudflare API MCP Server is maintained in [`cloudflare/mcp`](https://github.com/cloudflare/mcp):
6: | Server Name | Description | Server URL |
7: | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
8: | [**Cloudflare API MCP Server (recommended)**](https://github.com/cloudflare/mcp) | Best when you want broad access across Cloudflare's APIs through code execution | `https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp` |

35: best when you want broad access across Cloudflare's APIs through code execution.

37: best when you want curated, typed tools for a specific Cloudflare product area.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Create user or account token with resource rules and Read/Edit permissions; send Authorization: Bearer to v4 API.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
17: Determine if you want a user token or an Account API token. Use Account API tokens if you prefer service tokens that are not associated with users and your desired API endpoints are compatible.
18: From the Cloudflare dashboard ↗︎, go to My Profile > API Tokens for user tokens. For Account Tokens, go to Manage Account > API Tokens.
19: Select Create Token.
20: Add a token name to describe why or how the token is used.
21: Select a template from the available API token templates or start from scratch. Templates include policies with predefined permissions. The following example uses the Edit zone DNS template.
22: Create a policy to organize the token's permissions. Select a policy type (Account, User, or Zone), then select resource rules within the policy to specify which resources the permissions apply to, such as specific accounts or zones.
23: Choose the permissions to grant within the policy. Most permissions offer Edit or Read access. Edit is full CRUDL (create, read, update, delete, list) access, while Read is the read permission and list where appropriate. For example, Zone DNS Read for example.com allows the token to read DNS records only for that zone. Refer to the available token permissions for more information.
24: (Optional) Restrict how a token is used in the Token expiration and Client IP Address Filtering fields.
25: Select Continue to summary.
26: Review the token summary. Select Back to make adjustments. You can also edit a token after creation.
27: Select Create Token to generate the token's secret.
28: Copy the secret to a secure place.
29: Warning
30: The token secret is only shown once. Do not store the secret in plaintext where others can access it. Anyone with this token can perform the authorized actions against the resources that the token has access to.
31: The token secret page also includes an example command to test the token. Use the /user/tokens/verify endpoint to fetch the current status of the given token.
32: curl "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/user/tokens/verify" \
33: --header "Authorization: Bearer <API_TOKEN>"

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Squarespace Commerce APIs support generated API keys (requires Commerce Advanced plan; never expire while site is active) and OAuth 2.0 (required for Squarespace Extensions, which undergo OAuth client review and approval).
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
28: every request to Commerce APIs must be authenticated and have minimum permissions.
29: However, authenticated requests automatically have access to public site data,
30: such as site name, identifier, language, currency, time zone, and location.
31: Read the permission levels for each Commerce API below.
32: Then, depending on your development needs,
33: authenticate requests by using an API key or OAuth access token.
34: Remember: Requests only have access to data for
35: the website that owns the API key or OAuth access token.
36: API permission levels
37: Forms API
38: Read Only: View form submission data; for Zapier integration only
39: Inventory API
40: Read Only: View inventory stock levels
41: Read and Write: Manage inventory stock levels
42: Orders API
43: Read Only: View order, fulfillment, and customer information (name, email, address, and more)
44: Read and Write: View customer information (name, email, address, and more); manage order and fulfillment information
45: Products API
46: Read Only: View product information, including information for any images and variants; view Store Page information
47: Read and Write: Manage product information, including information for any images and variants; view Store Page information
48: Contacts API
49: Read Only: View contact records, address books, and marketing preferences
50: Read and Write: Manage contact records, address books, and marketing preferences
51: Discounts API
52: Read Only: View discount records
53: Read and Write: Manage discount records
54: Webhook Subscriptions API (OAuth only)
55: Read and Write: Create, update, delete, and test webhook subscriptions
56: Profiles API (maintenance mode — new integrations should use the Contacts API)
57: Read Only: View the name, address, email, marketing preferences, and other profile information of customers, subscribers, and other website users
58: Transactions API
59: Read Only: View transactional order, donation data, and customer information (email)
60: Authenticating requests
61: Depending on your development needs,
62: you can use a generated API key or start the OAuth process with Squarespace
63: to become a registered OAuth client. A Squarespace merchant site can use both
64: API keys and OAuth for data access, but Squarespace Extensions are required to use OAuth.
65: Custom applications
66: With Squarespace's Commerce Advanced plan,
67: you can develop a custom application for a Squarespace merchant site.
68: Follow the steps below to generate an API key for a custom application.
69: Log in to a Squarespace site.
70: In the left nav, click Settings; scroll down and click Advanced.
71: Click Developer API Keys.
72: Click the GENERATE KEY button.
73: In the dialog, add a key name under "KEY NAME",
74: and select one or more Commerce APIs under "PERMISSIONS" and permission level.
75: Record the generated key in a safe and secure place.
76: For security reasons, this is the only time the API key is visible.
77: API keys will never expire as long as the merchant site remains active.
78: Commercial development
79: Squarespace Extensions allow customers on any plan
80: to optimize and expand their site in a few clicks.
81: If you'd like to develop a new Extension,
82: start the OAuth client process here.
83: Once you've obtained OAuth credentials, you can use our OAuth 2.0 Guide to learn how to authorize your application to integrate with Squarespace and use Squarespace APIs.
84: Registering an OAuth client, and having it reviewed and approved, only allows OAuth connections with Squarespace.
85: It doesn't list your application in Squarespace Extensions, which is a separate process.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Orders API (GET /1.0/commerce/orders) supports paymentStates filtering (NOT_CHARGED, AUTHORIZED, PAID, REFUNDED, PARTIALLY_PAID) and order.create webhooks.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
48: PARTIALLY_PAIDA Payment Plan order with one or more installments still outstanding. An order enters this state as soon as the deposit is captured (before any installment has been collected) and remains in it while installments are still being collected.
49: PENDINGA payment is awaiting confirmation. The order will subsequently transition to PAID, PARTIALLY_PAID or FAILED.
50: FAILEDThe terminal state for an order whose payment was previously PENDING and ultimately did not succeed.
51: REFUND_PENDINGA refund has been initiated and is being processed. The order will subsequently transition to REFUNDED or REFUND_FAILED.
52: REFUNDEDThe order has had refund activity. This covers both full and partial refunds; a partial refund of any amount sets the order to REFUNDED. To determine the outstanding balance, compare the order's refundedTotal with grandTotal.
53: REFUND_FAILEDAn asynchronous refund attempt failed.
54: Filtering by payment state
55: The retrieve all orders endpoint accepts an optional paymentStates query parameter, a comma-separated list of the values above. If omitted, the endpoint defaults to NOT_CHARGED,AUTHORIZED,PAID,REFUNDED, which preserves the response set returned before Payment Plans existed and keeps existing integrations stable.
56: To include Payment Plan orders that are mid-collection, pass PARTIALLY_PAID explicitly:
57: Code
58: GET /1.0/commerce/orders?paymentStates=PAID,PARTIALLY_PAID
59: Working with Payment Plan orders
60: A few practical notes when integrating against Payment Plan orders:
61: Cancellations and refunds: sellers can cancel individual installments or an entire payment plan from the Orders panel. Canceling a plan stops future scheduled installments but does not automatically refund payments that have already been collected — those can be refunded individually. The Transactions API exposes per-payment refund detail.
62: Webhooks: to preserve backward compatibility with existing integrations, the order.create webhook for a Payment Plan order fires only when paymentState transitions to PAID (all installments collected), not when the order is initially placed. No webhook fires for the deposit or for intermediate installment captures. The order.update webhook continues to fire normally for FULFILLED, REFUNDED, CANCELED, MARKED_PENDING, and EMAIL_UPDATED events at any point in the order's lifecycle. For real-time visibility into newly placed Payment Plan orders, use the retrieve all orders endpoint with paymentStates=PARTIALLY_PAID.
63: Further reading
64: Become familiar with common commerce terms and how they're related to the API
65: Obtain an API key or use OAuth

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
28: every request to Commerce APIs must be authenticated and have minimum permissions.

53: Read and Write: Manage discount records

63: to become a registered OAuth client. A Squarespace merchant site can use both

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Orders API (GET /1.0/commerce/orders) supports paymentStates filtering (NOT_CHARGED, AUTHORIZED, PAID, REFUNDED, PARTIALLY_PAID) and order.create webhooks.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
48: PARTIALLY_PAIDA Payment Plan order with one or more installments still outstanding. An order enters this state as soon as the deposit is captured (before any installment has been collected) and remains in it while installments are still being collected.
49: PENDINGA payment is awaiting confirmation. The order will subsequently transition to PAID, PARTIALLY_PAID or FAILED.
50: FAILEDThe terminal state for an order whose payment was previously PENDING and ultimately did not succeed.
51: REFUND_PENDINGA refund has been initiated and is being processed. The order will subsequently transition to REFUNDED or REFUND_FAILED.
52: REFUNDEDThe order has had refund activity. This covers both full and partial refunds; a partial refund of any amount sets the order to REFUNDED. To determine the outstanding balance, compare the order's refundedTotal with grandTotal.
53: REFUND_FAILEDAn asynchronous refund attempt failed.
54: Filtering by payment state
55: The retrieve all orders endpoint accepts an optional paymentStates query parameter, a comma-separated list of the values above. If omitted, the endpoint defaults to NOT_CHARGED,AUTHORIZED,PAID,REFUNDED, which preserves the response set returned before Payment Plans existed and keeps existing integrations stable.
56: To include Payment Plan orders that are mid-collection, pass PARTIALLY_PAID explicitly:
57: Code
58: GET /1.0/commerce/orders?paymentStates=PAID,PARTIALLY_PAID
59: Working with Payment Plan orders
60: A few practical notes when integrating against Payment Plan orders:
61: Cancellations and refunds: sellers can cancel individual installments or an entire payment plan from the Orders panel. Canceling a plan stops future scheduled installments but does not automatically refund payments that have already been collected — those can be refunded individually. The Transactions API exposes per-payment refund detail.
62: Webhooks: to preserve backward compatibility with existing integrations, the order.create webhook for a Payment Plan order fires only when paymentState transitions to PAID (all installments collected), not when the order is initially placed. No webhook fires for the deposit or for intermediate installment captures. The order.update webhook continues to fire normally for FULFILLED, REFUNDED, CANCELED, MARKED_PENDING, and EMAIL_UPDATED events at any point in the order's lifecycle. For real-time visibility into newly placed Payment Plan orders, use the retrieve all orders endpoint with paymentStates=PARTIALLY_PAID.
63: Further reading
64: Become familiar with common commerce terms and how they're related to the API
65: Obtain an API key or use OAuth

47: Read and Write: Manage product information, including information for any images and variants; view Store Page information

53: Read and Write: Manage discount records

63: to become a registered OAuth client. A Squarespace merchant site can use both

67: you can develop a custom application for a Squarespace merchant site.

70: In the left nav, click Settings; scroll down and click Advanced.
71: Click Developer API Keys.
72: Click the GENERATE KEY button.
73: In the dialog, add a key name under "KEY NAME",
74: and select one or more Commerce APIs under "PERMISSIONS" and permission level.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Squarespace OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow uses https://login.squarespace.com/api/1/login/oauth/provider/authorize with scopes (including website.inventory, website.orders, website.contacts, website.contacts.read) and optional access_type=offline.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
50: Code
51: GET https://login.squarespace.com/api/1/login/oauth/provider/authorize
52: Query parameterRequirementValue
53: client_idRequired
54: Alphanumeric value for your_client_id that was supplied by
55: Squarespace in Step 1.
56: redirect_uriRequiredString; the full redirect URI sent to Squarespace in Step 1.
57: scopeRequired
58: String; comma-separated list of client permission values (see below)
59: for API access. The confirmation page always displays website(s) for
60: user selection for scope=website.*
61: website.orders
62: Send order data and mark orders as fulfilled.
63: website.orders.read
64: View order and fulfillment information.
65: website.transactions.read
66: Access transactional order and donation data.
67: website.inventory
68: View and update inventory stock levels.
69: website.inventory.read
70: View inventory stock levels.
71: website.products
72: View product information and modify products.
73: website.products.read
74: View product information.
75: website.contacts
76: View customer contact information and address book entries; create, update, and delete contacts and address book entries.
77: website.contacts.read
78: View customer contact information and address book entries.
79: website.discounts
80: View and manage discounts.
81: website.discounts.read
82: View discounts.
83: Example:
84: &scope=website.inventory,website.orders
85: stateRequired
86: Alphanumeric random value generated by client. You'll use it in
87: Step 3, Implement redirect URI, to prevent CSRF attacks.
88: website_idConditionally Required
89: Alphanumeric value for a Squarespace site ID.
90: When a logged-in user initiates an OAuth connection from Squarespace, this
91: value is appended as a query parameter on the provided initiate URL. Partners must
92: pass this parameter back to the GET /authorize endpoint.
93: If an OAuth connection is initiated by a logged-out user, Squarespace will not
94: include a website_id parameter on the initiate URL. Partners should not pass any
95: website_id parameter back to the GET /authorize
96: endpoint in these cases. Instead, the user will be prompted to select a website
97: on the confirmation page.
98: access_typeOptional
99: String; use offline for long-term API access. For more
100: information, see Token expiration and long-term access. Omit
101: parameter for short-term API access.
102: Authorize URL example with parameters
103: Note: Parameter values are in plain text and not URL-encoded for example purposes.
104: Code
105: https://login.squarespace.com/api/1/login/oauth/provider/authorize?client_id=fGBjMDBaUHli&redirect_uri=http://localhost:8090/oauth/callback&scope=website.inventory,website.orders&state=2BsmGS9AAzFppUmcoIagOLj4iKII
106: 3. Implement redirect URI
107: Both Allow or Deny on the confirmation page directs the user to the client redirect URI (i.e., the redirect_uri specified in Step 2) with query parameters appended by Squarespace. For Allow, the redirect URI should verify the state parameter and match it against state value that was appended for the /authorize endpoint. This verification prevents CSRF attacks. Squarespace doesn't provide guidelines for Deny implementation.
108: ParameterValue
109: error
110: String; access_denied if user selects Deny
111: on confirmation page. Parameter isn't appended if user selects
112: Allow.
113: state
114: Alphanumeric value; not present if user selects Deny.
115: code

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Documents X-MBX-APIKEY header with HMAC-SHA-256, RSA, and Ed25519 signing.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt: 94: ## What are RSA API Keys? 95: RSA API Keys are an alternative to the typical HMAC-SHA-256 API Keys that are used to authenticate 96: your requests on the Spot API. 97: Unlike HMAC-SHA-256 API Keys where we generate the secret signing key for you, with RSA API Keys, 98: _you_ generate a pair of public+private RSA keys, send us the public key, and sign your requests 99: with your private key. 100: 101: ## What type of RSA keys are supported? 102: We support RSA keys of any length from 2048 bits up to 4096 bits. We recommend **2048 bits keys** as 103: a good balance between security and signature speed. 104: When generating the RSA signature, use the **PKCS#1 v1.5** signature scheme. This is the default 105: when using OpenSSL. We currently do not support the PSS signature scheme. 106: 107: ## How can I use RSA API Keys? 108: Step 1: Generate the private key `test-prv-key.pem`. **Do not share this file with anyone!** 109: ``` 110: openssl genrsa -out test-prv-key.pem 2048 111: ``` 112: Step 2: Generate the public key `test-pub-key.pem` from the private key. 113: ``` 114: openssl rsa -in test-prv-key.pem -pubout -outform PEM -out test-pub-key.pem 115: ``` 116: The public key should look something like this: 117: ``` 118: -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- 119: bL4DUXwR3ijFSXzcecQtVFU1zVWcSQd0Meztl3DLX42l/8EALJx3LSz9YKS0PMQW 120: MIICIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAg8AMIICCgKCAgEAv9ij99RAJM4JLl8Rg47b 121: dJXMrv84WL1OK/gid4hCnxo083LYLXUpIqMmL+O6fmXAvsvkyMyT520Cw0ZNCrUk 122: WoCjGE4JZZGF4wOkWdF37JFWbDnE/GF5mAykKj+OMaECBlZ207KleQqgVzHjKuCb 123: hPMuBVVD3IhjBfIc7EEM438LbtayMDx4dviPWwm127jwn8qd9H3kv5JBoDfsdYMB 124: 3k39r724CljqlAfX33GpbV2LvEkL6Da3OFk+grfN98X2pCBRz5+1N95I2cRD7o+j 125: wtCr+65E+Gqjo4OI60F9Gq5GDcrnudnUw13a4zwlU6W+Cy8gJ4R0CcKTc4+VhYVX 126: 5wW2tzLVnDqvjIN8hjhgtmUv8hr19Wn+42ev+5sNtO5QAS6sJMJG5D+cpxCNhei1 127: Xm+1zXliaA1fvVYRqon2MdHcedFeAjzVtX38+Xweytowydcq2V/9pUUNZIzUqX7t 128: Zr3F+Ao3QOb/CuWbUBpUcbXfGv7AI1ozP8LRByyu6O8Z1dZNdkdjWVt83maUrIJH 129: jjc7jlZY9JbH6EyYV5TenjJaupvdlx72vA7Fcgevx87seog2JALAJqZQNT+t9/tm 130: rTUSEp3t4aINKUC1QC0CYKECAwEAAQ== 131: -----END PUBLIC KEY----- 132: ``` 133: Step 3: Register your public key on the Spot Test Network. 134: During registration, we will generate an API Key for you that you will have to put in the 135: `X-MBX-APIKEY` header of your requests, exactly the same way as you would do for HMAC-SHA-256 API 136: Keys. 137: Step 4: When you send a request to the Spot Test Network, sign the payload using your private key. 138: Here is an example Bash script to post a new order and sign the request using OpenSSL. You can adapt 139: it to your favorite programming language: 140: ```bash 141: #!/usr/bin/env bash 142: # Set up authentication: 143: API_KEY="put your own API Key here" 144: PRIVATE_KEY_PATH="test-prv-key.pem" 145: # Set up the request: 146: API_METHOD="POST" 147: API_CALL="api/v3/order" 148: API_PARAMS="symbol=BTCUSDT&side=SELL&type=LIMIT&timeInForce=GTC&quantity=1&price=0.2" 149: # Sign the request: 150: timestamp=$(date +%s000) 151: api_params_with_timestamp="$API_PARAMS×tamp=$timestamp" 152: signature=$(echo -n "$api_params_with_timestamp" \ 153: | openssl dgst -sha256 -sign "$PRIVATE_KEY_PATH" \ 154: | openssl enc -base64 -A) 155: # Send the request: 156: curl -H "X-MBX-APIKEY: $API_KEY" -X "$API_METHOD" \ 157: "https://testnet.binance.vision/$API_CALL?$api_params_with_timestamp" \ 158: --data-urlencode "signature=$signature" 159: ``` 160: 161: ## What are Ed25519 API keys? 162: Ed25519 API keys are an alternative to [RSA API keys](#what-are-rsa-api-keys), using asymmetric 163: cryptography to authenticate your requests on the Spot API. 164: Like RSA API keys, Ed25519 keys are _asymmetric_: you generate a keypair, share the public key with 165: Binance, and use your private key to sign requests. 166: 167: ## Why use Ed25519 instead of RSA API keys? 168: Ed25519 digital signature scheme provides security comparable to 3072-bit RSA keys, while having 169: much smaller signatures that are faster to compute: 170: | API key type | Signature size | Signature operation | 171: | -------------- | -------------- | ------------------- | 172: | HMAC-SHA-256 | 64 bytes | 0.00 ms | 173: | Ed25519 | 88 bytes | 0.03 ms | 174: | RSA (2048-bit) | 344 bytes | 0.55 ms | 175: | RSA (4096-bit) | 684 bytes | 3.42 ms | 176: 177: ## How can I use Ed25519 API keys? 178: Step 1: Generate the private key `test-prv-key.pem`. **Do not share this file with anyone!** 179: ``` 180: openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out test-prv-key.pem 181: ``` 182: Step 2: Compute the public key `test-pub-key.pem` from the private key. 183: ``` 184: openssl pkey -pubout -in test-prv-key.pem -out test-pub-key.pem 185: ``` 186: The public key should look something like this: 187: ``` 188: -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- 189: MCowBQYDK2VwAyEACeCSz7VJkh3Bb+NF794hLMU8fLB9Zr+/tGMdVKCC2eo= 190: -----END PUBLIC KEY----- 191: ``` 192: Step 3: Register your public key on the Spot Test Network. 193: During registration, we will generate an API key for you. Please put it in the `X-MBX-APIKEY` header 194: of your requests, exactly the same way as with other API key types. 195: Step 4: When you send a request to the Spot Test Network, sign the payload using your private key.

78: # Public Rest API for Binance
79: ## General API Information
80: - The following base endpoints are available. Please use whichever works best for your setup:
81: - **https://api.binance.com**
82: - **https://api-gcp.binance.com**
83: - **https://api1.binance.com**
84: - **https://api2.binance.com**
85: - **https://api3.binance.com**
86: - **https://api4.binance.com**
87: - The last 4 endpoints in the point above (`api1`-`api4`) should give better performance but have
88: less stability.
89: - Responses are in JSON by default. To receive responses in SBE, refer to the
90: [SBE FAQ](faqs/sbe_faq.md) page.
91: - Data is returned in **chronological order**, unless noted otherwise.
92: - Without `startTime` or `endTime`, returns the most recent items up to the limit.
93: - With `startTime`, returns oldest items from `startTime` up to the limit.
94: - With `endTime`, returns most recent items up to `endTime` and the limit.
95: - With both, behaves like `startTime` but does not exceed `endTime`.
96: - All time and timestamp related fields in the JSON responses are in **milliseconds by default.** To
97: receive the information in microseconds, please add the header `X-MBX-TIME-UNIT:MICROSECOND` or
98: `X-MBX-TIME-UNIT:microsecond`.
99: - We support HMAC, RSA, and Ed25519 keys. For more information, please see
100: [API Key types](faqs/api_key_types.md).
101: - Timestamp parameters (e.g. `startTime`, `endTime`, `timestamp`) can be passed in milliseconds or
102: microseconds.
103: - For APIs that only send public market data, please use the base endpoint
104: **https://data-api.binance.vision**. Please refer to
105: [Market Data Only](faqs/market_data_only.md) page.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Twilio SendGrid requires API keys passed via Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY> against https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
81: Twilio SendGrid supports API keys delivered via Bearer token or Basic authentication, depending on the Twilio SendGrid functionality you are using. In addition to Bearer API key authentication, Twilio SendGrid recommends two-factor authentication (2FA) to improve security.
82: API key
83: api-key page anchor
84: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
85: Authenticate to the Twilio SendGrid API by creating an API Key in the Settings section of the Twilio SendGrid console(link takes you to an external page).
86: Twilio SendGrid requires using API keys because they are a secure way to talk to the Twilio SendGrid API that is separate from your username and password. If your API key gets compromised, you can delete and create a new API key and update your environment variables with the new key. API key permissions can be set to provide access to different functions of your account, without providing access to your account as a whole.
87: To use an API key, pass an Authorization header with a value of Bearer <Your-API-Key-Here>, where you replace <Your-API-Key-Here> with the API Key that you created in the UI.
88: Example header:
89: Authorization header
90: authorization-header page anchor
91: Copy code block
92: 1
93: GET https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/resource HTTP/1.1
94: 2
95: Authorization: Bearer <Your-API-Key-Here>
96: Authenticated request with cURL
97: authenticated-request-with-curl page anchor
98: Copy code block
99: curl -X "GET" "https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/templates" -H "Authorization: Bearer <Your-API-Key-Here>" -H "Content-Type: application/json"

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
94: Twilio SendGrid API key limitations
95: Twilio supports a key longer than 69 characters. No exceptions can be made for third-party infrastructure.
96: Twilio limits accounts to 100 API keys.
97: You can't give an API key greater permissions than your own.
98: The Twilio SendGrid Console displays the API key only once at creation.
99: Treat your API key like a password and store it somewhere safe.
100: Twilio can't retrieve or restore an unknown or deleted API key.
101: To authenticate access to Twilio SendGrid services, use Application Programming Interface (API) keys.
102: They are the preferred alternative to using a username and password because you can revoke an API key at any time without having to change your username and password. We suggest that you use API keys for connecting to all of SendGrid's services.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Basic authentication uses username 'apikey' and API key as password; Basic auth is not possible for users/subusers/teammates with 2FA enabled (2FA required for all users).
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
100: Basic authentication
101: basic-authentication page anchor
102: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
103: Using basic authentication with your account password is not as secure as using an API key. If your credentials are compromised—for example, if you accidentally commit them to version control—it is more difficult to regain the security of your account when those credentials are your username and password rather than an API key. For this reason, Twilio SendGrid does not support Basic Authentication with a username and password. Twilio SendGrid supports Basic Authentication using an API key as your password value for some services.
104: When using Basic Authentication, your username will always be apikey, and your password will be your API key.
105: (information)
106: Info
107: If you are currently using Basic authentication, we recommend upgrading your authentication method to Bearer using API Keys and then enabling Two-Factor Authentication for improved security. For more information, see Upgrading your authentication method to API Keys.
108: Two-factor authentication
109: two-factor-authentication page anchor
110: Positive FeedbackNegative Feedback
111: To ensure the security of your account, Twilio SendGrid requires enabling two-factor authentication (2FA) for all users. To learn about setting up 2FA, see Two-factor authentication.
112: (information)
113: Info
114: It is not possible to use basic authentication for users, subusers, or teammates that enable 2FA.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Official MCP server supports OAuth 2.0 ADC with https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords scope or FastMCP OAuth proxy.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
47: Configure [Application Default Credentials (ADC)](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/provide-credentials-adc) for a user or service account with access to your Google Ads accounts. Credentials must include the Google Ads API scope (`https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords`). See [Manage OAuth Clients](https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/15549257) if you need to create an OAuth desktop or web client first.
48: - **Option 1 — User credentials with an OAuth client JSON file:**
49: ```shell
50: gcloud auth application-default login \
51: --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform \
52: --client-id-file=YOUR_CLIENT_JSON_FILE
53: ```
54: - **Option 2 — Service account impersonation:**
55: ```shell
56: gcloud auth application-default login \
57: --impersonate-service-account=SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL \
58: --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform
59: ```
60: When the command finishes, note the credentials path printed to the console (`Credentials saved to file: [PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON]`) for your MCP client configuration.
61: #### Mode B: Streamable HTTP with FastMCP OAuth Proxy
62: Setting `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` and `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` enables FastMCP's [OAuth proxy](https://gofastmcp.com/servers/auth/oauth-proxy) for dynamic per-user Google OAuth login and automatically switches the server transport from `stdio` to `streamable-http` (default endpoint: `http://localhost:8080/mcp`).
63: Run the server as a standalone process or container (see [Deployment](#deployment) and [Environment Variables Reference](#environment-variables-reference)), then point your MCP client at the HTTP endpoint—no server secrets are stored in client configs.

477: Test credentials
478: To minimize the risk of accidentally modifying production accounts when trying
479: to modify development accounts, we recommend maintaining a set of test
480: credentials that are separate from your production application credentials.
481: To create a set of test credentials, follow these steps:
482: Create an email account (for example, api.test@example.com) or a service
483: account that will be used only for testing purposes.
484: Add this user or service account as a valid user in the Google Ads accounts you
485: are running your tests against. Make sure you give appropriate access
486: levels to this user or service account. Don't give this
487: user or service account access to any production accounts.
488: If you are using the OAuth 2.0 user authentication flow, rather than the
489: service account flow, then generate a refresh token for
490: your test user account.
491: Use these new credentials when testing your application. The client ID and
492: client secret can be reused for testing purposes, since they have no effect
493: in determining which Google Ads accounts can be accessed. Store all credentials
494: and refresh tokens securely, and never commit them to source control.

473: Get started
474: Follow these steps to configure and run the Google Ads MCP server locally. To deploy
475: a shared remote service instead, see Deployment on Google
476: Cloud.
477: Prerequisites
478: Before you configure the server, complete the following prerequisites in your
479: local environment and the Google Cloud console:
480: Google Cloud project: Create or select a Google Cloud project with the
481: Google Ads API enabled. Enabling the API grants Test access for testing read
482: and mutate workflows against test accounts. To access
483: production accounts, check the Google Ads API overview page for
484: Explorer, Basic, or Standard access, or apply for one of these access
485: levels. Otherwise, production calls fail with an
486: AuthorizationError.CLOUD_PROJECT_NOT_APPROVED_FOR_PRODUCTION error. Google
487: sunset developer tokens (GOOGLE_ADS_DEVELOPER_TOKEN) on
488: September 9, 2026. The Google Cloud project that owns your OAuth client or
489: service account determines your API access level.
490: Credentials: Local stdio mode authenticates with Application Default
491: Credentials (ADC) from an OAuth 2.0 client secret JSON file or a
492: service account in your Cloud project. Set the GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
493: environment variable when needed to specify your default quota or ADC
494: project. Remote streamable-http deployments instead require an OAuth 2.0
495: Web application Client ID and Client secret (see Deploy to Google Cloud
496: Run).

1: # Google Ads MCP Server
2: An [MCP (Model Context Protocol)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server that enables LLMs and AI agents to query and manage [Google Ads](https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api) accounts.
3: ## Table of Contents
4: - [Overview](#overview)
5: - [Quickstart & Setup](#quickstart--setup)
6: - [1. Prerequisites](#1-prerequisites)
7: - [2. Choose an Authentication Mode](#2-choose-an-authentication-mode)
8: - [3. Configure Your MCP Client](#3-configure-your-mcp-client)
9: - [Tools & Resources](#tools--resources)
10: - [Available Tools](#available-tools)
11: - [Available Resources](#available-resources)
12: - [Configuration & Security](#configuration--security)
13: - [Propose & Confirm Safety Workflow](#propose--confirm-safety-workflow)
14: - [Configuring and Namespacing Tools](#configuring-and-namespacing-tools)
15: - [Tool Call Auditability](#tool-call-auditability)
16: - [Environment Variables Reference](#environment-variables-reference)
17: - [Deployment](#deployment)
18: - [Local Container Deployment (Docker / Podman)](#local-container-deployment-docker--podman)
19: - [Google Cloud Run Deployment](#google-cloud-run-deployment)
20: - [Try It Out](#try-it-out)
21: - [Contributing](#contributing)
22: ## Overview
23: The Google Ads MCP Server exposes [MCP Tools](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/concepts/tools) and [MCP Resources](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/concepts/resources) backed by the [Google Ads API](https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api/reference/rpc/latest/overview). It supports:
24: - **Read & reporting workflows**: GAQL queries, accessible customer discovery, resource field metadata, and API reference resources.
25: - **Guarded account mutations**: Asset creation, video uploads, and label management protected by a two-step **Propose & Confirm** workflow.
26: - **Flexible deployment**: Run locally over `stdio` with Application Default Credentials, or over **Streamable HTTP** with FastMCP's OAuth proxy and structured audit logging.
27: > **Notes:**
28: > - Connecting an LLM or agent to this server exposes your accessible Google Ads account data to that client.
29: > - API calls made by this server include an MCP telemetry header used by Google to collect usage statistics and improve the product.
30: > - Report bugs or feature requests on the [GitHub issue tracker](https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-mcp/issues).

473: Get started
474: Follow these steps to configure and run the Google Ads MCP server locally. To deploy
475: a shared remote service instead, see Deployment on Google
476: Cloud.
477: Prerequisites
478: Before you configure the server, complete the following prerequisites in your
479: local environment and the Google Cloud console:
480: Google Cloud project: Create or select a Google Cloud project with the
481: Google Ads API enabled. Enabling the API grants Test access for testing read
482: and mutate workflows against test accounts. To access
483: production accounts, check the Google Ads API overview page for
484: Explorer, Basic, or Standard access, or apply for one of these access
485: levels. Otherwise, production calls fail with an
486: AuthorizationError.CLOUD_PROJECT_NOT_APPROVED_FOR_PRODUCTION error. Google
487: sunset developer tokens (GOOGLE_ADS_DEVELOPER_TOKEN) on
488: September 9, 2026. The Google Cloud project that owns your OAuth client or
489: service account determines your API access level.
490: Credentials: Local stdio mode authenticates with Application Default
491: Credentials (ADC) from an OAuth 2.0 client secret JSON file or a
492: service account in your Cloud project. Set the GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT
493: environment variable when needed to specify your default quota or ADC
494: project. Remote streamable-http deployments instead require an OAuth 2.0
495: Web application Client ID and Client secret (see Deploy to Google Cloud
496: Run).
497: Local software (for stdio mode): Install Python 3.10 or
498: later, pipx, and the gcloud command-line
499: tool (used to generate user ADC files).
500: Configuration
501: Generate Application Default Credentials (ADC) using an OAuth
502: client from your API-enabled Google Cloud project and include the Google Ads API
503: scope:
504: gcloud auth application-default login \
505: --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform \
506: --client-id-file=PATH_TO_CLIENT_SECRET_JSON
507: Replace the following:
508: PATH_TO_CLIENT_SECRET_JSON: the path to your OAuth 2.0 client secret
509: JSON file.
510: This command prints Credentials saved to file: [PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON]
511: (such as ~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json on Linux
512: and macOS). To authenticate with a service account instead, skip this step
513: and point GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS to your service account key JSON
514: file, or pass --impersonate-service-account to gcloud auth
515: application-default login.
516: Add the server to your host's MCP configuration file (such as
517: ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json, ~/.gemini/settings.json, or
518: ~/.claude/settings.json):
519: {
520: "mcpServers": {
521: "google-ads-mcp": {
522: "command": "pipx",
523: "args": [
524: "run",
525: "--spec",
526: "google-ads-mcp==0.0.6",
527: "google-ads-mcp"
528: ],
529: "env": {
530: "GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT": "PROJECT_ID",
531: "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON"
532: }
533: }
