1: # Google Ads MCP Server
2: An [MCP (Model Context Protocol)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server that enables LLMs and AI agents to query and manage [Google Ads](https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api) accounts.
3: ## Table of Contents
4: - [Overview](#overview)
5: - [Quickstart & Setup](#quickstart--setup)
6: - [1. Prerequisites](#1-prerequisites)
7: - [2. Choose an Authentication Mode](#2-choose-an-authentication-mode)
8: - [3. Configure Your MCP Client](#3-configure-your-mcp-client)
9: - [Tools & Resources](#tools--resources)
10: - [Available Tools](#available-tools)
11: - [Available Resources](#available-resources)
12: - [Configuration & Security](#configuration--security)
13: - [Propose & Confirm Safety Workflow](#propose--confirm-safety-workflow)
14: - [Configuring and Namespacing Tools](#configuring-and-namespacing-tools)
15: - [Tool Call Auditability](#tool-call-auditability)
16: - [Environment Variables Reference](#environment-variables-reference)
17: - [Deployment](#deployment)
18: - [Local Container Deployment (Docker / Podman)](#local-container-deployment-docker--podman)
19: - [Google Cloud Run Deployment](#google-cloud-run-deployment)
20: - [Try It Out](#try-it-out)
21: - [Contributing](#contributing)
22: ## Overview
23: The Google Ads MCP Server exposes [MCP Tools](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/concepts/tools) and [MCP Resources](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/concepts/resources) backed by the [Google Ads API](https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api/reference/rpc/latest/overview). It supports:
24: - **Read & reporting workflows**: GAQL queries, accessible customer discovery, resource field metadata, and API reference resources.
25: - **Guarded account mutations**: Asset creation, video uploads, and label management protected by a two-step **Propose & Confirm** workflow.
26: - **Flexible deployment**: Run locally over `stdio` with Application Default Credentials, or over **Streamable HTTP** with FastMCP's OAuth proxy and structured audit logging.
27: > **Notes:**
28: > - Connecting an LLM or agent to this server exposes your accessible Google Ads account data to that client.
29: > - API calls made by this server include an MCP telemetry header used by Google to collect usage statistics and improve the product.
30: > - Report bugs or feature requests on the [GitHub issue tracker](https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-mcp/issues).
31: ---
32: ## Quickstart & Setup
33: ### 1. Prerequisites
34: 1. **Python & `pipx`** (for local non-container setups): Python 3.11+ and [`pipx`](https://pipx.pypa.io/stable/#install-pipx).
35: To run a specific released version from PyPI:
36: ```shell
37: pipx run --spec "google-ads-mcp==X.Y.Z" google-ads-mcp
38: ```
39: 2. **Google Cloud Project**: Enable the [Google Ads API](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/library/googleads.googleapis.com) in your Google Cloud project ([how to enable APIs](https://support.google.com/googleapi/answer/6158841)).
40: ### 2. Choose an Authentication Mode
41: The server supports two authentication and transport modes out of the box:
42: | Mode | Transport | Best For |
43: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
44: | **Mode A: Application Default Credentials (ADC)** | `stdio` | Single-user local CLI/IDE agents where the MCP client spawns the server directly. |
45: | **Mode B: FastMCP OAuth Proxy** | `streamable-http` | Shared/remote deployments or local containers where server credentials stay isolated from MCP client configs. |
46: #### Mode A: Local `stdio` with Application Default Credentials (ADC)
47: Configure [Application Default Credentials (ADC)](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/provide-credentials-adc) for a user or service account with access to your Google Ads accounts. Credentials must include the Google Ads API scope (`https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords`). See [Manage OAuth Clients](https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/15549257) if you need to create an OAuth desktop or web client first.
48: - **Option 1 — User credentials with an OAuth client JSON file:**
49: ```shell
50: gcloud auth application-default login \
51: --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform \
52: --client-id-file=YOUR_CLIENT_JSON_FILE
53: ```
54: - **Option 2 — Service account impersonation:**
55: ```shell
56: gcloud auth application-default login \
57: --impersonate-service-account=SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL \
58: --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform
59: ```
60: When the command finishes, note the credentials path printed to the console (`Credentials saved to file: [PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON]`) for your MCP client configuration.
61: #### Mode B: Streamable HTTP with FastMCP OAuth Proxy
62: Setting `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` and `GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` enables FastMCP's [OAuth proxy](https://gofastmcp.com/servers/auth/oauth-proxy) for dynamic per-user Google OAuth login and automatically switches the server transport from `stdio` to `streamable-http` (default endpoint: `http://localhost:8080/mcp`).
63: Run the server as a standalone process or container (see [Deployment](#deployment) and [Environment Variables Reference](#environment-variables-reference)), then point your MCP client at the HTTP endpoint—no server secrets are stored in client configs.
64: ### 3. Configure Your MCP Client
65: #### Connecting via Streamable HTTP (Mode B — Recommended for Shared or Container Setups)
66: - **Antigravity / Antigravity IDE** ([MCP setup docs](https://antigravity.google/docs/mcp)):
67: Use `serverUrl` (required for Streamable HTTP in current Antigravity releases; do not use `httpUrl`):
68: ```json
69: {
70: "mcpServers": {
71: "google-ads-mcp": {
72: "serverUrl": "http://localhost:8080/mcp"
73: }
74: }
75: }
76: ```
77: - **Codex CLI** ([Codex MCP docs](https://developers.openai.com/codex/mcp/)):
78: ```shell
79: codex mcp add google_ads --url http://localhost:8080/mcp
80: codex mcp login google_ads
81: ```
82: #### Spawning Locally via `stdio` + ADC (Mode A)
83: Add the following `mcpServers` block to your client configuration, replacing `PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON` and `YOUR_PROJECT_ID` ([how to find your project ID](https://support.google.com/googleapi/answer/7014113)):
84: ```json
85: {
86: "mcpServers": {
87: "google-ads-mcp": {
88: "command": "pipx",
89: "args": [
90: "run",
91: "--spec",
92: "git+https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-mcp.git",
93: "google-ads-mcp"
94: ],
95: "env": {
96: "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON",
97: "GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT": "YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
98: }
99: }
100: }
101: }
102: ```
103: > **Tip:** To pin a published PyPI release instead of tracking `main`, change `"git+https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-mcp.git"` to `"google-ads-mcp==X.Y.Z"`. Note that `stdio` mode stores the ADC file path in the client's config; prefer [Local Container Deployment](#local-container-deployment-docker--podman) if client configs are shared or synced across tools.
104: #### Manager Accounts (`login_customer_id`)
105: If you access client accounts through a Google Ads Manager Account (MCC), you can either:
106: 1. Pass `login_customer_id` per tool call (takes precedence when provided), or
107: 2. Set `GOOGLE_ADS_LOGIN_CUSTOMER_ID` in the server's `env` configuration as a default:
108: ```json
109: "env": {
110: "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS": "PATH_TO_CREDENTIALS_JSON",
111: "GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT": "YOUR_PROJECT_ID",
112: "GOOGLE_ADS_LOGIN_CUSTOMER_ID": "YOUR_MANAGER_CUSTOMER_ID"
113: }
114: ```
115: See [Google Ads API Call Structure (`login-customer-id`)](https://developers.google.com/google-ads/api/docs/concepts/call-structure#cid) for details.
116: #### Other MCP Clients (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code)
117: The `mcpServers` JSON format works across standard MCP clients—place it in the client's configuration file (for example, `~/.claude/settings.json` for Claude Code, `.cursor/mcp.json` for Cursor, or `.vscode/mcp.json` for VS Code).
118: ---
119: ## Tools & Resources
120: ### Available Tools
121: By default, tools are mounted with their category namespace prefix (`<namespace>_<tool>`). Namespaces and individual tools can be customized via `tools_config.yaml` (see [Configuring and Namespacing Tools](#configuring-and-namespacing-tools)).
122: | Default Tool Name | Namespace | Type | Description |
123: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
124: | `search_search` | `search` | Read | Queries Google Ads account data using GAQL (Google Ads Query Language). |
125: | `metadata_get_resource_metadata` | `metadata` | Read | Retrieves selectable, filterable, and sortable field metadata for a Google Ads API resource (e.g., `campaign`). |
126: | `customers_list_accessible_customers` | `customers` | Read | Lists customer IDs directly accessible to the authenticated user. |
127: | `assets_create_asset` | `assets` | Mutate | Creates Google Ads assets (`TEXT`, `IMAGE`, `YOUTUBE_VIDEO`, `SITELINK`, `CALLOUT`, `STRUCTURED_SNIPPET`, plus additional types via `extra_params`). Note: `image_asset_path` is local `stdio` only; use base64 `image_asset_data` over HTTP. |
128: | `assets_upload_video_asset` | `assets` | Mutate | Uploads a local video file to YouTube via a background task so it can be referenced by video assets (local `stdio` mode only). |
129: | `labels_manage_labels` | `labels` | Mutate | Creates, updates, and removes account labels. |
130: | `labels_manage_label_associations` | `labels` | Mutate | Creates and removes label associations on `CAMPAIGN`, `CUSTOMER`, `AD_GROUP`, and `AD_GROUP_CRITERION` resources. |
131: ### Available Resources
132: | Resource URI | Description |
133: | :--- | :--- |
134: | `resource://discovery-document` | Google Ads API REST discovery document describing the API surface, resources, methods, and schemas. (Prefer `metadata_get_resource_metadata` when looking up specific queryable GAQL fields.) |
135: | `resource://metrics` | Reference documentation for reporting metrics in the Google Ads API. |
136: | `resource://segments` | Reference documentation for reporting segments in the Google Ads API. |
137: | `resource://release-notes` | Release notes for the latest version of the Google Ads API. |
138: ---
139: ## Configuration & Security
140: ### Propose & Confirm Safety Workflow
141: All mutate tools (`assets_create_asset`, `assets_upload_video_asset`, `labels_manage_labels`, and `labels_manage_label_associations`) enforce a mandatory two-step safety workflow:
142: 1. **Propose (`validate_only=True`, default)**: Validates the operation (including a Google Ads API `validate_only` dry run where supported) without committing changes. Returns human-readable `change_items` and a cryptographic `checksum` bound to the `customer_id` and parameters.
143: 2. **Confirm (`validate_only=False`)**: After explicit user approval, pass the exact same parameters and `customer_id` along with the `checksum` from step 1. Missing or mismatched checksums are rejected before mutating the account.
144: ### Configuring and Namespacing Tools
145: Use `tools_config.yaml` to selectively enable or disable tool categories/tools and customize namespace prefixes. A default configuration with all categories enabled is bundled with the package.

39: MCP rate limits and public API rate limits are two separate limits. The public API limits requests per minute, per token. Without the Everything AI add-on, ClickUp MCP limits calls per rolling 24-hour period instead.
40: With the Everything AI add-on
41: If your Workspace has purchased the Everything AI add-on, your MCP rate limits are the same as the rate limits for our Public API which vary by plan.
42: On our new plans that include ClickUp AI, AI is included with your plan instead of as separate add-ons.
43: With the add-on, the rolling 24-hour limit no longer applies. Your MCP requests count toward the same per-minute, per-token limit as the public API:
44: Free Forever, Unlimited, and Business Plans: 100 requests per minute, per token.
45: Business Plus Plan: 1,000 requests per minute, per token.
46: Enterprise Plan: 10,000 requests per minute, per token.
47: On our new plans that include ClickUp AI, daily MCP limits differ by plan.
48: Without the Everything AI add-on
49: If your Workspace has not purchased the Everything AI add-on, your MCP usage is subject to the following daily rate limits by plan:
50: Free Forever Plan: 100 calls per 24 hours.
51: Unlimited Plan: 300 calls per 24 hours.
52: Business Plan: 1,000 calls per 24 hours.
53: Business Plus Plan: 2,500 calls per 24 hours.
54: Enterprise Plan: 5,000 calls per 24 hours.
55: Each person has their own daily limit. All the MCP clients you connect, such as Claude and Cursor, share that limit.
56: Every MCP request counts toward the limit, including everyday actions like reading, creating, and updating tasks. It isn't limited to AI-generated actions.
57: Rolling 24 hour rate limits
58: The rolling 24 hour rate limit begins with your first request.

151: GraphQL overview
152: The monday.com API is built with GraphQL, a flexible query language that allows you to return as much or as little data as you need. It's important to know that GraphQL is an application layer that parses the query you send it and returns (or changes) data accordingly.
153: Unlike REST APIs, where multiple endpoints return different data, GraphQL always exposes one endpoint and allows you to determine the structure of the returned data. Our API uses the following endpoint: https://api.monday.com/v2.
154: This document will walk through the GraphQL operations and object types to help you understand the essential components of a request. We will also discuss the GraphQL visual interface that enables you to test your queries and mutations, and finally, we cover where you can access the monday.com schema. Let's get started!
155: 👍
156: Pro tip
157: Check out this introduction to GraphQL to understand what all you can do with GraphQL!
158: Operations
159: There are two possible operations in GraphQL: queries and mutations.
160: Query
161: Queries perform the READ operation and do not change or alter any data. The result of each query will be formatted in the same way as the query itself. The following example retrieves the ID, title, and type of each column on board 1234567890.

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
151: Authentication
152: Learn about monday platform API token permissions, how to access tokens, and how to authenticate requests
153: The monday.com platform API utilizes personal V2 API tokens to authenticate requests and identify the user making the call. These tokens are unique to each user and have no explicit length.
154: Personal tokens allow you to interact with the API using your own user account. Their permissions mirror what you can do in the monday.com UI, ensuring that API access is consistent with your platform-level permissions.
155: If you don't have a monday.com account yet, create a free developer account to get an API token and start testing.
156: Token permissions
157: Personal tokens mirror all permission levels set in the monday.com UI, including board, column, item, or account access.
158: For example: If you don't have permission to access a certain workspace via the UI, you won't have permission using your personal API token either.
159: App tokens have an additional set of permission scopes that specify which queries and mutations it can access, while personal tokens have all permission scopes.
160: Accessing your token
161: You can access your API token in two ways, depending on your user type.
162: In the Developer Center (all users)
163: All users with API access can follow these steps to access their API token:
164: In your monday.com account, click on your profile picture in the top right corner.
165: Select Developers. This will open the Developer Center in another tab.
166: Click API token > Show.
167: Copy your personal token.
168: In the Administration tab (account admins only)
169: Account admins can use the Developer Center steps above or access their token via the Administration tab:
170: In your monday.com account, click on your profile picture in the top right corner.
171: Select Administration > Connections > Personal API token.
172: Copy your personal token.
173: Making requests with your token
174: Once you have your token, you can make requests with the API by passing the token in the Authorization header.

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
175: OAuth and Permissions
176: Authenticating monday apps with OAuth2 and defining permission scopes.
177: OAuth 2.0 is a protocol that lets your app request authorization to read or modify data in a user's monday account. At the end of the OAuth process, your app gets an access token that belongs to the user and grants access to specified permission scopes.
178: You can set up OAuth for your app in just two steps: configuring your app and going through the standard OAuth flow.
179: 🚧
180: A new OAuth 2.1 flow is available
181: monday.com now supports an improved OAuth 2.1 flow with expiring access tokens, refresh tokens, and token revocation. This page describes the current (legacy) flow. If you are building a new integration or want to upgrade your existing app, see Migrating to the new OAuth 2.1 flow.
182: Configure your scopes and redirect URLs
183: To start, you must first configure your app's scopes and redirect URLs. If you don't have an app, follow these steps to create an app in the monday UI and locate your client_id and client_secret.
184: Once your app has been created, set the scopes and redirect URLs in the OAuth tab in the Developer Center.
185: Permission scopes
186: OAuth scopes define what your app can and cannot do. Each endpoint in the monday API requires a certain permission scope, which can be found in our API reference.
187: When you ask a monday user to grant access to your app, you have to specify which of the following supported scopes you're requesting access to:
188: ScopeDescription
189: account:readRead general information about the account
190: assets:readRead data from assets the user has access to
191: boards:readRead a user's board data
192: boards:writeModify a user's board data
193: departments:readRead the account's department data
194: departments:writeModify the account's departments
195: docs:readRead a user's docs
196: docs:writeModify a user's docs
197: me:readRead a user's profile information
198: notifications:writeSend notifications on behalf of the user

151: GraphQL overview
152: The monday.com API is built with GraphQL, a flexible query language that allows you to return as much or as little data as you need. It's important to know that GraphQL is an application layer that parses the query you send it and returns (or changes) data accordingly.
153: Unlike REST APIs, where multiple endpoints return different data, GraphQL always exposes one endpoint and allows you to determine the structure of the returned data. Our API uses the following endpoint: https://api.monday.com/v2.
154: This document will walk through the GraphQL operations and object types to help you understand the essential components of a request. We will also discuss the GraphQL visual interface that enables you to test your queries and mutations, and finally, we cover where you can access the monday.com schema. Let's get started!

156: Pro tip

158: Operations
159: There are two possible operations in GraphQL: queries and mutations.
160: Query
161: Queries perform the READ operation and do not change or alter any data. The result of each query will be formatted in the same way as the query itself. The following example retrieves the ID, title, and type of each column on board 1234567890.

original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
138: Gorgias MCP Server
139: An MCP server for interacting with the Gorgias helpdesk API. This server provides tools and resources for managing tickets, customers, and other Gorgias functionality.
140: ## Setup
141: 1. Clone this repository
142: 2. Install dependencies:
143: ```
144: npm install
145: ```
146: 3. Create a `.env` file based on `.env.example` with your Gorgias credentials:
147: ```
148: GORGIAS_DOMAIN=your-domain.gorgias.com
149: GORGIAS_USERNAME=your-username
150: GORGIAS_API_KEY=your-api-key
151: ```
152: Or for OAuth apps:
153: ```
154: GORGIAS_DOMAIN=your-domain.gorgias.com
155: GORGIAS_ACCESS_TOKEN=your-oauth-access-token
156: ```
157: ## Running the Server
158: Start the server:
159: ```
160: npm run dev
161: ```
162: ## Testing with MCP Inspector
163: Test the server with the MCP Inspector:
164: ```
165: npm run inspect
166: ```
167: This will open a web interface where you can test all the available tools and resources.
168: ## Available Tools
169: ### Tickets
170: - `list_tickets`: List tickets from Gorgias helpdesk
171: - `get_ticket`: Get a specific ticket by ID
172: - `create_ticket`: Create a new ticket in Gorgias
173: - `add_message_to_ticket`: Add a message to an existing ticket
174: ### Customers
175: - `list_customers`: List customers from Gorgias
176: - `get_customer`: Get a specific customer by ID
177: ## Available Resources
178: - `gorgias://tickets`: List all tickets
179: - `gorgias://ticket/{id}`: Get a specific ticket by ID

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: Gorgias OAuth2 uses Authorization Code flow on tenant subdomains (https://{subdomain}.gorgias.com/oauth/authorize & /oauth/token) with 24-hour Bearer access tokens, non-expiring refresh tokens, and granular scopes (e.g., customers:read, tickets:read).

6: # OAuth2 authentication for creating apps with Gorgias 7: ## Introduction 8: In order to be able to have an approved public app with Gorgias, it is required that the app is using OAuth2 for authentication. 9: You can obtain the OAuth2 token by following these steps and requirements: 10:
    11:
  1. Creating an app on the partners’ account
    2. 12:
  2. Obtaining the client_id and client_secret
    3. 13:
  3. Redirect authorization
    4. 14:
  4. Post request to obtain the access token (has a 24 hours expiration time)
    5. 15:
  5. Refresh token used to obtain the next token (does not have expiration time)
    6. 16:
17: ## Partners account and retrieving client\_id and client\_secret 18: Once the application is created you will be able to retrieve the client\_id and client\_secret parameters. \*note that the client\_id and client\_secret are application-bound parameters, and if you are to create more than one application, you would have different parameter values per application. 19: 20: partners page screenshot for the client\_id and client\_secret 21: 22: ## Authorization redirection 23: Once the application is approved it will appear on the applications page in the helpdesk, and on that page, the connect app button will be available. The Gorgias users will click on the button to initiate the app installation and they will be redirected to the app URL which was specified on the app submission form in the partners’ account. After you have received that request, the app should send an authorization redirect to the following URL: https\://`{subdomain}`.gorgias.com/oauth/authorize 24: The app authorization is received through redirects. 25: Each Gorgias account has its own endpoint, which is defined by the subdomain. On these endpoints are sent all API requests, including the authorization requests. 26: The parameters which are required to be sent in this redirect are: 27:
    28:
  • response_type=code
    • 29:
  • client_id=`{your_app_client_id}`
    • 30:
  • redirect_uri=(app’s backend endpoint where to redirect once the app is authorized in order to obtain the tokes)
    • 31:
  • scope={scopes}
    • 32:
33: Additional parameters: 34:
    35:
  • state=(random string, protecting against CSRF attacks)
    • 36:
  • nonce=(random string, binds it with the token, so we identify the original request that issued it)
    • 37:
38: You can send multiple scopes in the requests, depending on the requirements of your app. 39: > 📘 Example for the redirect URL: 40: > 41: > https\://`{subdomain}`.gorgias.com/oauth/authorize?response\_type=code\&client\_id=6218fa8cfexxxxxxc5929712\&state=randomString1234Test\&scope=customers%3Aread%20tickets%3Aread%20integrations%3Aread\&redirect\_uri=`{apps_redirect_uri}` 42: 43: Authorization page screenshot 44: 45: ## Post request to obtain the access token 46: When the user accepts the authorization for the app, they will be redirected to the redirect\_uri that was set in the previous redirect. In this redirect, the code parameter will be sent as well as the state parameter you provided. The code parameter would be required for the POST request in order to obtain the access token. 47: ```http 48: curl -u : POST https://`{subdomain}`.gorgias.com/oauth/token 49: Content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded 50: grant_type:authorization_code 51: redirect_uri:(the same redirect URL you used during the authorization step) 52: code=`{received_in_redirect}` 53: ``` 54: After this request, you will receive a JSON response containing the access\_token as well as the refresh token. Bear in mind that this access token you receive has a 24 hours expiration time. 55:

17: LiveAgent exposes a built-in MCP server (Model Context Protocol) that lets you connect external AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Claude Desktop, Cursor, claude.ai, FlowHunt, or any other MCP-compatible client, directly with your LiveAgent account. Once connected, your own AI tools/agents can read ticket data and perform actions on your behalf, using your agent identity and permissions.
18: There are two ways to authenticate your MCP client - OAuth 2.1 (recommended), where the AI tool discovers the authorization server automatically and redirects you to a consent screen, or Bearer token, where you generate an MCP access token in your profile and paste it into the AI tool's configuration manually.

28: Finding MCP Integration in your profile
29: Click your avatar in the top-right corner of the LiveAgent panel and select Edit profile.
30: In the left-hand menu, navigate to the MCP Integration section.
31: This screen shows your connection details and access tokens. Use these values to configure any MCP-compatible client:
32: SettingValue
33: MCP server URLhttps://<your-liveagent-domain>/api/mcp
34: Transport protocolStreamable HTTP
35: AuthenticationOAuth 2.1 (Authorization Code + PKCE) or Bearer token
36: Connecting with OAuth
37: OAuth authentication lets AI tools connect to your LiveAgent MCP server without you having to generate, copy, and paste a token. The tool handles the entire authentication flow automatically using standard OAuth 2.1 with PKCE.
38: How it works
39: In your AI tool (for example Claude app), add a new MCP server/connector/plugin using your LiveAgent MCP server URL.
40: The AI tool calls that URL, receives a discovery hint, and fetches LiveAgent's OAuth server metadata automatically.
41: You are redirected to the LiveAgent login page (if not already logged in) and then to a consent screen asking you to approve the connection.
42: After you approve, the tool receives an access token and is ready to use.
43: Note: Your consent decision is remembered. If you remove and reconnect the same tool later, the consent screen is skipped and completes silently.
44: Managing authorized apps
45: The MCP Integration screen in your profile lists all OAuth clients you have approved under Authorized apps. You can revoke any authorized app. The tool will lose access immediately and will need to go through the OAuth flow again to reconnect.
46: Tip: Administrators or users with a custom role with the permission to manage agents can view and revoke authorized apps for other agents in the account.
47: Connecting with a bearer token
48: If your AI tool does not support OAuth authentication, you can use a bearer token to connect it. Bearer tokens are MCP access tokens you generate in your profile and paste directly into your MCP client. Bearer tokens are also used by scripts that require manual configuration.
49: Generating an access token
50: On the MCP Integration screen in your profile and click Generate token.
51: Copy the access token.
52: Paste the access token into your MCP client as the Bearer token value.
53: Important: Store the access token securely as soon as you generate it. If you lose it, you will need to revoke the existing token and generate a new one.
54: You can generate up to 10 active access tokens per account. Having multiple tokens is useful if you connect the same account to more than one tool or device.
55: Managing access tokens
56: The access token list on the MCP Integration screen shows each token's masked identifier and expiration date. Each can be revoked independently without affecting the others. Upon revoking a token, the corresponding MCP client/AI tool will lose access immediately.
57: Note: Access tokens expire automatically after two years from the date they were generated, regardless of how frequently they are used. Plan to rotate access tokens before they expire to avoid interruption.

17: LiveAgent exposes a built-in MCP server (Model Context Protocol) that lets you connect external AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Claude Desktop, Cursor, claude.ai, FlowHunt, or any other MCP-compatible client, directly with your LiveAgent account. Once connected, your own AI tools/agents can read ticket data and perform actions on your behalf, using your agent identity and permissions.
18: There are two ways to authenticate your MCP client - OAuth 2.1 (recommended), where the AI tool discovers the authorization server automatically and redirects you to a consent screen, or Bearer token, where you generate an MCP access token in your profile and paste it into the AI tool's configuration manually.

29: Click your avatar in the top-right corner of the LiveAgent panel and select Edit profile.
30: In the left-hand menu, navigate to the MCP Integration section.
31: This screen shows your connection details and access tokens. Use these values to configure any MCP-compatible client:
32: SettingValue
33: MCP server URLhttps://<your-liveagent-domain>/api/mcp
34: Transport protocolStreamable HTTP
35: AuthenticationOAuth 2.1 (Authorization Code + PKCE) or Bearer token
36: Connecting with OAuth
37: OAuth authentication lets AI tools connect to your LiveAgent MCP server without you having to generate, copy, and paste a token. The tool handles the entire authentication flow automatically using standard OAuth 2.1 with PKCE.
38: How it works
39: In your AI tool (for example Claude app), add a new MCP server/connector/plugin using your LiveAgent MCP server URL.
40: The AI tool calls that URL, receives a discovery hint, and fetches LiveAgent's OAuth server metadata automatically.
41: You are redirected to the LiveAgent login page (if not already logged in) and then to a consent screen asking you to approve the connection.
42: After you approve, the tool receives an access token and is ready to use.
43: Note: Your consent decision is remembered. If you remove and reconnect the same tool later, the consent screen is skipped and completes silently.
44: Managing authorized apps
45: The MCP Integration screen in your profile lists all OAuth clients you have approved under Authorized apps. You can revoke any authorized app. The tool will lose access immediately and will need to go through the OAuth flow again to reconnect.
46: Tip: Administrators or users with a custom role with the permission to manage agents can view and revoke authorized apps for other agents in the account.
47: Connecting with a bearer token
48: If your AI tool does not support OAuth authentication, you can use a bearer token to connect it. Bearer tokens are MCP access tokens you generate in your profile and paste directly into your MCP client. Bearer tokens are also used by scripts that require manual configuration.
49: Generating an access token
50: On the MCP Integration screen in your profile and click Generate token.
51: Copy the access token.
52: Paste the access token into your MCP client as the Bearer token value.
53: Important: Store the access token securely as soon as you generate it. If you lose it, you will need to revoke the existing token and generate a new one.
54: You can generate up to 10 active access tokens per account. Having multiple tokens is useful if you connect the same account to more than one tool or device.
55: Managing access tokens
56: The access token list on the MCP Integration screen shows each token's masked identifier and expiration date. Each can be revoked independently without affecting the others. Upon revoking a token, the corresponding MCP client/AI tool will lose access immediately.
57: Note: Access tokens expire automatically after two years from the date they were generated, regardless of how frequently they are used. Plan to rotate access tokens before they expire to avoid interruption.

original_evidence.observation: paraphrase: LiveAgent MCP integration gives external AI tools access to the full set of LiveAgent MCP tools under the agent's identity and role permissions, counting toward a shared AI budget.
original_evidence.snapshot_excerpt:
58: Permissions and available tools
59: Regardless of whether you connect via OAuth or bearer token, your AI tool has access to the full set of LiveAgent MCP tools. See the MCP tools reference for the complete list of tools and their detailed description.
60: All actions are performed under your agent identity and are subject to your role's permissions, exactly as if you had performed them in the LiveAgent panel. They appear in the ticket's activity history under your name.
61: Note: Unlike LiveAgent AI agents, which restrict the tool set per AI agent configuration, personal MCP integration gives access to all tools. Your role's permissions still apply - actions your role is not permitted to perform will be rejected.
62: Note: Actions performed through an MCP connection count toward a common AI budget shared by all users, which limits the number of tool calls. See the AI budgets article for details on how AI budgets work.
